translated_text:
It has been said concerning His words:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies it,”
“and failed indeed is the one who corrupts it,”

that the pronoun refers to Allah, meaning: “Successful indeed is the one whose soul Allah purifies, and failed indeed is the one whose soul Allah corrupts.” This contradicts the apparent meaning and departs considerably from the Quran’s characteristic manner of expression. The more fitting wording would then have been: “Successful indeed is she whom Allah purifies, and failed indeed is she whom He corrupts.” This is weak. Moreover, His words, “And inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness,” explain divine predestination. There is therefore no need to mention it again immediately afterwards in such a short surah.

For this reason, only this verse, rather than the latter passage, is reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as evidence establishing predestination. Thus, in Sahīh Muslim, Abū al-Aswad al-Du’alī reported:

‘Imrān ibn Husayn said to me, “Tell me about what people do today and strive to accomplish: is it something already decreed for them and settled by a prior decree, or is it something they face anew in response to what their Prophet has brought them and the proof established against them?”

I replied, “Rather, it is something already decreed for them and settled for them.”

He said, “Would that not then be injustice?”

I was greatly alarmed by this and said, “Everything is Allah’s creation and belongs to Him. He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.”

He said to me, “May Allah have mercy on you! I asked you this only to safeguard your understanding. Two men from Muzaynah came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, tell us about what people do today and strive to accomplish: is it something already decreed for them and settled concerning them as part of a decree

already determined, or is it something they face anew in response to what their Prophet has brought them and the proof established against them?’

He replied, ‘No. Rather, it is something already decreed for them and settled for them. This is confirmed in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:

“By the soul and the One Who fashioned it,
and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness.”’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus explained that Allah’s words, “And inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness,” confirm what he had stated concerning the decree. The hadith concerns the prior decree contained in Allah’s knowledge, His writing, and His speech; only the extreme Qadariyyah deny this. The Quranic passage, however, concerns Allah’s creation of people’s actions, which goes further, for the Magian-like Qadariyyah deny this. Thus, the Quranic passage establishes what the hadith states and more. This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, presented it as confirmation. This can be explained in several ways.

First: once a person knows that Allah is the One Who inspires wickedness and righteousness, and that this involves neither injustice, as the Iblīs-like Qadariyyah claim, nor any contradiction of divine commands and prohibitions, promises and threats, as the polytheistic Qadariyyah claim, he has no grounds relating to predestination for disputing that Allah recorded and decreed this before it came into existence. This is why most of the Qadariyyah who deny the creation of human actions have acknowledged the prior decree. No member of the Qadariyyah has affirmed that Allah creates people’s actions while denying, on grounds of predestination, that Allah is their Creator.

translated_text:
Second:

Once it is established that Allah creates a person’s actions and inspires wickedness and righteousness, these actions are part of His creation. The doubt that arose among the Qadariyyah, concerning which the two men from Muzaynah questioned the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, relates specifically to human actions for which people are rewarded or punished. They did not deny, on grounds of predestination, that Allah decreed what He Himself creates before its existence. Those among them who denied this did so only when the matter of human actions became unclear to them.

These people say that Allah decrees things before they exist, except for human actions, felicity and wretchedness. They maintain that He should not know these until they occur, because they consider it reprehensible for a ruler to issue a command when he knows that the person charged with it will not obey him and that it will instead cause that person harm. Various authors writing on the principles of jurisprudence and other subjects have reported the Muʿtazilah’s disagreement on this point. They say:

“Allah may command a person to do something He knows that person will not do, contrary to the position of the Muʿtazilah.”

This is because some among the Muʿtazilah dispute this, although most do not; only one group among them disagrees.

Since the Quran establishes that He inspires the soul with its wickedness and its righteousness, these are part of what He brings into being. Thus, the Qadariyyah’s objection to His having decreed this before its existence no longer stands, just as they have no objection to His predetermining the entities and attributes He creates. {فَأَلْهَمَهَا فُجُورَهَا وَتَقْوَاهَا}
 كَمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَدَرِ فَيَدُلُّ عَلَى الشَّرْعِ. فَإِنَّهُ لَوْ قَالَ 
" فَأَلْهَمَهَا أَفْعَالَهَا "
 كَمَا يَقُولُ النَّاسُ
translated_text:
have a different basis for their position, unrelated to the divine attributes.

Third:

He has inspired wickedness and righteousness, and He is the Creator of a person’s actions. He must therefore know what He creates before creating it, as He says:

“Does He who created not know?”

For an agent acting by choice wills what he does, and willing necessarily entails conceiving what is willed. This constitutes knowledge of the intended action. Since His creation of a thing necessarily entails His knowledge of it, this is the foundation of prior divine predestination. As for what Allah, glorified be He, has taught through His speech and His Books, there is no dispute about it. This is clear in all things, in this matter and others.

For when He, glorified be He, inspires wickedness and righteousness, the one who inspires must distinguish between wickedness and righteousness and know that this act He intends to bring about is wickedness, while that act He intends to bring about is righteousness. Otherwise, He could not inspire wickedness and righteousness. This makes clear how apt was the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that the verse confirms what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had reported concerning prior divine predestination.

His words, glorified be He,

“And inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness,”

indicate the divine law just as they indicate predestination. For had He said, “And inspired it with its actions,” as people say

translated_text:
“the Creator of people’s actions,” there would have been no distinction in this between good and evil, what is loved and what is hated, or what is commanded and what is forbidden. Rather, it would have provided an argument for the polytheists among the antinomians and the Jabriyyah, who reject commands and prohibitions, and moral goodness and badness; for He created people’s actions. But when He said:

“And inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness,”

these words distinguished between the good that is commanded and the evil that is forbidden, establishing that actions fall into good and evil, although He, exalted is He, is the Creator of both categories. This is the Quran’s approach in numerous passages: it mentions the believer and the disbeliever, their good and evil deeds, and His promise and warning; and it mentions that He is the Creator of both categories, as in His words:

“He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills,”

and similar passages.

It is concerning this principle that the Jabriyyah and the Qadariyyah have gone astray.

The Magian Qadariyyah said: Actions fall into good and evil because of qualities inherent in them, and the servant himself brings them into being, independently of Allah’s power and without His creating them.

The Jabriyyah, by contrast, said: Rather, the servant is compelled to act. Compulsion is a reality that necessitates the occurrence of his actions whenever the causes Allah creates are present, and makes their occurrence impossible whenever any of those causes is absent. If he is compelled, an action cannot be good or evil by virtue of any quality inherent in it.

translated_text:
This is the approach of Abū Abd Allāh al-Rāzī and others among the Jabriyyah who deny that actions are intrinsically divided into good and evil. The former is the approach of Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī and others among the Qadariyyah who maintain that the servant alone brings his action into being, that knowledge of this is either self-evident or inferential, and that actions are intrinsically divided into good and evil, knowledge of which is self-evident.

Abū al-Husayn is the leading authority among the later Muʿtazilah, possessing greater intellect and merit than most of his peers. Yet his knowledge of the Prophetic traditions, the meanings of the Quran, and the way of the early generations is limited. On this issue, he and Abū Abd Allāh al-Rāzī stand at opposite extremes, although each possesses some truth that the other lacks.

Abū al-Husayn claims that it is self-evident that the servant brings his action into being. Al-Rāzī likewise claims that it is self-evident that a newly originated, contingent action depends upon a determining factor whose presence necessitates the action’s occurrence and whose absence makes its occurrence impossible. Indeed, both speak truthfully concerning the self-evident knowledge they describe. Each side then believes that this self-evident knowledge invalidates what the other claims to be self-evident, but that is not so. Rather, both are truthful and correct concerning the self-evident knowledge they describe. Each errs only in denying what the other affirms regarding creation. For there is no incompatibility between the servant’s bringing his action into being and the fact that

this bringing into being is possible through the will of Allah Most High. Hence, the position of the adherents of the pure Sunnah is that the servant truly performs his action, just as Abū al-Husayn maintained was self-evident. They do not say that he does not truly act, or that he does not act at all, as those inclined toward compulsion say, such as the school of Abū Abd Allāh al-Rāzī.

At the same time, they maintain that Allah is the Creator of both this agent and his action, that He is the One who made him truly act, and that He creates the actions of His servants. In this they agree with those who affirm this among the Asharīs—the school of al-Rāzī—and others, rather than with the Qadariyyah, such as Abū al-Husayn and his followers, who say that Allah did not create the actions of His servants.

For this reason, the imams, such as Imam Ahmad and earlier imams such as al-Awzāī and others, explicitly rejected unqualified statements either affirming or denying compulsion. Thus, one should neither say, “Allah compelled His servants,” nor say, “He did not compel them.” The term “compulsion” has multiple meanings and is ambiguous. Saying “He compelled them” suggests that Allah compels them to do good and evil without their choosing; saying “He did not compel them” suggests that they do whatever they wish without His choosing. Both are erroneous. We have discussed this at length elsewhere.

The point here is that these two groups believed divine decree and revealed law to be incompatible, just as the Magians and polytheists believed. They therefore said: “If He creates the action, it is impossible

The Qadariyyah then said: “But actions do fall into these categories; therefore, He does not create them.”

The Jabriyyah said: “But He does create them; therefore, actions do not fall into these categories.”

However, those among the Jabriyyah who acknowledge the messengers recognize this distinction solely on the basis of the Lawgiver’s commands and prohibitions. They say: “He may command whatever He wills, without any inherent quality in it being the reason, and prohibit whatever He wills, without any inherent quality in it being the reason.” Regarding both His creation and His commands, they say: “He does whatever He wills and decrees whatever He wishes.”

As for someone overcome by personal opinion or desire, he casts off the Lawgiver’s authority once he sees actions as compelled. Such people say what the polytheists say:

“Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

Whoever acknowledges revealed law, commands and prohibitions, and moral good and evil, but not divine decree or Allah’s creation of actions—as is the position of the Mutazilah—belongs to the Magian Qadariyyah, who resemble the Magians. The Mutazilah bear considerable resemblance to the Magians and the Jews.

Whoever acknowledges divine ordainment and decree, Allah’s creation of actions, and His all-encompassing lordship, but denies right and wrong, guidance and misguidance, and good deeds and evil deeds, bears a resemblance to the polytheists and the Sabians.

Iblīs was the first to show enmity towards Allah, to transgress with regard to His creation and command, and to oppose an explicit revealed text with analogical reasoning.

For this reason, some of the early generations said:

“The first to reason by analogy was Iblīs.”

Allah commanded him to prostrate before Adam, but he objected to this command, saying, “I am better than him,” and refused to prostrate. He was thus the first to show enmity towards Allah. He was ignorant and unjust: ignorant of the wisdom in Allah’s command, and unjust through his arrogance, which combined rejection of the truth with contempt for others.

Then, in saying to his Lord, “Because You have led me astray, I shall surely do such and such,” he made Allah’s action—His leading him astray—a justification and a motive for leading the children of Adam astray. In this, he impugned Allah’s action and command, alleging that it was reprehensible: “So I too shall do what is reprehensible.” He thus drew an analogy between himself and his Lord and likened himself to his Lord. In this way, he sought to imitate divine lordship, as is established in Sahīh Muslim, on the authority of Jābir, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Iblīs sets up his throne upon the sea, then sends out his troops. Those who cause the greatest turmoil are closest to him in rank. One of them comes and says, ‘I persisted with him until he did such and such.’ Then another comes and says, ‘I persisted with him until I separated him from his wife.’ He then embraces him, draws him close, and says, ‘You are the one! You are the one!’”

translated_text:
The Qadariyya sought to declare Allah free of foolishness, and their intention in this was good. For He, glorified be He, is exalted far above what the wrongdoers—Iblīs and his hosts—say. He is a just Judge. Yet their understanding proved inadequate, and a measure of ignorance led them to believe that declaring Him free of such defects required denying His power over His servants’ actions, His creation of those actions, and the all-encompassing scope of His will. Thus, while they disputed with Iblīs and his party on one point, Iblīs gained mastery over them from another direction.

This is among the gravest perils of disputing about religion without knowledge or without adhering to the truth. This is the speculative theology condemned by the early generations: its practitioner counters falsehood with falsehood and innovation with innovation.

Then various groups who affirmed Allah’s all-encompassing power debated with them, seeking to establish that Allah is the Creator of all things; that whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; and that He has power over all things. Their capacity and knowledge likewise proved inadequate. They believed that this could not be established unless they denied Allah’s love and good pleasure, the good and bad qualities by which He has distinguished certain actions from others, and His wisdom and mercy. Accordingly, they deemed every act possible for Him, without holding Him to be above injustice or any other act.

Some went still further, entirely nullifying commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment. These inclined towards irjā (the Murji’ite doctrine), just as the former inclined towards the Wa‘īdiyya’s emphasis on threatened punishment.

The Wa‘īdiyya said:

translated_text:
“Every evildoer will remain in the Fire forever, never to leave it.” The Khawārij further said: “He is an unbeliever.”

The extremist Murji’a denied that anyone among the people of the qiblah would be punished. Those who openly avowed unbelief denied altogether the threatened punishment in the Hereafter, as various groups among the Ittihādiyya, the philosophizers, the Qarāmita and the Bātiniyya do. These determinist Murji’a showed greater disbelief in commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment than the Mu‘tazila, who upheld the doctrines of the Wa‘īdiyya and the Qadariyya. As for the moderate determinist Murji’a, who acknowledge commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment, and that some among the people of the qiblah will enter the Fire, they are the closest to Ahl al-Sunnah.

Al-Tirmidhī narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Qadariyya and the Murji’a were cursed on the tongues of seventy prophets, of whom I am the last.”

Nevertheless, the Mu‘tazila among the Qadariyya are sounder than the Jabriyya, the Murji’a and their like in their knowledge and practice of the Sharia. Their discussions of the principles of jurisprudence and of obedience to commands and prohibitions are better than those of the Murji’a among the Ash‘arīs and others. The latter’s discussions of the principles of jurisprudence are severely deficient; likewise, they fail to give due weight to acts of obedience and disobedience.

Yet in the fundamentals of religion, they are sounder than the former, for they affirm aspects of Allah’s attributes, power and creation that the former do not affirm. And this category ranks higher.

For this reason, the Murji’a were generally better than the Qadariyya. Indeed, even jurists from Kufa and elsewhere embraced the doctrine of the Murji’a, whereas none of the jurists or imams of the early generations adhered to Mu‘tazilism.

Section

If, then, error concerning divine decree has arisen sometimes through denying divine decree and Allah’s creation of acts, sometimes through denying the revealed Law and the threatened punishment, and sometimes through attributing injustice to the Lord, then this surah contains a refutation of all these groups. His statement, Exalted is He:

“Then inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness”

affirms divine decree through the words “Then inspired it.” It also affirms the servant’s actions by ascribing wickedness and righteousness to his own soul, making it clear that the soul itself is wicked or righteous. Furthermore, the words “its wickedness and its righteousness” affirm the distinction between good and evil, and between commands and prohibitions.

His subsequent statement:

“He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it”

affirms the servant’s actions, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment, through the success of whoever purifies his soul and the failure of whoever corrupts it. This explicitly refutes the Magian Qadariyya and the Jabriyya concerning the revealed Law or the servant’s actions. They are those who deny the truth.

As for those who accuse the Creator of injustice, He has demonstrated His justice through His words:

“By the soul and Him who proportioned it.”

Proportioning means giving a balanced form. He thus makes clear that He is just in fashioning the soul into which He inspired its wickedness and its righteousness. He then mentions the punishment of those who rejected His messengers and transgressed, and that He does not fear the consequences of His retribution against those who oppose His messengers. This makes clear that whoever denies either of these truths will face Allah’s retribution, and He does not fear its consequences, just as He exacted retribution upon Satan and his forces. Such a person’s complaints of injustice against his Lord and his imputing folly to Him only bring about his own destruction; he will not harm Allah in the least.

“For the servants will never be able to harm Allah, nor will they ever be able to benefit Him. Even if the first and last of them, humans and jinn alike, had the heart of the most righteous man among them, that would add nothing to His dominion. And even if the first and last of them, humans and jinn alike, had the heart of the most wicked man among them, that would diminish His dominion in no way.”

Thus, when ʿImrān ibn Husayn asked Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī about this to gauge his understanding—“Would that constitute injustice?”—he explained that this was not injustice on His part and expressed fear in view of His words:

“Glory be to Him! Exalted is He far above what they say!”

He also mentioned the hadith of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his citing this verse as evidence. It has thus become clear that the Qadariyya who engage in false disputation either deny what

the Lord has reported concerning His creation or His commands, or accuse Him of injustice in His judgment. Yet He, glorified be He, is truthful and just, as He, Most High, says:

“The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice. None can change His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

For speech is either performative or declarative. His declarations are true, never false; His performative speech—His commands bringing things into being and His legislative commands—is just, never unjust. The Magian Qadariyya denied what He reported concerning His creation and His legislation in matters of religion, while the Iblis-like Qadariyya accused Him of injustice in the two taken together, or in each separately.

It has thus become clear that those within the Muslim community who divide and disagree do so because they abandon some of the truth with which Allah sent His Prophet, embrace falsehood contrary to it, and share in falsehood that contradicts what the Messenger brought. This is akin to the unbelievers’ opposition to the believers, as He, Most High, says:

“Those messengers—some We have favored above others,”

through to His words:

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.”

When they share in a falsehood by which they oppose the believers who follow the messengers, they forget a portion of what they were reminded of. He then casts enmity and hatred among them, and they disagree with one another over another truth brought by the Messenger. Thus, one group believes in part of it and rejects another, while the other group believes in what the first rejects and rejects what the first believes. They shared the view that the Lord’s creation of the servant’s actions is incompatible with those actions being classified as good or bad. They shared this premise in their disputation, although it is neither true in itself nor supported by any sound proof. It is one of the two premises on which al-Rāzī relies in discussing the question of judging actions good or bad. In his al-Mahsūl and elsewhere, he held that the servant is compelled to act, that the action of someone compelled cannot be bad, and that therefore none of the servants’ actions can be bad.

This argument for denying such badness is rooted in the argument of the polytheists who denied the messengers and said:

“Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

By affirming divine decree, they denied the wrongfulness of associating partners with Allah and of forbidding good things that Allah had not forbidden. Yet those who invoke compulsion to negate rulings, if they acknowledge the revealed law, are not like the polytheists in every respect. Thus, the speculative theologians who acknowledge the revealed law are not like the polytheists, even though they share in some of the polytheists’ falsehood. translated_text:
they come to disbelieve in commands and prohibitions, promises and threats, reward and punishment, whether in speech or in their disposition and conduct. This most often occurs with actions that accord with their desires. By this they seek to escape blame and punishment, yet it only increases their blame and punishment—like someone seeking refuge from scorching ground in a fire.

No one can consistently put this view into practice. In their dealings with one another, human beings cannot do without wanting certain things and commanding them, and hating other things and forbidding them. Whoever seeks to treat alike what is loved and what is hated, what is pleasing and what is displeasing, justice and injustice, knowledge and ignorance, misguidance and guidance, sound judgment and error, can never maintain that position. Rather, when something happens that he dislikes and that harms him, he rushes to ward it off and punish its perpetrator by whatever means he can, even to the point of transgression.

They are thus among the most unjust of people: they judge reprehensible acts of injustice and indecency differently depending on whether they are committed by themselves or others, or by those they favor or those they do not. They invoke divine decree in their own defense, but not in defense of their adversaries. You will find that when one of them does something for which he is praised, the outlook of the Qadarites comes to dominate his heart: he regards himself, rather than Allah, as the one who brought it about, and forgets Allah’s favor to him

Ibn al-Qayyim—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

In this surah, Allah, glorified be He, mentioned Thamūd alone among the nations that rejected their messengers. Shaykh al-Islām Abū al-Abbās Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyyah said:

This—and Allah knows best—is an instance of drawing attention to the greater through the lesser. For none of the nations that rejected their messengers was less sinful or more lightly punished than they were (*), since He did not mention concerning them the sins He mentioned concerning ‘Ād, Midian, the people of Lot, and others. Thus, when He mentioned them alongside ‘Ād, He said:

“As for ‘Ād, they were arrogant in the land without right and said, ‘Who is mightier than us in strength?’ Did they not see that Allah, who created them, was mightier than them in strength? Yet they continued to reject Our signs.”

“As for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness to guidance.”

Likewise, when He mentions them alongside the nations that rejected their messengers, He does not attribute to them the tyranny, arrogance, and evil deeds that He attributes to those others, such as sodomy, giving short measure and weight, and spreading corruption in the land, as in Surahs Hūd and al-Shu‘arā’ and elsewhere. “Who is mightier than us in strength?”

Besides associating partners with Allah, the people of Midian dealt unjustly in matters of wealth; and Pharaoh’s people spread corruption in the land and exalted themselves.

Each nation’s punishment was commensurate with its sins and crimes. ‘Ād were punished with a fierce, raging wind that nothing could withstand. The people of Lot were subjected to forms of punishment inflicted on no other nation. He combined their destruction with pelting them with stones from the sky, obliterating their sight, overturning their dwellings upon them—turning them upside down—and causing the earth to swallow them into the lowest depths. He punished the people of Shu‘ayb with fire that consumed both them and the wealth they had acquired through injustice and aggression. As for Thamūd, He destroyed them with the mighty blast, and they died instantly.

If this was His punishment of these people, whose sin, besides associating partners with Him, was hamstringing the she-camel Allah had made a sign for them, then whoever violates Allah’s prohibitions, treats His commands and prohibitions with contempt, slaughters His servants, and sheds their blood will suffer a more severe punishment. Whoever considers the state of the world, past and present, and the punishments inflicted upon those who spread corruption in the land, shed blood unjustly, stir up strife, and disdain what Allah has made inviolable, will know that deliverance in this world and the Hereafter belongs to those who believe and are mindful of Allah.

Surah al-‘Alaq (The Clinging Clot)

The shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

The first revelation sent down to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained the foundations of religion: the rational proofs establishing the existence and oneness of the Creator, the truthfulness of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Resurrection—both its possibility and its occurrence.

We have discussed this principle several times previously, explaining that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, set out the rational and revealed proofs through which people are guided to their religion and to what brings them salvation and happiness in this world and the Hereafter. We have also explained that those who have devised foundations contrary to some of what he brought have laid the foundations of their own religion, not his. These foundations are invalid according to both reason and revelation, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

He also explained that many who associate themselves with religious knowledge and devotion are either deficient or negligent in their knowledge of what he brought in the way of

and falsehood. The Quran sets out the rational proofs for these matters and rebukes those who fail to reason from them. It explains that through reason one can recognize the Resurrection, the goodness of worshipping Him alone and thanking Him, and the evil of associating partners with Him and being ungrateful for His blessings, as I have discussed at length elsewhere.

Many people know this by their innate disposition, yet deny reason’s ability to discern good and evil when the fundamentals of religion are presented according to the approach of Jahm’s negationist, determinist followers. This is true of most of what the proponents of falsehood say: their innate disposition leads them to say things that contradict their innovated beliefs.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh Ibn al-Jadd al-Aʿlā mentioned that he heard Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī recite these two well-known verses at one of his preaching gatherings:

Suppose no messengers announcing resurrection had come to us, and Hell’s blazing fire had not been kindled—
Is it not an obligation, a duty owed, for servants to feel shame before their Benefactor?

Here he explicitly states that it is an obligation and a duty owed for created beings to feel shame before their Creator, who bestows blessings upon them. This explicitly affirms that thanking Him is an obligation and His due, even if there were no threat of punishment and no

message announcing recompense. This demonstrates that thanking Him is obligatory and due, even supposing there were no punishment. This is a disputed matter, which we have discussed elsewhere, explaining that this is the correct position.

The consequence of committing what is forbidden is a decline in rank and the loss of many blessings one previously enjoyed, even if one is not punished with harm. It also shows that what is obligatory and what is due can be known self-evidently. Thus, someone who neglects an obligation or commits an evil deed, even if not subjected to painful punishment such as the Fire, is deprived of blessings and the means of obtaining them as recompense. Such is the recompense of someone who fails to give thanks for a blessing and instead shows ingratitude for it: to be deprived of it. Gratitude preserves blessings and brings their increase. Ingratitude, once the proof has been established, entails punishment; before that, it diminishes blessings rather than increasing them. Nevertheless, a messenger must be sent, whereupon one becomes deserving of either bliss or punishment, for there is no abode other than Paradise or Hell. Allah Most High says:

“We have certainly created man in the finest form,
then We returned him to the lowest of the low,
except those who believe and do righteous deeds, for theirs is an unending reward.”

This is discussed at length in various places.

The point here is that these fundamental principles were explained in the earliest revelation of the Quran. For the first Quranic revelation was:

“Read in the name of your Lord,”

“O you wrapped in your cloak.”

This was reported from Jābir. The first view, however, is more sound. The hadith of ‘Ā’ishah in the two Sahīh collections makes clear that the first revelation was “Read in the name of your Lord,” which was revealed to him while he was in the cave of Hirā’, and that “The Cloaked One” was revealed later. This is indeed the fitting sequence, for His words “Read” command recitation, not the conveyance of the message; through this he became a prophet. His words “Arise and warn” command him to warn; through this he became a messenger charged with warning.

The two Sahīh collections relate, through al-Zuhrī, from ‘Urwah, that ‘Ā’ishah said:

“The revelation to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, began with true dreams during sleep. Every dream he saw would come true as clearly as the break of dawn. Then solitude was made dear to him. He would go to the cave of Hirā’ and devote himself to worship there for several nights before returning to his family, taking provisions for that purpose. Then he would return to Khadījah and replenish his provisions for a similar stay, until the truth came to him while he was in the cave of Hirā’.

“The angel came to him and said, ‘Read.’ He replied, ‘I cannot read.’ He related: ‘Then he seized me and squeezed me until I could bear no more. Then he released me and said, “Read.”

al-‘Uzzā, Khadījah’s cousin. He had embraced Christianity during the pre-Islamic era. He could write in Hebrew and would write out passages from the Gospel in Arabic, as much as Allah willed him to write. He was an elderly man who had become blind.

Khadījah said to him, ‘Cousin, listen to your nephew.’

Waraqah asked him, ‘My nephew, what do you see?’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, told him what he had seen.

Waraqah said to him, ‘This is the bearer of revelation who was sent down to Moses. If only I were a young man then! If only I were alive when your people drive you out!’

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked, ‘Will they drive me out?’

He replied, ‘Yes. No one has ever brought anything like what you have brought without being met with hostility. If I live to see that day of yours, I will give you steadfast support.’”

Soon afterward, Waraqah died, and revelation ceased for a time. Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī said, ‘I heard Abū Salamah ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān say that Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh had told him that he heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, speaking

about the pause in revelation:

“While I was walking, I heard a voice. I looked up towards heaven, and there was the angel who had come to me at Hirā’, sitting on a chair between heaven and earth. I went on until I fell to the ground. Then I came to my family and said, ‘Wrap me up! Wrap me up!’ So they wrapped me up. Then Allah Most High revealed, ‘O you wrapped in your cloak, arise and warn,’ down to His words, ‘And shun uncleanliness.’”’

This makes clear that Sūrat al-Muddaththir was revealed after that pause, and that this occurred after he saw the angel who had first come to him at Hirā’. He had thus seen the angel twice. This explains the hadith of Jābir transmitted through another chain, as the two compilers narrated from Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr, who said:

“I asked Abū Salamah ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān about the first passage of the Quran to be revealed.

“He replied, ‘O you wrapped in your cloak.’

“I said, ‘People say it was “Read in the name of your Lord who created.”’

“Abū Salamah said, ‘I asked Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh about that and said to him just what you have said. Jābir replied, “I will tell you only what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, told us. He said: ‘I stayed in retreat at Hirā’. When I had completed my retreat, I descended, and someone called out to me. I looked to my right but saw nothing. I looked to my left but saw nothing. I looked ahead of me but saw nothing. I looked behind me but saw nothing. Then I raised my head and saw something. I went to Khadījah and said, “Cover me up and pour cold water over me.” So they covered me up and poured cold water over me.

He said: Then the following was revealed: “O you wrapped in your cloak, arise and warn, and magnify your Lord.”’”’”

This hadith agrees with the preceding one: Sūrat al-Muddaththir was revealed after he had descended from the mountain, while he was walking, and after the angel had called out to him. In the other narration, he explained that this angel was the one who had come to him at Hirā’. ‘Ā’ishah explained that “Read” was revealed at that time in the cave of Hirā’.

It seems, however, that he did not know that “Read” had been revealed then. He only knew that the Prophet had seen the angel before that; yet he could have seen him without hearing from him. ‘Ā’ishah’s hadith, however, provides additional information: the angel’s command that he recite “Read.”

In al-Zuhrī’s narration, he called this the “pause in revelation,” an expression also found in ‘Ā’ishah’s hadith. Al-Zuhrī may therefore have paraphrased Jābir’s hadith, calling the interval between the two sightings the “pause in revelation,” as ‘Ā’ishah explained it. Otherwise, if Jābir himself called it the “pause in revelation,” how could he say that no revelation had yet come down?

In any event, al-Zuhrī possessed both ‘Urwah’s hadith from ‘Ā’ishah and Abū Salamah’s hadith from Jābir. Should he and Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr differ, al-Zuhrī has broader knowledge and a stronger memory. Yahyā, however, mentioned that he had asked Abū Salamah about the first revelation. Jābir thus related what he knew, not having known what had been revealed before that, whereas ‘Ā’ishah established and clarified the matter.

And the verses of “Read” and “The Cloaked One” make this clear. The two hadiths agree with one another, with the Quran, and with reason’s indication that this is the appropriate sequence. If the first revelation was:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—
created man from a clinging clot.
Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous,
who taught by the pen—
taught man that which he knew not,”

then the first verse affirms the Creator, exalted is He, as does the second. Both also provide evidence for the possibility of prophethood and for the prophethood of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

As for the first, He said, “Read in the name of your Lord who created,” then said, “Created man from a clinging clot.” He thus mentioned creation in general, then singled out the creation of man, stating that He created him from a clinging clot. This is something known to everyone: all people know that a human being comes into being in his mother’s womb and develops from a clinging clot. These are the descendants of Adam. The word “man” here is a generic noun encompassing all people; it does not include Adam, who was created from clay. The purpose of this verse is to present evidence for the Creator, exalted is He, and reasoning can proceed only from premises

known to the person drawing the inference. The aim is to direct people and guide them, and they all know that human beings are created from clinging clots. As for Adam’s creation from clay, that is known only through what the prophets reported or through other evidence. Hence some disbelievers among the Dahriyyah and others who do not acknowledge prophethood deny it. This differs from the mention of his creation in other surahs, where it is mentioned in connection with what establishes prophethood. This surah, however, was the first revelation, and prophethood is established through it. It therefore does not mention what is known through transmitted accounts, but instead presents evidence known through reason, observation, and—for those who have not seen clinging clots—mass-transmitted reports.

He, glorified is He, mentions the creation of man from clinging clots: ‘alaq is the plural of ‘alaqah, meaning a small piece of blood. Before that stage, it was a drop of semen. Such a drop may be discharged outside the womb, as when someone has a wet dream, or it may enter the womb and then be expelled before becoming a clot. At the clot stage, it has thus become the starting point of human creation, and it is known that the drop has become a clot from which a human being is to be created. He says in Surah al-Qiyāmah:

“Was he not a drop of semen emitted?
Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned him,
and made from him the two sexes, male and female.
Is He not able

to give life to the dead?”

Here He mentions this as evidence that the second creation, which will be from dust, is possible. Hence He says elsewhere:

“O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen.”

In Surah al-Qiyāmah, He adduces man’s creation from a drop of semen as evidence, since this is known to everyone. In Surah al-Hajj, He mentions man’s creation from dust, since this has been established by conclusive evidence. Mentioning the original creation provides stronger evidence that re-creation is possible.

Here, however, the purpose is to present evidence establishing the existence of the Creator, exalted is He, in the first place. He therefore mentions that He created man from clinging clots. Man develops from the blood clot into a lump of flesh—a piece of flesh like meat chewed in the mouth—then develops further and takes shape, as He, exalted is He, says:

“Then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, so that We may make things clear to you.”

The womb may expel it before it has taken shape. Thus He makes clear to people the beginning of their creation, which they see with their own eyes. This evidence—man’s creation from clinging clots—is shared by all people. People are the ones drawing the inference, yet they themselves are the evidence, the proof, and the sign. Man is both the evidence and the one who reasons from it, as He, exalted is He, says:

“And in yourselves—do you not see?”

And He says:

“We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.”

This is like His statement in another verse:

“Or were they created by nothing, or are they themselves the creators?”

And this is evidence that man knows from his own self and recalls whenever he reflects on himself and on the fellow human beings he sees. He thus reasons from it to the original creation and the resurrection, as Allah, exalted is He, says:

“Man says, ‘When I am dead, will I really be brought forth alive?’”

“Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“He presents an example to Us, forgetting his own creation. He says, ‘Who will give life to bones when they have crumbled away?’”

“Say, ‘He who brought them into being the first time will give them life, and He has full knowledge of every creation.’”

Likewise, Zechariah, astonished at having a child in old age, said:

“How can I have a son when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?”

“He said, ‘So it will be. Your Lord says: It is easy for Me; I created you before, when you were nothing.’”

It does not say, “It is easier for Him,” as He says concerning the original creation and the resurrection:

“It is He who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him.”

He, glorified is He, says:

“He created man from clinging clots,”

after saying:

“Who created.”

He thus speaks of creation in unrestricted terms, encompassing every created thing, and then singles out the creation of man. Everything known to have come into existence is therefore included in His words, “Who created.”

After creation, He mentions teaching: teaching by the pen and teaching man what he did not know. He singles out this teaching, from which one may infer the possibility of prophethood. Here the wording is not “guided,” which would refer to the general guidance encompassing human beings

and all other animals, as He says elsewhere:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,”
“Who created and proportioned,”
“And Who determined and guided.”

And as Moses said:

“Our Lord is He who gave each thing its form, then guided it.”

For this particular teaching necessarily entails general guidance, but the converse does not hold. It bears more directly on establishing prophethood, since prophethood is a kind of teaching. Making a human being a prophet is no greater than making a clinging clot into a living, knowing, rational human being, endowed with hearing, sight, and speech, who has acquired various kinds of knowledge. Likewise, originating creation is no easier for Him than repeating it. How could the One capable of the original creation be incapable of resurrection? And how could the One capable of this teaching be incapable of that teaching, when He knows all things and no one encompasses any of His knowledge except what He wills?

He, glorified is He, first says:

“Who taught by the pen.”

He thus speaks of both teaching and those taught in unrestricted terms, without singling out any particular class of learners. This encompasses the teaching of angels and others among humans and jinn, just as creation encompasses them all. He mentions teaching by the pen because it entails teaching writing. Writing corresponds to spoken expression, which is communication and speech. Spoken expression, in turn, signifies the intelligible meanings within the heart; thus, all knowledge within hearts is included.

Everything has a reality of its own, existing outside the mind; then

the mind and heart conceive it, then the tongue expresses it, and then the pen writes it down. Thus, it has external, mental, verbal, and written existence: existence in external reality, in minds, on tongues, and through fingertips. Yet the first is the thing itself, whereas the other three are representations corresponding to it. The first is the created thing, while the other three convey knowledge of it. He therefore mentions creation and teaching so as to encompass all four levels, saying:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created,”
“Created man from a clinging clot.”
“Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous,”
“Who taught by the pen,”
“Taught man what he did not know.”

People have disputed whether essences are made or not, and whether the essence of each thing is something additional to its existence. This has been discussed at length elsewhere, where the correct position has been explained: there is only what is conceived in the mind and what exists in external reality. If by ‘essence’ one means what is conceived in the mind, and by ‘existence’ what is in external reality—or vice versa—then essence is distinct from existence, if what is in external reality differs from what is in the mind. But if ‘essence’ refers to what is in the mind, or in external reality, or both, and ‘existence’ is used likewise, then existence in external reality is the very essence existing in external reality. The same applies in the mind: the one is the other. There are not two things in external reality.

He—glorified be He—knows what is in minds and has created what exists in external reality; both are made by Him. Yet He brings about what exists externally by creating it, and what exists in the mind by teaching it. He is the One who “created,” “created man from a clinging clot,” and He is “the Most Generous,” “who taught by the pen,” “taught man what he did not know.”

His words, “taught by the pen,” include His teaching the recording angels and His teaching the writing of the revealed Books. Through the pen, He taught how to write down His speech which He revealed, such as the Torah and the Quran. Indeed, He Himself wrote the Torah for Moses.

The fact that Muhammad was an unlettered prophet makes what he brought all the more miraculous and extraordinary, and demonstrates all the more clearly that the teaching he received surpasses all other teaching. As the Most High said:

“You did not recite any Scripture before it, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise, those who follow falsehood would have doubted.”

Others know what others have written—such is people’s knowledge of what they write—whereas Allah taught him this through what He revealed to him. This speech revealed to him is a sign and proof of his prophethood, for neither mankind nor jinn can produce it:

“Say, ‘If mankind and jinn gathered to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like, even if they supported one another.’”

“Or do they say, ‘He fabricated it’? Say, ‘Then produce a surah like it and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.’”

And in the other verse: “Then produce ten surahs

like it that you have fabricated, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.”

“But if they do not respond to you, then know that it was revealed with Allah’s knowledge and that there is no deity except Him. Will you then submit?”

Section

We have discussed at length elsewhere the methods people use to establish the existence of the Creator and the truth of prophethood. We have shown that every method containing something contrary to the Sunnah is rationally invalid, just as it is contrary to revelation. The well-known method among speculative theologians is to infer the temporal origination of bodies from the temporal origination of accidents. We have examined this method in several places and shown that it contradicts both revelation and reason.

Many people know that it is an innovation in religion but do not know that it is rationally unsound. Some suppose that it is sound according to both reason and revelation, and that it was the method of Abraham, Allah’s close friend, peace be upon him. The invalidity of this has been demonstrated elsewhere.

They therefore argued from the creation of man, but instead of treating his creation as evidence, as the verse does, they treated it as something requiring proof. They supposed that the temporal origination of the accidents of the drop of semen was known self-evidently and through sense perception. As for its constituent atoms, they believed that all bodies are composed of indivisible atoms, and that creating man and other things consists merely in bringing accidents into existence in those atoms by combining and separating them, rather than bringing an entity itself into existence. Thus, they sought to establish by inference that man is created.

Once they had established that he is created, they said that he has a Creator. They argued that he is created by appealing to accidents: the drop of semen, the clot, and the lump of flesh are never free of temporally originated accidents. For, in their view, these consist of atoms that are sometimes combined and sometimes separated. They are therefore never free of combination and separation, both of which are temporally originated. Thus, man is never free of temporally originated events, and whatever is never free of such events is itself temporally originated, since a beginningless succession of events is impossible.

Since these atoms are never free of temporally originated events, they are themselves temporally originated. This method depends on all bodies being of this nature.

This is the well-known method followed by the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, and those who followed them among later scholars affiliated with the four schools and others among the followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad. It was set out by al-Qādī and Ibn ‘Aqīl, among others; by Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī and the author of *The Supplement*, among others; by Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī and Abū Bakr ibn al-‘Arabī, among others; and by Abū Mansūr al-Māturīdī and al-Sābūnī, among others.

However, those who argued from the creation of man applied this argument specifically to man, supposing that this was the Quran’s method. They elaborated at length and in minute detail, going so far as to argue that man’s very entity and constituent atoms are created, because they supposed that sense perception and self-evident reason establish only the temporal origination of accidents, not of atoms. They claimed that, in everything Allah brings into being—clouds, rain, crops, fruit, man, and animals—He brings into existence only accidents, namely, the combination and separation of atoms that already existed.

translated_text:
They also claimed that no one knows, through observation or self-evident reason, that other concrete entities come into being; rather, this can only be known by reasoning as they did. They said:

“These are temporally originated accidents inhering in atoms, and those atoms have never been free of accidents, since atoms cannot be devoid of accidents.”

They then said:

“Whatever is never free of temporally originated events is itself temporally originated.”

They based this on the premise that bodies consist of individual, indivisible atoms. They also said that bodies cannot be transformed into one another.

The majority of rational people among the early generations and the various classes of scholars, as well as most speculative thinkers, disagree with their affirmation of indivisible atoms. They affirm that bodies can be transformed into one another and maintain that the Lord continually brings concrete entities into being, as the Quran indicates.

Thus, this method is invalid both rationally and according to revelation; indeed, it obstinately defies reason. For it is self-evident to everyone that man is created and originated, coming into existence after not having existed. Everyone knows that he came into being in his mother’s womb after not having existed, and that his very being came into existence. As the Exalted says:

“I created you before, when you were nothing.”

And the Exalted says:

“Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?”

translated_text:
This is not something that requires proof, for it is clearer and more evident than the argument offered to establish it, even if that argument were sound. How much more so when it is false!

Their claims that only accidents come into being and that man is composed of indivisible atoms are both false. Their truth is not known; rather, their falsity is known. It is known that man’s very substance—and likewise that of other beings—comes into existence from the material from which he was created, namely clinging substance, as He says:

“He created man from a clinging substance.”

The claim that man is composed of indivisible atoms is not correct. Even if it were correct, it could only be known through subtle arguments that cannot constitute the foundation of religion, which consists of primary premises. Those premises must be clear, fundamental, and self-evidently known.

Their method thus entails denying what is known—namely, that concrete entities come into being, something known to people—and affirming what is not known, but is in fact false: that bringing these entities into being consists merely of combining and separating atoms, and that it is nothing more than bringing accidents into being.

For this reason, the leading scholars of the religion condemned their use of the method of substances and accidents in this manner and explained that they were introducing innovations in this regard. Indeed,

they demonstrated their misguidance on both scriptural and rational grounds. The statements of the early generations and the leading scholars against them have been set out at length elsewhere, for they are numerous. The Quran bases its argument on what people already know:

“He created man from a clinging substance.”

Yet these people approached this known fact and claimed that it was not known, but doubtful. They then claimed to present the proof by which it would become known. However, they offered an invalid argument that does not establish that man came into existence. It is taken for a proof, but is merely a specious argument with false implications. Thus, they denied what is known through reason and, furthermore, through revelation, while claiming to offer a method established by reason, although it is invalid according to both reason and revelation. They thereby resembled those of whom Allah says:

Likewise, in establishing prophethood and its possibility, and resurrection and its possibility, they turned away from the guiding path that yields certain knowledge—the path by which Allah guided His servants—to a path that breeds doubt, specious arguments, and bewilderment.

Hence it has been said:

“The ultimate outcome for proponents of innovation among speculative theologians is doubt, and among Sufis, ecstatic excesses.”

Whenever they do offer a sound proof, it agrees with what the Messenger brought, even if the wording differs. Thus, one of them may offer a proof, whether sound or unsound, only for another to attack it and claim to offer something better, while actually offering something inferior. This frequently happens with their definitions: some attack the definitions of others, then offer definitions that are equivalent or inferior. Yet all these definitions belong to the same category and are valid if their purpose is to distinguish the thing defined from other things.

As for those who claim that definitions convey a conception of the essence of the thing defined, as the logicians maintain, they are mistaken and misguided, as has been explained at length elsewhere. A definition merely identifies the thing defined and points to it, much as a name does, but it sets out in detail what the name conveys in general terms. It is therefore a kind of indication, as has been explained at length elsewhere. The purpose here is simply to draw attention to the distinction between a path that yields knowledge and certainty, such as the one explained in the Quran, and the paths of the proponents of innovation that do not, and that are invalid according to both revelation and reason.

Section

Those who built the foundation of their religion upon the argument from accidents, using them to infer that bodies came into existence, have fallen into considerable inconsistency, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Besides opposing the law revealed from heaven, each of them inevitably also contradicts clear reason and obstinately denies the obvious, becoming one of those who neither listen nor reason. A proposition has necessary consequences; if it is false, it may entail other falsehoods whose falsity is evident. Its proponent seeks to establish those consequences, thereby revealing his opposition to sensory experience and reason.

Such are those who affirmed indivisible atoms and maintained that motions do not intrinsically differ as fast or slow, since, in their view, motion is divided just as the moving body is, and likewise time and its parts. For them, a motion and a moving body are each a single indivisible unit. Thus, if two moving bodies are equal, yet one moves faster than the other, they say: “That is only because periods of rest intervene.”

They maintained that when a millstone, a wheel, or any circular object rotates, its circumference and a smaller ring within it move for the same length of time, although the circumference has more parts. so they claimed that the parts separate and then rejoin. This is an obstinate denial of the obvious, akin to “al-Nazzām’s leap.” Likewise, those who maintained that an accident does not persist for two successive moments contradicted sensory experience and what rational people know by the self-evident dictates of reason. Everyone knows that the colour of his body a moment ago is this same colour, and likewise the colour of the sky, mountains, wood, paper, and other things. Among the considerations that drove them to this was their supposition that, if both persisted, neither could be brought out of existence. For they were perplexed about how Allah causes things to perish when He wills to do so, just as they were perplexed about His bringing them into existence. Their perplexity concerning annihilation is even more evident.

One says: “He creates annihilation that inheres in no substrate; it is the opposite of those things, and they perish through their opposite.” Another says: “He deprives them of accidents altogether, or of the persistence without which they cannot endure; thus they perish because the condition of their continued existence is lost.”

One cause of this is their supposition—or the supposition of some among them—that things which come into existence need Allah only when they are brought into existence, not while they continue to exist. Yet they affirmed that He has the power to annihilate them, and so they contrived these false doctrines. These people do not argue for the Lord’s everlasting existence on the basis of the world’s dependence upon Him, but rather on the grounds that He is beginningless, and whatever is necessarily beginningless cannot cease to exist. Apart from that, in their view, an enduring thing has no need of the Lord while it continues to exist.

These people are worse than those who asked Moses, “Does your Lord sleep?” Allah gave them an illustration with two glass vessels. After Moses had remained awake for several nights, He commanded him to hold the two vessels. When he held them, sleep overcame him, and they shattered. Allah thus showed him that, were drowsiness or sleep to overtake Him, the world would collapse. Yet according to these people’s view, were drowsiness or sleep to overtake Him, what already endures would not cease to exist.

Some of them, however, say that an enduring thing depends upon accidents being brought into existence in succession, since, in their view, an accident does not persist for two successive moments. It is on this basis that such a person argues that, were drowsiness or sleep to overtake Him, the accidents through which bodies persist would not come into existence—not because, in his view, bodies themselves depend upon Him while they continue to exist.

Likewise, they say that the divine will does not pertain to what is beginningless or to what continues to exist. In their view, power likewise does not pertain to what continues to exist. Nor, according to them, can incapacity properly be spoken of with respect to what continues to exist or is beginningless, since they hold that incapacity can only concern something over which power is possible.

These people say that the reason for dependence upon the Creator is simply having come into existence. Others among the philosophers say that it is simply contingency, and claim that something beginningless and eternal, which has always existed and will always exist, depends upon the Maker. Thus the former claims that an enduring thing which came into existence has no such dependence, while the latter claims that an enduring, beginningless thing does have such dependence.  إنَّهَا تَعْدَمُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ لِامْتِنَاعِ وُجُودِ حَوَادِثَ لَا آخِرَ لَهَا كَمَا تَقُولُهُ الْجَهْمِيَّة. وَهَذَا مِمَّا أَنْكَرَهُ عَلَيْهِمْ السَّلَفُ وَالْأَئِمَّةُ كَمَا قَدْ ذُكِرَ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ.
 وَهَؤُلَاءِ إنَّمَا قَالُوا هَذَا طَرْدًا لِقَوْلِهِمْ بِامْتِنَاعِ دَوَامِ جِنْسِ الْحَوَادِثِ وَقَالُوا:
 مَا وَجَبَ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَهُ ابْتِدَاءٌ وَجَبَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَهُ انْتِهَاءٌ كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ هَذَا وَبَيَّنَ فَسَادَ هَذَا الْأَصْلِ.
translated_text:
unsound, as has been explained at length elsewhere. The truth is that everything besides Allah has come into existence and depends upon Him at all times. He sustains it and brings it to nonexistence, just as He brings it into being and originates it. Thus He brings things into existence from dust and other things, then causes them to perish and transforms them into dust and other things. Many of these people have claimed that everything besides Allah will cease to exist and then be restored.

Some of them have said: “This is possible, but establishing it depends upon revelation, and revelation has neither affirmed nor denied it.” This is their conception of the resurrection. Yet neither the Book nor the Sunnah has taught this, nor has reason established it. Rather, the Book and the Sunnah make clear that Allah transforms the world from one state to another: He splits the heaven, makes the mountains like wool, rolls up the sun, and does the other things He has foretold in His Book. He has not stated that all things will cease to exist and then be restored.

Some of them further say that these things will cease to exist thereafter, because an endless succession of events is impossible, as the Jahmiyyah maintain. This is among the views for which the early generations and the leading scholars condemned them, as has been discussed elsewhere.

They said this only to carry through the implications of their claim that a perpetual succession of originated events is impossible. They said: “Whatever must have a beginning must also have an end.” This has been explained at length, and the unsoundness of this principle has been demonstrated.

Section

He, glorified be He, sometimes mentions the creation of man in general terms and sometimes describes it in detail, as when He says:

“We created man from an extract of clay. Then We placed him as a drop of sperm in a secure resting place. Then We made the drop into a clinging clot, then made the clot into a lump of flesh, then made the lump into bones, then clothed the bones with flesh, then brought him into being as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.”

He then mentions the two returns—the lesser and the greater—saying:

“Then, after that, you will surely die. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised.”

Some people ask: Why does the emphatic lām occur in the statement about death, which is witnessed, but not in the statement about resurrection, which is unseen and therefore calls for emphasis?

The reason—and Allah knows best—is that the purpose of mentioning death and resurrection is to announce recompense and the return, the first stage of which is death. Thus He draws attention to belief in the return and preparation for what comes after death. He says only, “you will be raised,” not “you will be recompensed”; nevertheless, it is known that resurrection is for recompense.

This also draws attention to how man is overpowered and humbled. He says: “After this

all, you will indeed die and be returned to the lowest of the low—except those who believe and do righteous deeds.” As He says:

“We have certainly created man in the finest form.”

“Then We returned him to the lowest of the low.”

“Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, for they will have an uninterrupted reward.”

This return takes place through death, for man descends to the lowest of the low, except those who believe and do righteous deeds. As He says:

“No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjīn.”

And He says:

“Indeed, the record of the righteous is in Illiyyīn.”

There are two interpretations of His words, “the lowest of the low.” One is that they refer to decrepit old age; the other is that they refer to punishment after death. The latter is what the verse definitively indicates, for He places man among the lowest of the low, with the exception of the believers.

People fall into two categories: after death, the disbeliever is punished among the lowest of the low, while the believer is in Illiyyīn. As for the first interpretation, it is open to question. Not everyone other than the believers reaches decrepit old age and is thus returned to the lowest of the low. Rather, many disbelievers die before reaching decrepitude, while many believers do reach it. Even if the believer’s condition in old age is better than the disbeliever’s, the believer’s condition is likewise better than the disbeliever’s in youth. Thus, interpreting the return to the lowest of the low as occurring at the end of life, and restricting it to disbelievers, is a weak interpretation. Hence some have said that, on this interpretation, the exception is disjunctive; this, too, is

translated_text:
weak. A disjunctive exception cannot occur in an affirmative statement. Were this permissible, anyone could claim that any exception he wished was disjunctive. Moreover, in a disjunctive exception, the category excepted is not part of the original category, whereas believers are part of humankind.

Some have explained the verse, according to the first interpretation, as meaning that when a believer becomes incapable of performing deeds, he continues to be credited for what he used to do.

Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī said:

“When a believer becomes so old that he can no longer perform deeds, Allah credits him for what he used to do. This is what He means by His words, ‘For they will have an uninterrupted reward.’”

Ibn Qutaybah said:

“The meaning is: ‘Except those who believe’ while they possess strength and ability. Their reward is not diminished in old age, even if they become incapable of acts of obedience. Allah knows that, had He not taken away their strength, they would not have ceased doing good, so He continues to grant them its reward.”

In reply, one may say: This also holds true during youth, when a young person becomes unable to act because of illness or travel. As reported in the two Sahīh collections, Abū Mūsā narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a servant falls ill or travels, Allah credits him with the deeds he used to perform while healthy and resident.”

Others have explained it by citing the report that Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“Whoever recites the Quran will not be reduced to decrepit old age.”

In reply, one may say: This applies specifically to someone who recites the Quran, whereas the verse excepts those who believe and do righteous deeds, whether they recite the Quran or do not

recite it. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“The believer who recites the Quran is like a citron: its taste is pleasant and its fragrance is pleasant. The believer who does not recite the Quran is like a date: its taste is pleasant, but it has no fragrance.”

It may also be said: Senescence is not peculiar to human beings; other animals likewise become decrepit as they age. Moreover, although an elderly person’s body grows weak, his intellect is stronger than a young person’s. Even supposing that some of his faculties decline, this does not amount to being reduced to the lowest of the low. Allah, glorified be He, describes old age only in terms of weakness, as when He says:

“Then, after strength, He brought weakness and grey hair.”

And:

“Whoever We grant a long life, We reverse his development.”

Thus, He returns him to a state of weakness. It is well known that a child is not among the lowest of the low; the same holds for an elderly person, with even greater reason. Rather, those in the lowest of the low are those who will be in Sijjīn, not in Illiyyīn, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire.”

Further clarification comes in His words:

“What, then, makes you deny the Judgment?”

This must be connected to what precedes it, since it is introduced by the particle fa (“then”). If the preceding passage referred only to a person’s being reduced to decrepit old age, rather than to what happens after death, there would be no reference here to judgment and recompense, unlike

the case in which the passage states that, after death, man is reduced to the lowest of the low, except for the believer who does righteous deeds. This conveys that Allah will judge His servants after death, honouring the believers and humiliating the disbelievers.

Moreover, He, glorified be He, has affirmed this with solemn oaths: by the fig, the olive, Mount Sinai, and this secure city. These are the places from which Muhammad, the Messiah, and Moses came, and where Allah sent these messengers as bearers of glad tidings and warnings. Such an oath would not concern mere senescence, which everyone knows, but rather unseen matters that are confirmed by oaths. For Allah’s oaths concern tidings of the unseen.

The very subject by which the oath is sworn—the sending of these messengers—confirms what the oath affirms: reward and punishment after death, since the messengers conveyed this. It also encompasses recompense in this world, such as Allah’s destruction of those disbelievers whom He destroyed. Through their destruction in this world, He reduced them to the lowest of the low. This also draws attention to the loss of blessings when sins are committed, as in the case of someone brought low in this world as recompense for his sins.

 قَالَ عِكْرِمَةُ يَقُولُ:
 فَمَا يُكَذِّبُك بَعْدُ بِهَذِهِ الْأَشْيَاءِ الَّتِي فَعَلْت بِك.
 وَعَنْ مُقَاتِلٍ:
translated_text:
His words,

“What, then, makes you deny the Recompense after this?”

refer to recompense for deeds in this world, the intermediate realm after death, and the Hereafter. For He has sworn by the places of these messengers, who were sent with clear signs indicating Allah’s commands and prohibitions, His promises and warnings, bringing glad tidings to the believers and warning the disbelievers. By these places, He has sworn that man, after being created in the best form, will have an unending reward if he believes and does righteous deeds; otherwise, he will be among the lowest of the low. Thus, the surah explains the message entrusted to these messengers by whose places He swore.

Swearing by the places of their trials honours them, for if a person’s place is honoured on his account, that person is even more deserving of honour. Hence correspondence uses expressions such as, “To the lofty and exalted assembly, residence, or the like.” The place is mentioned with deference and veneration, while its occupant is intended.

Thus, His words,

“What, then, makes you deny the Recompense after this?”

indicate that the preceding passage has explained what should preclude denial of the Recompense. There are two interpretations of His word yukadhdhibuka.

One is that it addresses man, as stated by Mujāhid, ‘Ikrimah, and Muqātil. Al-Baghawī mentions no other interpretation. ‘Ikrimah said: “He is saying: What, after this, makes you deny these things that I have done for you?”

And it is reported from Muqātil:

“What, then, makes you deny recompense?” He claimed that it was revealed concerning ‘Ayyāsh ibn Abī Rabī‘ah.

The second interpretation is that it addresses the Messenger, and this is more evident. Man has only been spoken about, not directly addressed. It is to the Messenger that the Quran was revealed, and he is the one addressed in these surahs, as in His words:

“Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor despised you.”

And His words:

“Have We not expanded your breast for you?”

And His words:

“Read in the name of your Lord.”

When man is addressed, he is told:

“O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?”

“O man, you are striving hard towards your Lord.”

Moreover, if we suppose that this addresses man, it must address mankind as a whole, as in His words, “O man, you are striving.” According to these interpreters, however, it addresses only the disbeliever who denies the Recompense.

Furthermore, His words, “calls you a liar, after this, concerning the Recompense,” mean “declares you to be a liar.” This is the familiar usage in Arabic. The expression kadhdhaba ghayrahu, meaning “he accused another of lying and declared him a liar,” is well known, and the Quran abounds in this usage. Whenever Allah mentions the deniers’ rejection of the messengers, or rejection of the truth and the like, this is what He means.

translated_text:
Yet this verse presents a difficulty because He says:

“Calls you a liar, after this, concerning the Recompense.”

Here He mentions both the person accused of lying and the matter denied. This is uncommon, though a similar construction occurs in His words:

“They have indeed declared you liars in what you say.”

In most passages, however, He mentions only one of the two: either the person accused of lying, as in His words:

“The people of Noah denied the messengers,”

or the matter denied, as in His words:

“Rather, they deny the Hour.”

Mentioning both the person accused of lying and the matter denied together is uncommon. This is why this verse proved confusing to those who took it as addressing man and interpreted His words, “What, then, makes you a liar?” as meaning, “What makes you a denier?” Others expressed it as, “What makes you a liar?”

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: “The majority of exegetes said that the person addressed is the disbelieving man. That is: What makes you a liar concerning the Recompense, setting up rivals to Allah and claiming that there is no resurrection, after these proofs?”

(I say: Neither interpretation is known in Arabic usage—that one should say, “Kadhdhabaka means ‘he made you one who is disbelieved.’” Rather, kadhdhabaka means “he declared you a liar.” To say “he declared you a liar” means that he deemed you untruthful in what you reported, just as the disbelievers deemed the messengers untruthful in what they reported and thus accused them of lying. This interpreter, however, says:
