translated_text:
“He made you a liar concerning the Recompense.” He thus takes the man’s lying to consist in his associating partners with Allah and denying the Resurrection. Yet this is the opposite of being a denier. The former interpretation makes him a denier of the Recompense; the latter makes him a liar concerning it. The first is unsound in terms of Arabic usage, and the second is unsound in meaning. For the Recompense is the requital that the disbeliever denied. The disbeliever denied it; he did not himself accuse anyone of lying concerning it.

Furthermore, when referring to someone who conveys a report, it is not established usage to say, “Kadhabtu bihi” (“I lied concerning him”); rather, one says, “Kadhdhabtuhu” (“I declared him a liar”). Moreover, the established meaning of declaring someone a liar is to accuse him of lying, not to cause lying to arise in him. All of this is strained interpretation unknown in the language; established usage is, rather, the opposite. He did not say, “Fa-mā yukadhdhibuk” (“What, then, declares you a liar?”), nor did He say, “Fa-mā kadhdhabak” (“What, then, declared you a liar?”). This is why the scholars of Arabic adopted the first position.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said:

“There is disagreement over who is addressed in His words, ‘What, then, calls you a liar?’ Qatāda, al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash said that it is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Allah said to him: ‘What, then, declares you a liar in what you report about requital and resurrection—which is the Recompense—after this lesson, reflection upon which establishes the truth of what you have said?’”

He said: “According to this interpretation, ‘the religion’ may also encompass the entirety of his revealed law and religion.”

" لَا تُكَذِّبْ "
translated_text:
I say:

On the assumption that Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the one addressed, there are two interpretations. The first is Qatāda’s. He said concerning “What, then, makes you deny the Recompense after this?”: “That is, be certain, for clarification has come to you from Allah.” This is how Ibn Abī Hātim transmitted it from him through a reliable chain of transmission.

Al-Mahdawī likewise cited it:

“‘What, then, makes you deny the Recompense after this?’ That is, be certain, in light of what has come to you from Allah, that He is the wisest of judges. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the one addressed.”

He attributed this interpretation to Qatāda, then said:

“It has also been said that the meaning is: ‘What, then, makes you deny, O you who doubt Allah’s power?’—meaning the disbelievers. What induces you to do so after His power has become clear to you?”

He said: “Al-Farrā’ said: ‘Who, then, can declare you a liar concerning reward and punishment?’ This is the interpretation preferred by al-Tabarī.”

(I say:

This interpretation transmitted from Qatāda is what caused Mujāhid to recoil from the view that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was being addressed. As various scholars, including Ibn Abī Hātim, transmitted from al-Thawrī, from Mansūr, who said:

“I asked Mujāhid: ‘In “What, then, makes you deny the Recompense after this?”, did He mean the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?’

“He replied: ‘Allah forbid! He meant man.’”

Mujāhid was right to hold the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, above being told, “What, then, makes you deny?”—meaning, “Be certain and do not deny.” For if he were told, “Do not deny,”

translated_text:
that would have been of the same kind as commanding him to believe and fear Allah, and forbidding him from doing what Allah has forbidden. But as for saying, “What, then, makes you deny the Recompense after this?”, he never denied the Recompense. Rather, he is the one who proclaimed it and believed in it. He is “the one who brought the truth and believed in it.” How, then, could he be asked, “What makes you deny the Recompense after this?” This interpretation is therefore unsound in both wording and meaning.

Moreover, the wording I have seen transmitted from Qatāda through a chain of transmission does not explicitly support this interpretation. Rather, he may have intended it as an address to man, for concerning “What, then, makes you deny the Recompense after this?”, he said: “Be certain, for clarification has come to you.” Every human being is addressed by this. If this is what Qatāda intended, the meaning is sound. However, they reported him as saying that this is addressed to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. On that understanding, the meaning is false. The Messenger cannot be asked, “What, then, makes you deny the Recompense?”—even if the mind should entertain such an interpretation—for there are indications here that demonstrate its unsoundness. This is why Mujāhid sought refuge in Allah from it.

The correct interpretation is that stated by al-Farrā’, al-Akhfash and others. It is the interpretation preferred by Abū Ja‘far Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī and other scholars, as mentioned above. Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī likewise cited it from al-Farrā’, saying:

On this interpretation, mā (“what”) in His words “What, then” describes persons. It is as though it were said: “What kind of person, then, denies the Recompense after this?” That is, anyone with this description and these qualities is ignorant and wrongs himself. Allah will judge between His servants concerning their disagreements about this momentous news. As for His word “after,” it has been said that it means “after the proofs of the Recompense that He has mentioned.”

translated_text:
Yet it may be asked: Has He done more than announce it and state that people are of two kinds—those in the lowest of the low and those who will have an unfailing reward? He has thus mentioned glad tidings and warnings, and the messengers were sent as bearers of glad tidings and warners. Whoever rejects you after this, his judgment rests with Allah, the most just of judges, while you have conveyed what you were obliged to convey.

His words, “Who, then, can deny your account?” do not mean that no such rejection occurs, for it has indeed occurred. Rather, it may be said that they express astonishment at it, as in His words:

“If you are astonished, then astonishing is their saying, ‘When we have become dust, will we really be created anew?’”

It may also be said that this belittles the denier’s importance and diminishes his standing because of his ignorance and wrongdoing, just as one might say, “Who is so-and-so?” or “Who but an ignorant person would say this?” Yet He uses mā (“what”), because it indicates the person’s qualities, which are what is intended; his individual identity is of no concern. It is as though He said: “What sort of person, then—what ignorant person—denies your account of the Recompense after this? He is indeed among those who will be returned to the lowest of the low.”

His words, “Is Allah not the most just of judges?” indicate that He is the Judge between the one who denies the Recompense and the one who believes in it. The decision in this matter belongs to Him, glorified and exalted be He.

The wonders of the Quran never cease. Allah, glorified be He, has made His intent clear with perfect precision. Confusion arises, however, for those who are not firmly grounded in understanding the evidence and what it indicates. This surah, like others, contains inexhaustible wonders. Among them is that His statement,

“Who, then, can deny your account of the Recompense after this?”

mentions both the Messenger who is denied and the Recompense that is denied. The surah encompasses both matters. It includes an oath by the places associated with the messengers, which testify to their greatness and to the signs they brought—signs that establish their truthfulness and require belief. They foretold the Resurrection mentioned in this surah. Allah has sworn to its occurrence, just as He does elsewhere, and just as He commanded His Prophet to swear to it in such statements as:

“Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, ‘Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected.’”

And:

“Those who disbelieve say, ‘The Hour will never come upon us.’ Say, ‘Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you.’”

Since the surah encompasses both matters, He mentions both kinds of denial, saying:

“Who, then, can deny your account of the Recompense after this?”

And Allah, glorified be He, knows best.

Moreover, he bears no sin for that, whereas the Quran intends to make clear that this return is a recompense for his sins. Hence He says, “Except those who believe and do

righteous deeds.” As He says:

“Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds and counsel one another to truth and counsel one another to patience.”

Here, however, He mentions only loss, so He describes those excepted as counselling one another to truth and patience, in addition to their faith and righteousness. There, He mentions “the lowest of the low,” which is punishment. A believer who acts righteously will not be punished, even if he has neglected certain things and thereby lost them; had he preserved them, he would have gained rather than lost. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that He, glorified be He, mentions the creation of man both in general terms and in detail. At times, He mentions giving him life, as in His statement, Most High:

“How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were lifeless and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then bring you back to life, and then to Him you will be returned.”

This is like the statement of His intimate friend, peace be upon him:

“My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death.”

For the creation of life, together with all that it entails and presupposes, is greater and more clearly demonstrates power, blessing, and wisdom.

Section

His words:

“Recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man that which he knew not.”

After declaring that He created, He named and described Himself as generous, indeed as the Most Generous, to make clear that He bestows blessings upon His creatures and brings them to praiseworthy ends. As He says elsewhere:

“Who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided.”

And as Moses, peace be upon him, said:

“Our Lord is He who gave each thing its form, then guided it.”

And as His intimate friend, peace be upon him, said:

“Who created me, and He guides me.”

Creation thus encompasses the beginning, while generosity encompasses the culmination. Likewise, in the Mother of the Quran, He says:

“Lord of the worlds,”

then says:

“The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.”

The word karam (nobility and generosity) encompasses all fine and praiseworthy qualities. It does not mean merely giving; rather, giving completes its meaning, for doing good to others brings fine qualities to their perfection. Karam is the abundance and ready availability of goodness. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not call grapes al-karm (‘the noble one’), for al-karm is the believer’s heart.”

They called grapes “al-karm” (“the noble one”) because they are the most beneficial of fruits: they are eaten fresh or dried, and pressed to make various products. Grapevines are also more widespread than date palms, growing in most countries, whereas date palms grow only in hot countries. Thus, concerning human sustenance, Allah says:

“Let man consider his food: We poured down water abundantly, then split the earth open, and caused grain to grow in it, and grapes and herbage, and olives and date palms, and gardens of dense foliage, and fruit and pasture, as provision for you and your livestock.”

He thus mentioned grapes first. And in describing Paradise, He says:

“Indeed, the righteous will have triumph: gardens and grapevines.”

Nevertheless, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade calling grapes al-karm, saying:

“Al-karm is the believer’s heart.”

For nothing in this world contains more or greater goodness than the believer’s heart. The quality of karam (nobility) is ascribed to anything fine and praiseworthy. Allah Most High says:

“Have they not looked at the earth—how many noble kinds We have caused to grow in it?”

Ibn Qutaybah said: “Of every fine kind.” Al-Zajjāj said: “Zawj means ‘type,’ and karīm means ‘praiseworthy.’” Others explained “of every kind” as “of every class and variety,” and “noble” as “fine,” referring to plants eaten by people and livestock. One says “a noble date palm” when its fruit is good, and “a noble she-camel” when its milk is abundant.

It is also reported from al-Sha‘bī:

“People are among the things that grow from the earth: whoever enters Paradise is noble, and whoever enters the Fire is base.”

The Quran indicates that some people are noble in Allah’s sight and He honors them, while others He humiliates. He, Most High, says:

“Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”

He, Most High, also says:

“Whomever Allah humiliates, none can honor. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal:

“Beware of taking the choicest of their possessions, and beware the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and Allah.”

The choicest possessions are those dear to their owners because they need them and benefit from them, whether livestock or other property.

He, glory be to Him, has declared that He is “the Most Generous,” using the superlative with the definite article. This indicates that He alone is the Most Generous, unlike saying, “Your Lord is more generous,” which would not indicate exclusivity. His saying “the Most Generous” does indicate exclusivity. Nor did He say, “more generous than such-and-such.” Rather, He left the name unrestricted to make clear that He is the Most Generous absolutely, without qualification. This indicates that He possesses the utmost generosity, beyond which there is nothing greater and in which there is no deficiency.

 وَهَذَا لِأَنَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ. وَقَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَى هَذَا فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ وَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ أَهْلَ السُّنَّةِ يَصِفُونَهُ بِالْقُدْرَةِ الْإِلَهِيَّةِ وَالْحِكْمَةِ وَالرَّحْمَةِ. وَهُمْ الَّذِينَ يَعْبُدُونَهُ وَيَحْمَدُونَهُ وَأَنَّهُ يَجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ هُوَ الْمُسْتَحِقُّ لَأَنْ يُعْبَدَ دُونَ مَا سِوَاهُ وَالْعِبَادَةُ تَتَضَمَّنُ غَايَةَ الذُّلِّ وَغَايَةَ الْحُبِّ.
translated_text:
reassurance, as though He were saying: ‘Proceed with what you have been commanded to do. Your Lord is not like these other lords; rather, He is the Most Generous, untouched by any deficiency. He will support you and grant you victory.’”

I say: Some of the early Muslims said:

“None of you should offer Allah what he would be ashamed to offer someone he esteems, for Allah is the most generous of the generous.”

That is, He is more deserving of honor than anything else, since He is more generous than anything else. He, glory be to Him, is the Possessor of Majesty and Honor. He therefore deserves to be revered and honored. Reverence entails exaltation, while honor entails praise and love.

This resembles what has been said in describing the believer: he has been endowed with sweetness of character and an awe-inspiring presence. In the report of Hind ibn Abī Hālah describing the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, it says:

“Whoever saw him at first sight stood in awe of him, and whoever came to know him through close association loved him.”

This is because sovereignty and praise belong to Him, glory be to Him. This has been discussed at length elsewhere, and it has been explained that Ahl al-Sunnah describe Him as possessing divine power, wisdom, and mercy. They are the ones who worship and praise Him. It has also been explained that worship must be His due alone, to the exclusion of all else, and that worship entails the utmost humility and the utmost love.

and that the real implication of the position of the Jahmiyyah and those who agree with them in denying that He loves is that He does not deserve to be worshipped, just as their claim that He acts without wisdom or mercy implies that He is not to be praised. They describe Him only as possessing power and irresistible might. This entails reverence alone, not honor, love, or praise. Yet He, glory be to Him, is the Most Generous. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, your Lord’s punishment is severe. Indeed, it is He who originates creation and brings it back.”

Then He says:

“And He is the All-Forgiving, the All-Loving, Owner of the Throne, the Glorious, Doer of whatever He wills.”

And Shuayb said:

“Seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful, Loving.”

In the first revelation, He described Himself as the One who created and as the Most Generous. The Jahmiyyah affirm nothing beyond His being the Creator, despite their shortcomings even in affirming this. They do not describe Him as possessing generosity, mercy, or wisdom. Even when they use these terms, they do not intend their meanings. Rather, they use them because they occur in the Quran, then deviate concerning His names and distort words from their proper places.

At times they say that wisdom is power; at other times, that it is will; and at still other times, that it is knowledge. Yet wisdom, although it includes and entails these, is something more

than that. Not everyone who possesses power or will is wise, nor is everyone who possesses knowledge wise unless he acts upon his knowledge.

Ibn Qutaybah and others said: Wisdom is knowledge and acting upon it. It is also sound speech. Thus, it encompasses sound speech and upright, righteous action. The Lord Most High is the wisest of judges and the wisest of the wise. The precision evident in His creation is proof of His knowledge. They, along with all the other groups, infer knowledge from this precision. Yet it indicates knowledge only if the agent is wise and acts for a wise purpose. They, however, say that He does not act for a wise purpose, but acts solely by a will that singles out one of two equivalent alternatives without any reason necessitating that choice. This contradicts wisdom; indeed, it is foolishness. He has declared Himself free of this in His words:

“Had We intended to take a pastime, We would have taken it from what is with Us—if We were to do so.

“Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, whereupon it vanishes. And woe to you for what you attribute to Us!”

He has also stated that He created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them only in truth, and that He

did not create them in vain, and that such is the supposition of those who disbelieve. He says:

“Did you think that We created you without purpose?”

He also says:

“Does man think that he will be left without responsibility?”

That is, left unattended, neither commanded nor forbidden. This rhetorical question rebukes anyone who considers such a thing possible for the Lord. Yet the Jahmiyyah who espouse absolute determinism consider it possible for Him. They do not declare Him above any act, even if it is reprehensible. Nor do they ascribe to Him what His generosity, mercy, wisdom, and justice necessarily entail, whereby it would be known that He does what befits these attributes and does not do what contradicts them. Rather, they consider it possible for anything within His power either to occur or not to occur. They affirm one of these alternatives with certainty only on the basis of a revealed report or an established pattern, despite their inconsistencies in reasoning from reports—the reports of the messengers—and from the Lord’s customary ways. This has been explained at length elsewhere, including in discussions of the prophets’ miracles, the sending of messengers, commands and prohibitions, the resurrection, and similar matters pertaining to His acts and decrees that proceed from His will.

For these proceed from His wisdom and His mercy, and His will necessarily entails both. He wills only with a will that encompasses wisdom. He is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child, as is established in the authentic hadith in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah is indeed more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child.”

" إنَّ الْقَادِرَ يُرَجِّحُ أَحَدَ مَقْدُورَيْهِ عَلَى الْآخَرِ بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ "

translated_text:
Thus, in reality, they do not acknowledge that He is the Most Generous. The will they affirm is supported by neither revelation nor reason. For no will is known to favor one thing over another without a cause that necessitates that preference. Whoever among the Jahmiyyah and Muʿtazilah says, “An agent capable of acting favors one of two alternatives within his power over the other without any determining factor,” is obstinately denying the obvious.

The examples they give—a hungry person taking one of two loaves, or a fleeing person taking one of two roads—are evidence against them. Such a choice occurs only when one alternative has an advantage: either it is easier for him, it is the one that occurred to him and that he pictured, or he thought it more beneficial. One must therefore have some advantage over the other, whether in terms of his ability or his conception and awareness. He then gives preference to willing that option, while he does not will the other. How, then, can it be said that his will favored one over the other without any determining factor, or that he favored willing this over willing that without any determining factor? This is impossible, and its impossibility becomes evident once it is properly conceived.

But when they advanced invented doctrines concerning the origin of creation, contradicting both revelation and reason, they found themselves compelled to resort to this obstinate denial, as has been explained at length elsewhere. This also gave the philosophers an opening against them from another direction. Thus, they neither defended Islam nor defeated the philosophers.

Sound reason clearly establishes that if one who is capable of acting neither wills an act nor performs it, and then comes to will and perform it, something must have occurred to bring this about. The discussion here concerns two issues.

The first concerns action and speech in general: did He begin acting and speaking by His will after not having done so, or has He always acted and spoken by His will? This is discussed at length under the questions of divine speech and actions, in connection with the Quran and the world's coming into existence.

The second concerns willing and performing a particular act, as in His words, Most High:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

And His words:

“So your Lord willed that they should reach maturity and recover their treasure.”

And His words:

“When We will to destroy a town, We command its affluent inhabitants, but they transgress within it; then the sentence against it becomes justified, and We destroy it utterly.”

And His words:

“When Allah wills harm for a people, there is no averting it.”

And His words:

“If Allah touches you with harm, none can remove it except Him; and if He wills good for you, none can repel His bounty.”

And His words:

“Say, ‘Have you considered those you invoke besides Allah? If Allah willed harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He willed mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?’”

When He, glorified be He, wills any such thing, people hold various views concerning this.

It has been said that the will is single, eternal, and beginningless, and that only its relation to what is willed is renewed

translated_text:
and its relation to all things willed is the same, yet one of the distinctive properties of the will is that it determines particulars without a determining factor. This is the view of Ibn Kullāb, al-Ashʿarī, and their followers.

Many rational thinkers say that the falsity of this is self-evident. Indeed, Abū al-Barakāt went so far as to say, “No rational thinker has held this view.” He was unaware that it was the view of a large group of speculative thinkers and theologians.

Its invalidity is evident on several grounds: in treating the will for this as different from the will for that; in making the will determine particulars by its very nature; and in positing nothing new arising when temporal events occur that could account for a particular determination or its absence. Rather, only a relation devoid of actual existence is renewed. This is not anything real, so nothing new has arisen. Temporal events thus occur and take their particular forms without any newly arising cause or determining factor.

The second view is that of those who, like the preceding group, affirm a single eternal will, but say that as new acts occur, particular wills arise within His essence through that eternal will. This is the position of the Karrāmiyyah and others. They are closer to the truth insofar as they affirm wills pertaining to particular acts. Nevertheless, they face the same difficulties as the preceding group: they affirm temporal events without a newly arising cause, and particular determinations without a determining factor; and they make that will a single will relating to all newly arising wills

{فَإِذَا عَزَمْتَ فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ}
 بِالضَّمِّ. وَفِي الْحَدِيثِ
translated_text:
and also held that its particular determinations are intrinsic to it. They did not posit anything newly arising when the new wills come into existence that would enable those wills to determine the occurrence of events.

The third view is that of the Jahmiyyah and Muʿtazilah, who deny that will subsists in Him. They either deny will altogether, interpret it as nothing other than command and action, or affirm that a will comes into existence without inhering in any subject, as the Basrans hold. All these views, too, are known to be invalid.

The fourth view is that He has always willed through successive acts of will. Will as a kind is therefore eternal, whereas He wills each particular thing only at its appointed time. He, glorified is He, decrees things and records them, then subsequently creates them. When He decrees them, He knows what He will do and wills to do it at a future time, but He does not will to do it at that moment. When its time comes, He wills to do it. The former is resolve, and the latter is intention.

There are two views on whether He may be described as having resolve. The first disallows this, as held by al-Qādī Abū Bakr and al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā. The second permits it, and this is the more correct view. A number of the early generations recited, with a dammah (u-vowel):

“When I have resolved, then put your trust in Allah.”

And in the hadith

original_text:
الصَّحِيحِ مِنْ حَدِيثِ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ:
 
{ثُمَّ عَزَمَ اللَّهُ لِي}
 .
 وَكَذَلِكَ فِي خُطْبَةِ مُسْلِمٍ:
 
{فَعَزَمَ لِي}
 . وَسَوَاءٌ سُمِّيَ 
" عَزْمًا "
 أَوْ لَمْ يُسَمَّ فَهُوَ سُبْحَانَهُ إذَا قَدَّرَهَا عَلِمَ أَنَّهُ سَيَفْعَلُهَا فِي وَقْتِهَا وَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَفْعَلَهَا فِي وَقْتِهَا. فَإِذَا جَاءَ الْوَقْتُ فَلَا بُدَّ مِنْ إرَادَةِ الْفِعْلِ الْمُعَيَّنِ وَنَفْسِ الْفِعْلِ وَلَا بُدَّ مِنْ عِلْمِهِ بِمَا يَفْعَلُهُ. ثُمَّ الْكَلَامُ فِي عِلْمِهِ بِمَا يَفْعَلُهُ هَلْ هُوَ الْعِلْمُ الْمُتَقَدِّمُ بِمَا سَيَفْعَلُهُ وَعِلْمُهُ بِأَنَّ قَدْ فَعَلَهُ هَلْ هُوَ الْأَوَّلُ فِيهِ قَوْلَانِ مَعْرُوفَانِ. وَالْعَقْلُ وَالْقُرْآنُ يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّهُ قَدْرٌ زَائِدٌ كَمَا قَالَ 
{لِنَعْلَمَ}
 فِي بِضْعَةَ عَشَرَ مَوْضِعًا وَقَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ: إلَّا لِنَرَى. وَحِينَئِذٍ فَإِرَادَةُ الْمُعَيَّنِ تَتَرَجَّحُ لِعِلْمِهِ بِمَا فِي الْمُعَيَّنِ مِنْ الْمَعْنَى الْمُرَجِّحِ لِإِرَادَتِهِ. فَالْإِرَادَةُ تَتْبَعُ الْعِلْمَ. وَكَوْنُ ذَلِكَ الْمُعَيَّنِ مُتَّصِفًا بِتِلْكَ الصِّفَاتِ الْمُرَجَّحَةِ إنَّمَا هُوَ فِي الْعِلْمِ وَالتَّصَوُّرِ لَيْسَ فِي الْخَارِجِ شَيْءٌ. وَمِنْ هُنَا غَلِطَ مَنْ قَالَ 
" الْمَعْدُومُ شَيْءٌ "
 حَيْثُ أَثْبَتُوا ذَلِكَ الْمُرَادَ فِي الْخَارِجِ. وَمَنْ لَمْ يُثْبِتْهُ شَيْئًا فِي الْعِلْمِ أَوْ كَانَ لَيْسَ عِنْدَهُ إلَّا إرَادَةٌ
translated_text:
authenticated on the authority of Umm Salamah:

“Then Allah resolved on my behalf.”

Likewise, in Muslim’s introduction:

“He resolved on my behalf.”

Whether or not this is called “resolve,” when He, glorified is He, decrees things, He knows that He will do them at their appointed times and wills to do them at those times. When the time comes, there must be both the will to perform the particular act and the act itself, and He must know what He is doing.

There are two well-known views concerning whether His knowledge of what He is doing is the same as His prior knowledge of what He would do, and whether His knowledge that He has done it is the same as that earlier knowledge. Reason and the Quran indicate that this involves something additional, as He says, “so that We may know,” in more than ten passages. Ibn ʿAbbās explained: “Only so that We may see.”

Thus, His willing a particular thing is favored by His knowledge of the consideration within it that favors His willing it. Will therefore follows knowledge. That particular thing’s possession of those favoring attributes exists only in knowledge and conception; it has no external existence. This is where those who said, “The nonexistent is a thing,” went wrong: they affirmed that the object of will existed externally. As for someone who does not affirm it as a thing in knowledge, or who holds that there is only a will

original_text: وَاحِدَةٌ وَعِلْمٌ وَاحِدٌ لَيْسَ لِلْمَعْلُومَاتِ وَالْمُرَادَاتِ صُورَةٌ عِلْمِيَّةٌ عِنْدَ هَؤُلَاءِ. فَهَؤُلَاءِ نَفَوْا كَوْنَهُ شَيْئًا فِي الْعِلْمِ وَالْإِرَادَةِ وَأُولَئِكَ أَثْبَتُوا كَوْنَهُ شَيْئًا فِي الْخَارِجِ. وَتِلْكَ الصُّورَةُ الْعِلْمِيَّةُ الْإِرَادِيَّةُ حَدَثَتْ بَعْدَ أَنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ. وَهِيَ حَادِثَةٌ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ كَمَا يُحْدِثُ الْحَوَادِثَ الْمُنْفَصِلَةَ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ. فَيُقَدِّرُ مَا يَفْعَلُهُ ثُمَّ يَفْعَلُهُ. فَتَخْصِيصُهَا بِصِفَةِ دُونَ صِفَةٍ وَقَدَرٍ دُونَ قَدَرٍ هُوَ لِلْأُمُورِ الْمُقْتَضِيَةِ لِذَلِكَ فِي نَفْسِهِ. فَلَا يُرِيدُ إلَّا مَا تَقْتَضِي نَفْسُهُ إرَادَتَهُ بِمَعْنَى يَقْتَضِي ذَلِكَ وَلَا يُرَجِّحُ مُرَادًا عَلَى مُرَادٍ إلَّا لِذَلِكَ. وَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُرَجِّحَ شَيْئًا لِمُجَرَّدِ كَوْنِهِ قَادِرًا. فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ قَادِرًا قَبْلَ إرَادَتِهِ وَهُوَ قَادِرٌ عَلَى غَيْرِهِ. فَتَخْصِيصُ هَذَا بِالْإِرَادَةِ لَا يَكُونُ بِالْقُدْرَةِ الْمُشْتَرَكَةِ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ غَيْرِهِ وَلَا يَجُوزُ أَيْضًا أَنْ تَكُونَ الْإِرَادَةُ تُخَصِّصُ مِثْلًا عَلَى مِثْلٍ بِلَا مُخَصِّصٍ. بَلْ إنَّمَا يُرِيدُ الْمُرِيدُ أَحَدَ الشَّيْئَيْنِ دُونَ الْآخَرِ لِمَعْنَى فِي الْمُرِيدِ وَالْمُرَادِ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمُرِيدُ إلَى ذَلِكَ أَمْيَلَ وَأَنْ يَكُونَ فِي الْمُرَادِ مَا أَوْجَبَ رُجْحَانَ ذَلِكَ الْمَيْلِ.
translated_text:
that is single, together with a single knowledge, the objects of knowledge and will have no representation in knowledge in their view. These people thus deny that it is a thing in knowledge and will, while the others affirm that it is a thing in external reality.

That representation in knowledge and will came into being after not having existed. It comes into being by His will and power, just as He brings into being events distinct from Himself by His will and power. He determines what He will do, then does it. His assigning them one attribute rather than another, and one measure rather than another, is due to considerations within Himself that call for this. Thus, He wills only what His own self calls for Him to will, on account of a consideration that calls for it; and He favors one object of will over another only on that account.

He cannot favor something merely because He has the power to bring it about, for He had that power before willing it, and He also has power over other things. Singling this out as the object of His will therefore cannot be due to the power that applies equally to it and to other things. Nor can will single out one of two like things over the other without a determining factor. Rather, one who wills chooses one thing rather than another only because of a consideration in both the one willing and the object of will. The one willing must be more inclined toward it, and the object of will must contain something that makes that inclination prevail.

original_text:
وَالْقُرْآنُ وَالسُّنَّةُ تُثْبِتُ الْقَدَرَ وَتَقْدِيرَ الْأُمُورِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَخْلُقَهَا وَأَنَّ ذَلِكَ فِي كِتَابٍ وَهَذَا أَصْلٌ عَظِيمٌ يُثْبِتُ الْعِلْمَ وَالْإِرَادَةَ لِكُلِّ مَا سَيَكُونُ وَيُزِيلُ إشْكَالَاتٍ كَثِيرَةً ضَلَّ بِسَبَبِهَا طَوَائِفُ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ فِي مَسَائِلِ الْعِلْمِ وَالْإِرَادَةِ.
 فَالْإِيمَانُ بِالْقَدَرِ مِنْ أُصُولِ الْإِيمَانِ كَمَا ذَكَرَهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي حَدِيثِ جِبْرِيلَ قَالَ:
 
{الْإِيمَانُ أَنْ تُؤْمِنَ بِاَللَّهِ. وَمَلَائِكَتِهِ وَكُتُبِهِ وَرُسُلِهِ وَبِالْبَعْثِ بَعْدَ الْمَوْتِ. وَتُؤْمِنَ بِالْقَدَرِ خَيْرِهِ وَشَرِّهِ}
 وَقَدْ تَبَرَّأَ ابْنُ عُمَرَ وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ مِنْ الْمُكَذِّبِينَ بِالْقَدَرِ. وَمَعَ هَذَا فَطَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ لَا تُثْبِتُ الْقَدَرَ إلَّا عِلْمًا أَزَلِيًّا وَإِرَادَةً أَزَلِيَّةً فَقَطْ. وَإِذَا أَثْبَتُوا الْكِتَابَةَ قَالُوا إنَّهَا كِتَابَةٌ لِبَعْضِ ذَاكَ.
 وَأَمَّا مَنْ يَقُولُ إنَّهُ قَدَّرَهَا حِينَئِذٍ كَمَا فِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{قَدَّرَ اللَّهُ مَقَادِيرَ الْخَلَائِقِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَخْلُقَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ بِخَمْسِينَ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ وَكَانَ عَرْشُهُ عَلَى الْمَاءِ}
 فَقَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ.
translated_text:
The Quran and Sunnah affirm divine decree, His determining all matters before He creates them, and their being recorded in a Book. This is a fundamental principle that affirms His knowledge and will concerning everything that will come to pass. It also resolves many difficulties that have led various groups astray in this area concerning questions of knowledge and will.

Belief in divine decree is therefore one of the foundations of faith, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, stated in the hadith of Gabriel:

“Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and resurrection after death, and to believe in divine decree, both its good and its evil.”

Ibn Umar and other Companions disavowed those who denied divine decree. Nevertheless, a group of speculative theologians and others affirm nothing in divine decree beyond eternal knowledge and an eternal will. When they affirm its being written down, they say that this records only part of that.

As for those who say that He determined these matters at that time—as related in Sahīh Muslim from Abd Allāh ibn Amr, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who said:

“Allah determined the decrees of all creation fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water”—

this has been discussed at length elsewhere.

This is like His saying:

“And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict grievous torment upon them.”

And His saying:

“I will surely fill Hell with you and all those among them who follow you.”

And His saying:

“Were it not for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord and an appointed term, punishment would have been inevitable.”

And His saying:

“Our word has already gone forth to Our servants, the messengers: they will surely be helped, and Our forces will surely prevail.”

And His saying:

“Had it not been for a prior decree from Allah, a tremendous punishment would have befallen you for what you took.”

The written record itself cannot have existed from eternity.

In a hadith transmitted by Hammād ibn Salama, from al-Ash‘ath ibn Abd al-Rahmān al-Jarmī, from Abū Qilāba, from Abū al-Ash‘ath al-San‘ānī, from Shaddād ibn Aws, the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah wrote a book two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. From it He sent down two verses with which He concluded Sūrat al-Baqara.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated it and described it as singular.

Allah, glorified is He, sent down the Quran on the Night of Decree from the Preserved Tablet to the House of Honour in the lowest heaven. Many works on the foundations of religion and speculative theology contain innovated views but omit the position conveyed by the Quran and Sunnah. Thus al-Shahrastānī, despite his writings on religions and sects, lists, on the question of speech

وَالْإِرَادَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمَا أَقْوَالًا لَيْسَ فِيهَا الْقَوْلُ الَّذِي دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ وَإِنْ كَانَ بَعْضُهَا أَقْرَبَ.
وَقَبِلَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ كِتَابُهُ فِي اخْتِلَافِ الْمُصَلِّينَ مِنْ أَجْمَعِ الْكُتُبِ وَقَدْ اسْتَقْصَى فِيهِ أَقَاوِيلَ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ. وَلَمَّا ذَكَرَ قَوْلَ أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ وَالْحَدِيثِ ذَكَرَهُ مُجْمَلًا غَيْرَ مُفَصَّلٍ. وَتَصَرَّفَ فِي بَعْضِهِ فَذَكَرَهُ بِمَا اعْتَقَدَهُ هُوَ أَنَّهُ قَوْلُهُمْ مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَكُونَ ذَلِكَ مَنْقُولًا عَنْ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ.

Before him was Abū al-Hasan, whose book on disagreements among Muslims is among the most comprehensive works. In it, he exhaustively surveyed the views of the people of innovation. Yet when he presented the position of the people of Sunnah and hadith, he gave only a general account, without elaboration. He also reworked parts of it, presenting what he himself believed to be their position without this having been transmitted from any of them.

The position closest to his own is that of Ibn Kullāb. Ibn Kullāb’s position, however, is mingled with that of the Jahmiyyah: it combines the position of the people of Sunnah with that of the Jahmiyyah. The same applies to al-Ashʿarī’s position on the divine attributes. As for divine decree and faith, his position is that of Jahm.

As for the position he reported from the people of Sunnah and hadith, concerning which he said, “We affirm everything we have mentioned of their position, and we adopt it,” this comes closest to the truth among the positions he mentioned. Some of it he reported accurately from them; other parts he reworked and mixed with views of Jahm concerning the divine attributes and divine decree, since he himself believed those principles to be sound. His followers who understood and accepted his views on those fundamental principles openly expressed the opposition to the people of Sunnah and hadith that their position necessarily entailed. They did not stand in awe of the people of Sunnah and hadith, revere them, or believe their doctrines to be sound, as he had done. Both groups—the people of Sunnah and the Jahmiyyah—say that this is contradictory. From the Sunni perspective, however, his agreement with the people of hadith is praiseworthy, while his agreement with the Jahmiyyah is blameworthy; from the Jahmī perspective, his agreement with the people of hadith is blameworthy, while his agreement with the Jahmiyyah is praiseworthy. Thus, his later followers, such as Abū al-Ma‘ālī and others, were more overtly Jahmī and more pronounced in their negation of the divine attributes than their predecessors.

These are subtle matters in which Allah forgives those who err after exercising scholarly judgment. Yet what is correct is what the Messenger conveyed; the truth can never lie in anything contrary to it. And Allah knows best.

The unalloyed truth is what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—conveyed; the truth cannot lie in anything contrary to it.

Yet complete guidance is attained through knowing this and understanding it clearly. Disagreement sometimes arises from misunderstanding and insufficient knowledge, and sometimes from ill intent. People disagree concerning knowledge and will, regarding their multiplicity and their being brought into existence. It is well known that, with regard to the willing of things that subsists in the soul, one cannot say, “Knowing this is knowing that,” or, “Willing this is willing that.” Such a claim is obstinate denial of the obvious. Distinguishing one instance of knowledge from another, or one act of willing from another, does not mean that one is separate from the other. and power and will, are not separate from one another when they subsist in a single subject. Rather, they share the same subject, just as taste, colour and fragrance subsist in a single citron, or in other fruits and things of this kind. Thus, when one speaks of “instances of knowledge and acts of willing,” there is no physical separation between one and another; rather, it is a single kind subsisting in the soul.

When someone comes to know one thing after knowing another, this kind has increased and become more abundant—or, if you wish, greater. Here, the increase in quantity does not exceed the increase in quality. Rather, one speaks of “abundant knowledge and great knowledge,” with greatness referring to its strength, the nobility of what is known, and similar considerations.

Thus the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb:

“Do you know which verse of the Book of Allah that you know is the greatest?”

He replied: “Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all.”

He said: “May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!”

Salmān wrote to Abū al-Dardāʾ: “Goodness does not lie in having abundant wealth and children. Rather, goodness lies in having abundant knowledge and great forbearance.”

The addition of knowledge to knowledge, willing to willing, and power to power resembles the joining of continuous bodies, as when water is added to water and its amount increases. Yet this is a continuous quantity, not a discrete one, unlike dirhams.

“The guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me are like rain that falls upon a land…”—to the end of the hadith.

Allah also says:

“He sent down water from the sky, and valleys flowed according to their capacity,”

through to His words:

“Thus does Allah set forth examples.”

Whatever the Lord, Exalted is He, has created, He sees; and He hears the voices of His servants. All rational people agree that what is nonexistent cannot be seen.

The Sālimiyyah, such as Abū Tālib al-Makkī and others, did not say that it is seen as something subsisting independently. They said only that the Lord sees it within Himself, even though it has no existence in the nonexistent thing itself. Thus, they take the object of vision to be its conceptual representation subsisting within the knower

translated_text:
, which is not sheer nonexistence.

Although they erred in some of what they said, they did not say that sheer nonexistence, which is nothing at all, can be seen; no rational person would say this. In reality, when something is seen, it is only its conceptual representation that is seen, not the thing itself. When this question was raised, Abū al-Shaykh al-Asbahānī instructed people to refrain from discussing it. Before a thing comes into existence, it is not seen; after it ceases to exist, it is not seen. It is seen only while it exists. This is perfection in seeing. Likewise, the voices of His servants are heard when they exist, not after they have faded away or before they arise. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“And say, ‘Work, for Allah will see your deeds, as will His Messenger and the believers.’”

He also says:

“Then We made you successors in the land after them, so that We might see how you would act.”

Section

Allah, Exalted is He, sent the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—as guidance and mercy to all worlds. Just as He sent him with knowledge, guidance, and proofs drawn from reason and revelation, He also sent him to show kindness and mercy to people without seeking anything in return, and to be patient in the face of the harm they inflict

and to endure it. Thus He sent him with knowledge, generosity, and forbearance—a knowledgeable guide, generous and benevolent, forbearing and forgiving. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“And indeed, you guide to a straight path—the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth. Surely, to Allah all matters return.”

He, Exalted is He, also says:

“A Book We have sent down to you so that you may bring people out of darkness into light, by their Lord’s permission, to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“And thus We have revealed to you a spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Scripture was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants.”

There are many similar passages. He also says:

“Say, ‘I ask you for no reward for it.’”

And He says:

“Say, ‘Whatever reward I may have asked of you is yours. My reward rests with Allah alone.’”

And He says:

“Say, ‘I ask you for no reward for it.’”

He thus possesses knowledge, gives guidance, reforms hearts, and directs them toward what will set them right in this world and the Hereafter, without seeking anything in return. This is the description of all the messengers; each says:

“I ask you for no reward for it.”

Hence the man mentioned in Surah Yā-Sīn said:

“O my people, follow the messengers. Follow those who ask you for no reward and are themselves rightly guided.”

This is also the path of those who follow him, as Allah says:

“Say, ‘This is my path: I call to Allah with clear insight—I and those who follow me.’”

As for those who oppose them, Allah says of those who claim affiliation with them while practicing religious innovation:

“Indeed, many rabbis and monks devour people’s wealth unjustly and turn people away from the path of Allah.”

These people took their wealth and barred them from Allah’s path—the opposite of what the Messenger did. What, then, of those who are worse than these, such as pagan scholars, sorcerers, and soothsayers? They devour people’s wealth unjustly and turn people away from Allah’s path even more than the rabbis and monks do. Yet Allah, Glorified is He, says:

“Indeed, many rabbis and monks…”

Thus, not all of them are like this. Rather, He says elsewhere:

“And you will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers to be those who say, ‘We are Christians.’ That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.”

He also says in describing the Messenger:

“Nor does he withhold knowledge of the unseen.”

There are two readings here. According to the reading bi-zanīn (“suspected”), the meaning is that he is not suspected of falsehood concerning the unseen; rather, he is truthful and trustworthy in what he reports. According to the reading bi-danīn (“withholding”), the meaning is that he is not miserly, imparting it only in return for payment, like those who demand payment for what they know. Thus, Allah describes him as speaking the truth, neither lying nor concealing it. He has described the People of the Book, by contrast, as making it into sheets which they display while concealing much, and as exchanging it for a paltry price.

“I have been forbidden to recite the Quran while bowing or prostrating. When bowing, magnify the Lord; when prostrating, strive earnestly in supplication, for then your supplications are likely to be answered.”

When he raises his head, he praises Allah, saying:

“Allah hears whoever praises Him. Our Lord, to You belongs all praise.”

Thus, he praises Him during this standing just as he praises Him during the first standing when reciting the Mother of the Quran. Praising Allah and affirming His oneness take precedence over magnification alone. This is why al-Fātihah encompasses these meanings: its beginning is praise and its middle is glorification. Then, while bowing, one magnifies the Lord, whereas while standing, one praises Him, extols Him, and glorifies Him. This shows that magnification alone is subordinate to His being praised and worshipped. For He loves to be praised and worshipped, and magnification must accompany this, since it necessarily entails magnifying Him.

Magnification, however, may be detached from praise and worship, according to the principle of the Jahmiyyah. Such magnification is not commanded, nor does it make a servant a believer, a worshipper, or obedient.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh Ibn al-Khatīb al-Rāzī assigns majesty to attributes of negation and honor to affirmative attributes, calling the former “attributes of majesty” and the latter “attributes of honor.” This, however, is his own terminology, not what is meant in His words:

“And the Face of your Lord, possessed of majesty and honor, will remain.”

And His words:

“Blessed is the Name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honor.”

In the codex of the people of Syria, the wording is: “Blessed is the Name of your Lord, possessed of majesty and honor,” with dhū al-jalāl wa-l-ikrām. This is the reading of Ibn ‘Āmir. Thus, the name itself is described as possessing majesty and honor. In all other codices and in the reading of the majority, the wording is dhī al-jalāl (“possessed of majesty”), referring to the One named Himself.

In the earlier verse, “And the Face of your Lord, possessed of majesty and honor, will remain,” it is His Face—glorified is He—that is described as possessing these qualities. This necessarily entails that He Himself possesses majesty and honor. For if His Face possesses majesty and honor, this points to His being so, just as, if His name possesses majesty and honor, this points to the One named.

This makes clear that what is meant is that He deserves to be revered and honored. For the name itself is glorified and mentioned, while what is intended is the One named. The name itself does nothing: it neither bestows honor nor performs any other act. Hence, the Quran does not attribute any acts or blessings to the name.

Rather, it says:

“Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High.”

“Blessed is the Name of your Lord.”

And similar expressions. For Allah’s name is blessed, and blessing is attained through it. The servant glorifies the Name of his Lord, the Most High, saying:

“Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.”

This is like His words:

“Say, ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever name you call upon, to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.’”

The supplicant says, “O Allah,” or “O Most Merciful,” intending the One named. His words “Whichever” mean whichever of the two names you invoke; invoking the name is invoking the One it names.

This is what those among Ahl al-Sunnah who said, “The name is the One named,” intended. They meant that when a name is invoked or mentioned, it is the One named who is intended. When someone praying says, “Allah is the Greatest,” he has mentioned his Lord’s name, intending the One named. They did not mean that the utterance itself is the actual entity existing outside the mind. The absurdity of this is obvious to anyone who understands it: if that were so, anyone who said “fire” would have his tongue burned. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point is that majesty and honor are like sovereignty and praise, and like love and veneration. This applies to both affirmative and negative attributes, for every negation entails

an affirmation. Pure negation, however, contains no praise. This exposes the error of those who assign one of the two to negation and the other to affirmation, especially those among the Jahmiyyah who deny love of Him and affirm no attributes of His that call for love and praise. Rather, they affirm only what entails subjugation, such as power. Thus, they have believed in part and disbelieved in part, and have deviated concerning His names and signs to the extent that they have rejected the truth. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Section

In the first revelation, Allah Most High says:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created.”

And He says:

“Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous.”

In both places, He refers to Himself through a possessive construction that makes the expression definite and indicates that He is known to those addressed. For the Lord Most High is known to the servant without inferring His existence from the fact that He created. Although created things constitute evidence and point to the Creator, He is known through the natural disposition before this inference is made. Knowledge of Him is innate, implanted in the natural disposition—necessary, self-evident, and primary. And His command, “Read,” although addressed first to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is

an address to everyone, whether His words,

“Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous,”

are addressed to humanity in general—with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, being the first to hear this address, or one of those it addresses—or specifically to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as has been suggested regarding comparable passages. For example, His words,

“Whatever good comes to you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself,”

have been understood as addressed either to him or to humanity generally. There are other such examples. Even if the address is understood as directed to him, it is established that commands and prohibitions addressed to him also address his community, unless there is evidence that they apply exclusively to him.

This makes clear that the words of Allah Most High,

“So if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to you, ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you,”

also encompass others besides him. Indeed, many commentators have said: “The address is directed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but others are intended.” That is, they are the ones intended to ask because of their doubts, whereas he was not intended to ask, since he had no doubt.

There is no question that this does not preclude his being addressed and intended by the address. Indeed, this is what the wording explicitly states, so it is not permissible to say that the address did not include him. Moreover, the address does not command him to ask unconditionally; rather, he is commanded to do so if he has any doubt. This does not entail that he had any doubt, nor that he was commanded to ask

unconditionally; rather, he was commanded to do so if such doubt existed. A ruling dependent on a condition does not apply when that condition is absent.

Likewise, concerning His words,

“The truth is from your Lord, so never be among those who doubt,”

and His words,

“And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites,”

and similar passages, many commentators say that the address is directed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but others are intended. That is, others might doubt and obey those people, and so are forbidden to do so, whereas he would neither doubt nor obey them. Yet even assuming this to be so, he too is addressed by these words and is subject to this prohibition.

Allah, glorified be He, has forbidden him to commit what He has made unlawful: associating partners with Him, speaking about Him without knowledge, wrongdoing, and acts of indecency. Through Allah’s prohibition of these things and his obedience to Allah in this regard, he became deserving of an immense reward. Were it not for the prohibition and his obedience, he would not have deserved that reward.

It is not necessary that someone who receives commands and prohibitions be a person whose obedience is in doubt and who might disobey the Lord—or disobey Him altogether and never obey Him. Rather, Allah commanded the angels while knowing that they would obey Him, and He commands the prophets while knowing that they will obey Him. Likewise, everything in which the believers obey Him is something He has commanded them to do, while knowing that they will obey Him.

Nor should it be said, “He has no need of the command.” Rather, it is through the command that he becomes obedient and deserving of an immense reward. A prohibition, however, presupposes that he is capable of doing what is forbidden and that, were he to will it, he would do it, so that when he refrains from it, he may be rewarded for doing so. It may also presuppose the presence of a motive urging him to do it, in which case he is forbidden to do it. Through the prohibition and Allah’s help in obeying it, he refrains from what he has been forbidden, even when a motive urging him towards it is present.

Likewise, concerning His words,

“Ask the Children of Israel,”

it has been said that this is a command to the Messenger, intended to include both him and the believers. It has also been said that it is a command to everyone accountable before Allah. Thus, His command in this surah,

“Read,”

is like His command at its conclusion,

“Prostrate and draw near,”

and His words,

“So do not oppress the orphan,”

“And do not rebuff the one who asks,”

“And proclaim the blessings of your Lord.”

This encompasses the entire Muslim community. His words,

“O you wrapped in garments,”

“Stand in prayer at night, except for a little,”

were addressed to all the believers. The same applies to His words,

“O you covered in your cloak,”

“Arise and warn,”

when the Messenger was commanded to convey the warning revealed to him. This is a collective obligation. The Muslim community must therefore convey what was revealed to him and warn as he warned. Allah Most High says:

“Why, then, should not a group from each section of them go forth to gain understanding of the religion and warn their people when they return to them, so that they may

be on their guard.” When the jinn heard the Quran,

“they returned to their people as warners.”

Since this is so, every person has knowledge of his Lord within his heart. When he is told,

“Read in the name of your Lord,”

he knows the Lord in whose name he is commanded to read, just as he knows that he is a created being. The existence of a created being necessarily implies a Creator and points to Him. This has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it has been explained that acknowledging and recognizing the Creator is innate and self-evident within human souls. Some people, however, may experience something that corrupts their innate disposition, so that they need rational inquiry to acquire this knowledge. This is the view of most people, including the most accomplished rational thinkers: knowledge is sometimes attained immediately and sometimes through rational inquiry, as several leading speculative theologians have acknowledged.

This verse also indicates that rational inquiry is not the first obligation. Rather, the first thing Allah enjoined upon His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was:

“Read in the name of your Lord.”

He did not say, “Engage in rational inquiry and seek proof until you come to know the Creator.” Likewise, this surah was the first thing the Prophet conveyed. Those to whom it was conveyed were therefore addressed by this verse before anything else, yet it did not command them to engage in rational inquiry or seek proof. Many speculative theologians, however, have maintained that the soul can acknowledge the Creator and affirm His existence only through rational inquiry.

original_text:
ثُمَّ كَثِيرٌ مِنْهُمْ جَعَلُوا ذَلِكَ نَظَرًا مَخْصُوصًا وَهُوَ النَّظَرُ فِي الْأَعْرَاضِ وَأَنَّهَا لَازِمَةٌ لِلْأَجْسَامِ فَيَمْتَنِعُ وُجُودُ الْأَجْسَامِ بِدُونِهَا.

 وَمَا لَا يَخْلُو عَنْ الْحَوَادِثِ أَوْ مَا لَا يَسْبِقُ الْحَوَادِثَ فَهُوَ حَادِثٌ. ثُمَّ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ اعْتَقَدَ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْمُقَدِّمَةَ بَيِّنَةٌ بِنَفْسِهَا بَلْ ضَرُورِيَّةٌ وَلَمْ يُمَيِّزْ بَيْنَ الْحَادِثِ الْمُعَيَّنِ وَالْمَحْدُودِ وَبَيْنَ الْجِنْسِ الْمُتَّصِلِ شَيْئًا بَعْدَ شَيْءٍ إمَّا لِظَنِّهِ أَنَّ هَذَا مُمْتَنِعٌ أَوْ لِعَدَمِ خُطُورِهِ بِقَلْبِهِ. لَكِنْ وَإِنْ قِيلَ هُوَ مُمْتَنِعٌ فَلَيْسَ الْعِلْمُ بِذَلِكَ بَدِيهِيًّا. وَإِنَّمَا الْعِلْمُ الْبَدِيهِيُّ أَنَّ الْحَادِثَ الَّذِي لَهُ مَبْدَأٌ مَحْدُودٌ كَالْحَادِثِ. وَالْحَوَادِثُ الْمُقَدَّرَةُ مِنْ حِينٍ مَحْدُودٌ فَتِلْكَ مَا لَا يَسْبِقُهَا فَهُوَ حَادِثٌ. وَمَا لَا يَخْلُو مِنْهَا لَمْ يَسْبِقْهَا فَهُوَ حَادِثٌ. فَإِنَّهُ إذَا لَمْ يَسْبِقْهَا كَانَ مَعَهَا أَوْ مُتَأَخِّرًا عَنْهَا. وَعَلَى التَّقْدِيرَيْنِ فَهُوَ حَادِثٌ. وَأَمَّا إذَا قَدَّرَ حَوَادِثَ دَائِمَةً شَيْئًا بَعْدَ شَيْءٍ فَهَذَا إمَّا أَنْ يُقَالَ هُوَ مُمْكِنٌ وَإِمَّا أَنْ يُقَالَ هُوَ مُمْتَنِعٌ.
 لَكِنَّ الْعِلْمَ بِامْتِنَاعِهِ يَحْتَاجُ إلَى دَلِيلٍ وَلَمْ تَعَلُّمِ طَائِفَةٍ مَعْرُوفَةٍ مِنْ الْعُقَلَاءِ قَالُوا:
 إنَّ الْعِلْمَ بِامْتِنَاعِ هَذَا بَدِيهِيٌّ ضَرُورِيٌّ وَلَا يَفْتَقِرُ إلَى دَلِيلٍ.
translated_text:
Many of them further restricted this to a particular form of rational inquiry: examining accidents and their inseparability from bodies, such that bodies cannot exist without them. They said:

“Whatever is never free of events that come into being, or does not precede such events, must itself have come into being.”

Some of them then believed this premise to be self-evident—indeed, necessarily known. They did not distinguish between a particular, bounded event and events considered as a kind, occurring continuously one after another, either because they thought the latter impossible or because it had never occurred to them. Yet even if it is said to be impossible, knowledge of its impossibility is not self-evident.

What is self-evident is only that an event with a definite beginning is like any other event that comes into being. As for events reckoned from a definite point in time, whatever does not precede them must itself have come into being. Whatever is never free of them does not precede them and must therefore have come into being. For if it does not precede them, it must exist either alongside them or after them. In either case, it must have come into being.

If, however, one supposes a perpetual succession of events, one after another, this must be said to be either possible or impossible. But knowledge of its impossibility requires proof. No known group of rational thinkers has said:

“Knowledge that this is impossible is self-evident and necessary, requiring no proof.”

translated_text:
Indeed, many people do not fully conceive of this. Whenever they conceive of an event that comes into being, they posit a starting point in their minds, then imagine something before it, then something before that—but only to finite limits, according to what their minds envisage. This is like the mind imagining one number after another: whatever it imagines is finite. Some people, when told of “beginningless eternity,” or that “this existed in beginningless eternity,” conceive of it in this way. This is mistaken. “Beginningless eternity” has no beginning, just as “endless eternity” has no end. Whatever limit the mind points to, beginningless eternity lies beyond it. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that those who said that knowledge of the Lord can be attained only through rational inquiry, and then said that it can be attained only through this particular inquiry, are the Jahmī and Qadarī speculative theologians and their followers. The early generations of the Muslim community, its leading scholars, and the majority of scholars, both speculative theologians and others, have agreed that these people are mistaken in making this particular form of inquiry obligatory and in claiming that knowledge of the Lord depends upon it. For it is necessarily known from the religion of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he neither made this obligatory upon the Muslim community nor commanded them to undertake it. Indeed, neither he nor any of the community’s early generations even followed this method to attain such knowledge. Now, concerning this rational inquiry—this argument—people hold three views.

original_text:
قِيلَ:

 وَقِيلَ:

 ثُمَّ مِنْ الْمُوجِبِينَ لِلنَّظَرِ مَنْ يَقُولُ:
 هُوَ أَوَّلُ الْوَاجِبَاتِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَقُولُ: بَلْ الْمَعْرِفَةُ الْوَاجِبَةُ بِهِ وَهُوَ نِزَاعٌ لَفْظِيٌّ.
 كَمَا أَنَّ بَعْضَهُمْ قَالَ:
 أَوَّلُ الْوَاجِبَاتِ الْقَصْدُ إلَى النَّظَرِ كَعِبَارَةِ أَبِي الْمَعَالِي.
 وَمِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ مَنْ قَالَ:
 بَلْ الشَّكُّ الْمُتَقَدِّمُ كَمَا قَالَهُ أَبُو هَاشِمٍ. وَقَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْأَقْوَالِ وَغَيْرِهَا فِي مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ.
translated_text:
One view is that it is obligatory and that knowledge depends upon it, as these people maintain.

Another view is that knowledge can be attained without it, but that it offers another path to knowledge. This is held by many who consider this method valid but do not regard it as obligatory, such as al-Khattābī, Judge Abū Yaʿlā, and Abū Jaʿfar al-Simnānī, the judge of Mosul and teacher of Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī. Al-Simnānī used to say: “Making rational inquiry obligatory is a remnant of Muʿtazilism that remained with Shaykh Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī.”

These are the people who do not regard this particular rational inquiry as obligatory. Some of them do not regard rational inquiry as obligatory at all, such as al-Simnānī, Ibn Hazm, and others. Others regard it as obligatory in general, such as al-Khattābī and Abū al-Faraj al-Maqdisī. Judge Abū Yaʿlā sometimes adopts one position and sometimes the other; indeed, at times he even maintains that this particular form of inquiry is obligatory, as do Abū al-Maʿālī and others.

Among those who consider rational inquiry obligatory, some say that it is the first obligation. Others say: “Rather, it is the knowledge that must be attained through it.” This is a merely verbal dispute.

Similarly, some have said that the first obligation is the intention to undertake rational inquiry, as expressed by Abū al-Maʿālī. Others among them have said: “Rather, it is the doubt that precedes it,” as Abū Hāshim maintained. These and other views have been discussed at length elsewhere.

 فَيُقَالُ لَهُمْ:
 وَلَيْسَ فِيمَا قَصَّ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا مِنْ أَخْبَارِ الرُّسُلِ أَنَّ مِنْهُمْ أَحَدًا أَوْجَبَهَا بَلْ هِيَ حَاصِلَةٌ عِنْدَ الْأُمَمِ جَمِيعِهِمْ.
وَلَكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ الرُّسُلِ افْتَتَحُوا دَعْوَتَهُمْ بِالْأَمْرِ بِعِبَادَةِ اللَّهِ وَحْدَهُ دُونَ مَا سِوَاهُ كَمَا أَخْبَرَ اللَّهُ عَنْ نُوحٍ وَهُودٍ وَصَالِحٍ وَشُعَيْبٍ. وَقَوْمُهُمْ كَانُوا مُقِرِّينَ بِالْخَالِقِ لَكِنْ كَانُوا مُشْرِكِينَ يَعْبُدُونَ غَيْرَهُ كَمَا كَانَتْ الْعَرَبُ الَّذِينَ بُعِثَ فِيهِمْ مُحَمَّدٌ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. وَمِنْ الْكُفَّار مَنْ أَظْهَرَ جَحُودَ الْخَالِقِ كَفِرْعَوْنَ حَيْثُ قَالَ {يَا أَيُّهَا الْمَلَأُ مَا عَلِمْتُ لَكُمْ مِنْ إلَهٍ غَيْرِي فَأَوْقِدْ لِي يَا هَامَانُ عَلَى الطِّينِ فَاجْعَلْ لِي صَرْحًا لَعَلِّي أَطَّلِعُ إلَى إلَهِ مُوسَى وَإِنِّي لَأَظُنُّهُ مِنَ
translated_text:
and it has been shown that all these views are mistaken, contrary to the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations and the leading scholars—indeed, they are also rationally unsound. This verse is among the evidence for that, for the first obligation Allah imposed upon His Messenger and the believers was what He commanded in His words:

“Recite in the name of your Lord who created.”

Those who maintain that knowledge can be attained only through rational inquiry argue: “If it could be attained otherwise, the obligation to attain it would lapse.” Judge Abū Bakr and others have stated this.

They may be answered as follows: Nothing in the accounts of the messengers that Allah has related to us indicates that any of them made this knowledge obligatory. Rather, all nations already possessed it.

Most messengers, however, began their call by commanding people to worship Allah alone and none besides Him, as Allah relates concerning Noah, Hūd, Sālih, and Shuayb. Their peoples acknowledged the Creator, but they associated partners with Him, worshipping others besides Him. Such was also the case with the Arabs among whom Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent.

Some unbelievers professed denial of the Creator, such as Pharaoh, who said:

“O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself. So, Hāmān, fire bricks for me and build me a lofty tower, so that I may look upon the God of Moses; indeed, I think he is one of

the liars.” He also said:

“I am your lord, the Most High.”

And he said to Moses:

“If you take a god other than me, I will surely imprison you.”

He also said:

“O Hāmān, build me a lofty tower so that I may reach the pathways—the pathways of the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses; indeed, I think he is a liar.”

Yet Allah commanded Moses to say what He relates in the Quran:

“And when your Lord called Moses, ‘Go to the wrongdoing people—the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?’ He said, ‘My Lord, I fear that they will deny me, and my chest tightens and my tongue is not fluent, so send for Aaron. They also have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me.’ He said, ‘No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. We are with you, listening. Go to Pharaoh and say, “We are messengers from the Lord of all worlds: send the Children of Israel with us.”’ Pharaoh said, ‘Did we not raise you among us as a child, and did you not spend years of your life among us? And you committed that deed of yours, and you were ungrateful.’ Moses said, ‘I did it then, when I was among those who were astray. So I fled from you when I feared you; then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers.’”

Pharaoh said, in denial and rejection:

“And what is the Lord of all worlds?”

Moses said:

“The Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, if you have certainty.”

“Pharaoh said to those around him, ‘Do you not hear?’ Moses said, ‘Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers.’ Pharaoh said, ‘This messenger of yours who has been sent to you is surely mad.’ Moses said, ‘The Lord of the east and the west and everything between them’”—and the following verses.

Some people have supposed that Pharaoh’s question, “And what is the Lord of all worlds?” was a question about the Lord’s essence, like someone asking for the definitions of things: “What is a human being? What is an angel? What is a jinni?” and so forth.

They said: “Since the One being asked about has no essence, Moses turned from answering the question to explaining how He may be known, saying: ‘The Lord of the heavens and the earth.’” This view, advanced by some later scholars, is false. Pharaoh’s question expressed denial and rejection. He was not asking about the essence of a Lord whose existence he acknowledged; rather, he denied and rejected Him. Hence, later in the exchange, he said:

“If you take a god other than me, I will surely imprison you.”

He also said:

“Indeed, I think he is a liar.”

His question thus expressed denial and rejection, as though he were saying: “The worlds have no Lord who could send you. Who, then, is this?” He was denying Him. Moses therefore made clear that Pharaoh and those present knew Him, and that His signs were manifest and clear, leaving no grounds for denying Him: “You merely deny with your tongues what you know in your hearts.” As Moses said to Pharaoh elsewhere:

“You know well that none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth has sent down these signs as clear proofs.”

And Allah Most High said:

“They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance. So see what was the end of those who spread corruption.”

Nor did Pharaoh ask, “And who is the Lord of all worlds?” For “who” asks about someone’s particular identity: it is used by someone who knows that the one being asked about belongs to the category of beings endowed with knowledge, but is unsure of that individual’s identity. Thus, one might ask a messenger known to have come from a human being, “Who sent you?”

“What,” however, asks about a description. He was saying: “What sort of thing is this? What is this that you have called ‘the Lord of all worlds’?” He said this in denial and rejection of Him. Since his question expressed denial, Moses answered that He was too well known to be denied and too evident to be doubted or questioned. He said:

“The Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that lies between them, if you have certainty.”

He did not say, “Certainty about such-and-such,” but left it unrestricted. Whatever certainty you have about anything, the foremost certainty is certainty about this Lord, as the messengers said to their peoples:

“Can there be any doubt about Allah?”

If you say, “We have no certainty about anything; rather, we have been deprived of all knowledge,” this is the claim of universal skepticism, and anyone making it is plainly lying. For knowledge is inseparable from every human being: every rational human being must possess some knowledge. For this reason,

the intellect has been defined as self-evident knowledge, which no rational person lacks.

Pharaoh’s statement, “Your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad,” exemplifies the slanders that those who reject the messengers direct against them. Whenever the messengers departed from the customs that their opponents considered praiseworthy, they accused them of madness. They openly professed denial of the Creator, or misgivings and doubt about Him. Such was the condition of the people generally and the character of their religion, which they considered good. Their only god, whom they obeyed, was Pharaoh. Thus he said:

“Your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad.”

Moses therefore made it clear to him: it is you who have been deprived of beneficial reason, and you are more deserving of this description. He said:

“The Lord of the east and the west and all that lies between them, if you use your reason.”

For reason necessarily entails certain, self-evident knowledge, foremost among which, in the innate human disposition, is acknowledgment of the Creator. Having first explained that whoever is certain of anything is certain of Him—and certainty about anything is inseparable from reason—he then explained that acknowledging Him is inseparable from reason.

What is praiseworthy, however, is beneficial knowledge upon which its possessor acts. If he does not act upon it, he is said to have no reason. It is likewise said of someone who does not follow what he knows with certainty:

translated_text:
“He has no certainty.” For certainty can mean knowledge firmly established in the heart, and it can also mean acting upon that knowledge. Thus, only someone in whose heart both knowledge and action are firmly established is described as “certain.” Pharaoh’s people did not follow what they knew, so they had neither reason nor certainty.

Moses’ words imply both points: if you have certainty, you already know Him; and if you have reason, you already know Him. If you claim that you have neither certainty nor reason, and that the same is true of your people, then you are admitting that you lack the distinguishing quality of a human being. Someone in such a condition is unfit to make the claim to divinity that you make. Moreover, this claim of yours is false, for you are certain of Him, as the Most High said:

“They denied them, though their souls were certain of them, out of injustice and arrogance.”

You also possess reason by which you know Him, but your desire for supremacy and corruption on earth prevents you from following what reason requires. In this sense, you have no reason, just as the inhabitants of the Fire said:

“If only we had listened or used our reason, we would not be among the inhabitants of the Blaze.”

The Most High also said of the disbelievers:

“Or do you think that most of them listen or use their reason? They are only like cattle; rather, they are further astray.”

The Most High said of Pharaoh and his people:

“He made fools of his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a people

who were defiantly disobedient.” A person who is easily swayed is a fool who does not act upon his knowledge but follows his desires. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that none of the messengers began calling his people by saying: “You are commanded to seek knowledge of the Creator, so reflect and reason until you come to know Him.” They were not initially charged either with acquiring this knowledge itself or with examining the proofs leading to it, since their hearts already knew and acknowledged Him. Every child is born upon the innate disposition, but influences arise that alter it. When a person is reminded, he recalls what is within his innate disposition. Hence Allah said when addressing Moses:

“Both of you speak to him gently, so that perhaps he may be reminded”

of the knowledge within his innate disposition by which he knows his Lord, recognizes His blessings and kindness towards him, and knows his own dependence upon Him. This calls him to faith.

“Or become fearful”

of the punishment of which he is warned; this too calls him to faith. As the Most High said:

“Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition.”

Wisdom makes the truth known, so that it is accepted on account of its truth, without resistance. Whoever encounters resistance from his own desires is admonished through encouragement and warning. Knowledge of the truth calls the one who possesses it to follow it, for truth is beloved to the innate disposition. It is dearer to it, more exalted in its eyes, and more delightful to it than falsehood, which has no reality. The innate disposition does not love such falsehood.

If the truth and knowledge of it do not move him to follow it, he is warned of the consequences of denial and disobedience and the punishment they entail, for the soul naturally fears punishment. Every living being flees what harms it, unlike what benefits it. Some people, however, follow their desires, choosing what is inferior over what is superior. Likewise, some deny the punishment of which they are warned or deliberately disregard it so that they can do what they desire. For if a person believed in it and kept it in mind, he would not urge his soul to pursue its desires. There must therefore be some heedlessness and ignorance for him to follow them. Hence everyone who disobeys Allah is ignorant, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The purpose here is to draw attention to the fact that His words,

“Read in the name of your Lord,”

indicate that the Lord is already known to those addressed and that the innate disposition acknowledges Him. This is also indicated by His words,

“And when your Lord brought forth from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves,”

and the rest of the verse, which has been discussed at length elsewhere. Likewise, the messengers’ words,

“Can there be any doubt about Allah?”

express a negation: there is no doubt about Allah. This is a question calling for acknowledgment: it calls upon the nations to affirm what they already acknowledge—that there is no doubt about Allah. Thus, it is a question calling for acknowledgment.
