فَإِنَّ حَرْفَ الِاسْتِفْهَامِ إذَا دَخَلَ عَلَى حَرْفِ النَّفْيِ كَانَ تَقْرِيرًا كَقَوْلِهِ:
 
{أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ}
 
{أَلَمْ نَجْعَلْ لَهُ عَيْنَيْنِ}
 
{أَلَمْ يَأْتِهِمْ نَبَأُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ}
 وَمِثْلُهُ كَثِيرٌ. بِخِلَافِ اسْتِفْهَامِ فِرْعَوْنَ فَإِنَّهُ اسْتِفْهَامُ إنْكَارٍ لَا تَقْرِيرَ إذْ لَيْسَ هُنَاكَ إلَّا أَدَاةُ الِاسْتِفْهَامِ فَقَطْ وَدَلَّ سِيَاقُ الْكَلَامِ عَلَى أَنَّهُ إنْكَارٌ.
فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 إذَا كَانَتْ مَعْرِفَتُهُ وَالْإِقْرَارُ بِهِ ثَابِتًا فِي كُلِّ فِطْرَةٍ فَكَيْفَ يُنْكِرُ ذَلِكَ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ النُّظَّارِ نُظَّارِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَهُمْ يَدَّعُونَ أَنَّهُمْ الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الْأَدِلَّةَ الْعَقْلِيَّةَ عَلَى الْمَطَالِبِ الْإِلَهِيَّةِ؟
 فَيُقَالُ أَوَّلًا:
 أَوَّلُ مَنْ عُرِفَ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ بِإِنْكَارِ هَذِهِ الْمَعْرِفَةِ هُمْ أَهْلُ الْكَلَامِ الَّذِي اتَّفَقَ السَّلَفُ عَلَى ذَمِّهِ مِنْ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْقَدَرِيَّةِ. وَهُمْ عِنْدَ سَلَفِ الْأُمَّةِ مِنْ أَضَلِّ الطَّوَائِفِ وَأَجْهَلِهِمْ. وَلَكِنْ انْتَشَرَ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ أُصُولِهِمْ فِي الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ الَّذِينَ يُوَافِقُونَ السَّلَفَ عَلَى كَثِيرٍ مِمَّا خَالَفَهُمْ فِيهِ سَلَفُهُمْ الْجَهْمِيَّة. فَصَارَ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ يَظُنُّ أَنَّ هَذَا قَوْلٌ صَدَرَ فِي الْأَصْلِ عَنْ عُلَمَاءِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ إنَّمَا صَدَرَ أَوَّلًا عَمَّنْ ذَمَّهُ أَئِمَّةُ الدِّينِ وَعُلَمَاءُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ.
الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ قَدْ يَقُومُ بِنَفْسِهِ مِنْ الْعُلُومِ وَالْإِرَادَاتِ وَغَيْرِهَا مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ مَا لَا يَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ قَائِمٌ بِنَفْسِهِ فَإِنَّ قِيَامَ الصِّفَةِ بِالنَّفْسِ غَيْرُ
translated_text:
For when an interrogative particle precedes a negative particle, the question calls for acknowledgment, as in His words:

“Have We not expanded your breast for you?”

“Have We not given him two eyes?”

“Has the news of those before them not reached them?”

There are many similar examples. Pharaoh’s question, by contrast, expresses denial rather than calling for acknowledgment: it contains only an interrogative particle, and the context indicates that it expresses denial.

If it is asked:

“If knowledge and acknowledgment of Him are inherent in every innate disposition, how can so many speculative thinkers, both Muslim and non-Muslim, deny this, when they claim to be the very ones who establish rational proofs concerning theological questions?”

The first answer is:

The first people known in Islam to deny this knowledge were the adherents of the speculative theology that the early generations unanimously condemned: the Jahmiyyah and the Qadariyyah. The early generations of this ummah regarded them as among the most misguided and ignorant sects. Yet many of their principles spread among later thinkers who agree with the early generations on many matters in which their own Jahmī predecessors opposed those generations. Some people thus came to suppose that this position originally came from Muslim scholars. That is not so: it first came from those whom the leading authorities of the religion and the Muslim scholars condemned.

The second answer is:

A person may possess knowledge, intentions, and other attributes without knowing that they are present within him. For an attribute’s presence in the soul is distinct from

original_text: شُعُورِ صَاحِبِهَا بِأَنَّهَا قَامَتْ بِهِ. فَوُجُودُ الشَّيْءِ فِي الْإِنْسَانِ وَغَيْرِهِ غَيْرُ عِلْمِ الْإِنْسَانِ بِهِ. وَهَذَا كَصِفَاتِ بَدَنِهِ فَإِنَّ مِنْهَا مَا لَا يَرَاهُ كَوَجْهِهِ وَقَفَاهُ. وَمِنْهَا مَا يَرَاهُ إذَا تَعَمَّدَ النَّظَرَ إلَيْهِ كَبَطْنِهِ وَفَخِذِهِ وَعَضُدَيْهِ. وَقَدْ يَكُونُ بِهِمَا آثَارٌ مِنْ خِيلَانٍ وَغَيْرِ خِيلَانٍ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَحْوَالِ وَهُوَ لَمْ يَرَهُ وَلَمْ يَعْرِفْهُ لَكِنَّ لَوْ تَعَمَّدَ رُؤْيَتَهُ لَرَآهُ. وَمِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ لَا يَسْتَطِيعُ رُؤْيَةَ ذَلِكَ لِعَارِضِ عَرَضَ لِبَصَرِهِ مِنْ العشى أَوْ الْعَمَى أَوْ غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ. كَذَلِكَ صِفَاتُ نَفْسِهِ قَدْ يَعْرِفُ بَعْضَهَا وَبَعْضُهَا لَا يَعْرِفُهُ. لَكِنَّ لَوْ تَعَمَّدَ تَأَمُّلَ حَالِ نَفْسِهِ لَعَرَفَهُ. وَمِنْهَا مَا لَا يَعْرِفُهُ وَلَوْ تَأَمَّلَ لِفَسَادِ بَصِيرَتِهِ وَمَا عَرَضَ لَهَا. وَاَلَّذِي يُبَيِّنُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ الْأَفْعَالَ الِاخْتِيَارِيَّةَ لَا تُتَصَوَّرُ إلَّا بِإِرَادَةِ تَقُومُ بِنَفْسِ الْإِنْسَانِ. وَكُلُّ مَنْ فَعَلَ فِعْلًا اخْتِيَارِيًّا وَهُوَ يَعْرِفُهُ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يُرِيدَهُ كَاَلَّذِي يَأْكُلُ وَيَشْرَبُ وَيَلْبَسُ وَهُوَ يَعْرِفُ أَنَّهُ يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يُرِيدَهُ. فَالْفِعْلُ الِاخْتِيَارِيُّ يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ بِغَيْرِ إرَادَةٍ. وَإِذَا تَصَوَّرَ الْفِعْلَ الَّذِي يَفْعَلُهُ وَقَدْ فَعَلَهُ لَزِمَ أَنْ يَكُونَ مُرِيدًا لَهُ وَقَدْ تَصَوَّرَهُ. وَإِذَا كَانَ مُرِيدًا لَهُ وَقَدْ تَصَوَّرَهُ امْتَنَعَ أَنْ لَا يُرِيدَ مَا تَصَوَّرَهُ وَفَعَلَهُ.
translated_text:
the person’s awareness that it is present within him. Something’s existence within a person or elsewhere is distinct from his knowledge of it. This is like his bodily attributes: some he does not see, such as his face and the back of his neck; others he sees if he deliberately looks at them, such as his abdomen, thigh, and upper arms. His upper arms may bear moles and other marks, or exhibit other conditions, which he has neither seen nor known about. Yet if he deliberately looked, he would see them. Some people cannot see such things because their eyesight has been affected by dimness of vision, blindness, or some other impairment.

Likewise, he may know some attributes of his soul but not others. Yet if he deliberately reflected on the state of his soul, he would recognize them. Some, however, he would not recognize even upon reflection, because of the corruption of his insight and the impairments that have affected it.

What makes this clear is that voluntary actions are inconceivable without an intention present within the person’s soul. Anyone who performs a voluntary action while knowing what he is doing must intend it. Someone who eats, drinks, or dresses while knowing that he is doing so must intend to do so. A voluntary action cannot occur without an intention. If he has conceived of the action he performs and has actually performed it, he must intend it, having conceived of it. If he intends it and has conceived of it, it is impossible for him not to intend what he has conceived of and performed.

original_text: فَالْإِنْسَانُ إذَا قَامَ إلَى صَلَاةٍ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّهَا الظُّهْرُ فَمِنْ الْمُمْتَنِعِ أَنْ يُصَلِّيَ الظُّهْرَ وَهُوَ يَعْلَمُ هَذَا لَمْ يَنْسَهُ وَلَا يُرِيدُ صَلَاةَ الظُّهْرِ. وَكَذَلِكَ الصِّيَامُ إذَا تَصَوَّرَ أَنَّ غَدًا مِنْ رَمَضَانَ وَهُوَ مُرِيدٌ لِصَوْمِ رَمَضَانَ امْتَنَعَ أَنْ لَا يَنْوِيَ صَوْمَهُ. وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا أَهَلَّ بِالْحَجِّ وَهُوَ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ مُهِلٌّ بِهِ امْتَنَعَ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ مُرِيدًا لِلْحَجِّ. وَكَذَلِكَ الْوُضُوءُ إذَا عَلِمَ أَنَّهُ يَتَوَضَّأُ لِلصَّلَاةِ وَهُوَ يَتَوَضَّأُ امْتَنَعَ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ مُرِيدًا لِلْوُضُوءِ. وَمِثْلُ هَذَا كَثِيرٌ نَجِدُ خَلْقًا كَثِيرًا مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ دَعْ الْعَامِّيَّةَ يَسْتَدْعُونَ النِّيَّةَ بِأَلْفَاظِ يَقُولُونَهَا وَيَتَكَلَّفُونَ أَلْفَاظًا وَيَشُكُّونَ فِي وُجُودِهَا مَرَّةً بَعْدَ مَرَّةٍ وَيَخْرُجُونَ إلَى ضَرْبٍ مِنْ الْوَسْوَسَةِ الَّتِي يُشْبِهُ أَصْحَابُهَا الْمَجَانِينَ. وَالنِّيَّةُ هِيَ الْإِرَادَةُ. وَهِيَ الْقَصْدُ وَهِيَ مَوْجُودَةٌ فِي نُفُوسِهِمْ لِوُجُودِهَا فِي نَفْسِ كُلِّ مَنْ يُصَلِّي فِي ذَلِكَ الْمَسْجِدِ وَالْجَامِعِ وَمَنْ تَوَضَّأَ فِي تِلْكَ الْمَطْهَرَةِ. أُولَئِكَ يَعْلَمُونَ هَذَا مِنْ نُفُوسِهِمْ وَلَمْ يَحْصُلْ لَهُمْ وَسْوَاسٌ وَهَؤُلَاءِ ظَنُّوا أَنَّ النِّيَّةَ لَمْ تَكُنْ فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ يَطْلُبُونَ حُصُولَهَا مِنْ قُلُوبِهِمْ.
translated_text:
Thus, when a person stands to pray, knowing that it is the noon prayer, it is impossible for him to perform that prayer while knowing this, without having forgotten it, yet not intend to perform it. The same applies to fasting: if he recognizes that tomorrow is a day of Ramadan and wishes to fast Ramadan, it is impossible for him not to intend to fast that day. Likewise, if he announces his entry into Hajj, knowing that this is what he is doing, it is impossible for him not to intend Hajj. Similarly, if he knows that he is performing ablution for prayer and is actually doing so, it is impossible for him not to intend ablution.

There are many such examples. We find a great many scholars, let alone ordinary people, trying to summon intention through words they utter. They labor over verbal formulas and repeatedly doubt whether the intention is present, descending into a kind of obsessive doubt whose sufferers resemble the insane.

Yet intention is simply the will to act—one’s purpose. It is present within them, for it is present within everyone who prays in that mosque or congregational mosque, and everyone who performs ablution at that ablution facility. The former recognize this within themselves and have not developed obsessive doubts, whereas the latter suppose that intention is absent from their hearts and seek to bring it about within them.

translated_text:
Yet they know that stating the intention aloud is not obligatory; what is obligatory is simply that the will to act be present in the heart. It is already present, but despite this they believe it is not. If one of them is told, “The intention is already present in your heart,” he will not accept it because of the false belief he holds, which contradicts his innate disposition.

Likewise, love for Allah and His Messenger is present in the heart of every believer. So long as he is a believer, he cannot banish it from his heart. Signs of his love for Allah and His Messenger become apparent when someone begins to insult and disparage the Messenger, or to insult Allah and speak of Him in an unworthy manner. The believer becomes far angrier at this than he would if his own father and mother were insulted.

Nevertheless, many adherents of speculative theology and rationalist thought have denied love in relation to Allah, saying, “It is impossible for Him to love or to be loved.” They made this a fundamental tenet of religion, adding, “In opposition to the advocates of divine indwelling”—as though only the advocates of divine indwelling affirmed that Allah loves. Yet it is well known that this is the religion of the prophets and messengers, the Companions, their successors, and all believers. The Quran and Sunnah establish this, as we have explained at length elsewhere.

This love for Allah and His Messenger is present in the hearts of most of those who deny it—indeed, in the heart of every believer—even if he denies it because of a misconception that has occurred to him.

Likewise, knowledge of Allah is present in these people’s hearts. Those who denied love for Him are the very ones who said, “Knowledge of Him can be attained only through rational reflection.” Thus they denied the knowledge and love of Him present in their innate dispositions and hearts. This denial may then prevent them from recognizing these within themselves. The knowledge and love once present in a person’s heart may also disappear, for the innate disposition can become corrupted: it may disappear, or it may remain present yet go unseen.

“For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but the hearts within the breasts.”

Allah Most High also says:

“So direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth—in accordance with the natural disposition with which Allah created mankind. There is no changing Allah’s creation. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know. Turn to Him in repentance, fear Him, establish prayer, and do not be among those who associate partners with Him.”

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Every child is born upon the innate disposition. Then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to an intact offspring. Do you see any mutilation in it?”

Abū Hurayrah would then say: “Recite, if you wish: ‘The natural disposition with which Allah created mankind.’”

The innate disposition necessarily entails knowing Allah, loving Him, and singling Him out as the most beloved of all things

 . فأخبر أَنَّهُ خَلَقَهُمْ حُنَفَاءَ وَذَلِكَ يَتَضَمَّنُ مَعْرِفَةَ الرَّبِّ وَمَحَبَّتَهُ وَتَوْحِيدَهُ. فَهَذِهِ الثَّلَاثَةُ تَضَمَّنَتْهَا الْحَنِيفِيَّةُ وَهِيَ مَعْنَى قَوْلِ 
" لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ "
. فَإِنَّ فِي هَذِهِ الْكَلِمَةِ الطَّيِّبَةِ الَّتِي هِيَ 
{كَشَجَرَةٍ طَيِّبَةٍ أَصْلُهَا ثَابِتٌ وَفَرْعُهَا فِي السَّمَاءِ}
 فِيهَا إثْبَاتُ مَعْرِفَتِهِ وَالْإِقْرَارِ بِهِ. وَفِيهَا إثْبَاتُ مَحَبَّتِهِ فَإِنَّ الْإِلَهَ هُوَ الْمَأْلُوهُ الَّذِي يَسْتَحِقُّ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَأْلُوهًا؛ وَهَذَا أَعْظَمُ مَا يَكُونُ مِنْ الْمَحَبَّةِ. وَفِيهَا أَنَّهُ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا هُوَ. فَفِيهَا الْمَعْرِفَةُ وَالْمَحَبَّةُ وَالتَّوْحِيدُ. وَكُلُّ مَوْلُودٍ يُولَدُ عَلَى الْفِطْرَةِ وَهِيَ الْحَنِيفِيَّةُ الَّتِي خَلَقَهُمْ عَلَيْهَا. وَلَكِنَّ أَبَوَاهُ يُفْسِدَانِ ذَلِكَ فَيُهَوِّدَانِهِ وَيُنَصِّرَانِهِ وَيُمَجِّسَانِهِ وَيُشْرِكَانِهِ.
translated_text:
to the servant. This is the affirmation of Allah’s oneness, and this is the meaning of the statement, “There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.” As an explanatory wording states: “Every child is born upon this religion.” Another narration reads: “Upon the religion of Islam.”

In Sahīh Muslim, ‘Iyād ibn Himār reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘I created My servants as pure monotheists, but the devils led them astray, forbade them what I had made lawful for them, and commanded them to associate with Me that for which I had sent down no authority.’”

He thus states that He created them as pure monotheists. This entails knowing the Lord, loving Him, and affirming His oneness. These three are encompassed by pure monotheism, which is the meaning of the statement, “There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.”

For this good word, which is “like a good tree whose root is firmly fixed and whose branches reach into heaven,” affirms knowing Him and acknowledging Him. It also affirms loving Him, for a deity is an object of worship who deserves to be worshipped, and this is the highest degree of love. It further affirms that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him. Thus it encompasses knowledge, love, and the affirmation of His oneness.

Every child is born upon the innate disposition: the pure monotheism upon which He created them. But the child’s parents corrupt this, making him a Jew, a Christian, a Magian, or one who associates partners with Allah.

" الشَّهْوَةُ الْخَفِيَّةُ "
.
 قَالَ شَدَّادُ بْنُ أَوْسٍ:
 يَا بَقَايَا الْعَرَبِ إنَّ أَخْوَفَ مَا أَخَافُ عَلَيْكُمْ الرِّيَاءُ وَالشَّهْوَةُ الْخَفِيَّةُ.
 قِيلَ لِأَبِي دَاوُد السجستاني:
 مَا الشَّهْوَةُ الْخَفِيَّةُ؟
 قَالَ:
 حُبُّ الرِّيَاسَةِ. فَهِيَ خَفِيَّةٌ تَخْفَى عَلَى النَّاسِ وَكَثِيرًا مَا تَخْفَى عَلَى صَاحِبِهَا. بَلْ كَذَلِكَ حُبُّ الْمَالِ وَالصُّورَةِ فَإِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ قَدْ يُحِبُّ ذَلِكَ وَلَا يَدْرِي. بَلْ نَفْسُهُ سَاكِنَةٌ مَا دَامَ ذَلِكَ مَوْجُودًا فَإِذَا فَقَدَهُ ظَهَرَ مِنْ
translated_text:
Likewise, they make him a Jahmī, causing him to deny the knowledge of the Lord, love for Him, and affirmation of His oneness that are within his heart. He then seeks that knowledge through evidence, while denying love altogether. The affirmation of Allah’s oneness that encompasses love is denied by those who do not understand it; only His oneness as Creator is affirmed. The polytheists used to acknowledge this oneness and this association of partners with Allah. Thus, his parents make him a polytheist, a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian. This hadith and people’s views concerning it have been discussed at length elsewhere.

Another illustration of how much of a person’s inner state can remain hidden from him, without his awareness, is that many people harbour a latent love of leadership without knowing it. Indeed, a person may be sincere in his worship while his faults remain hidden from him. Much has been said about this, and it is well known. This is why it has been called “the hidden desire.”

Shaddād ibn Aws said:

“O remaining Arabs! What I fear most for you is showing off and the hidden desire.”

Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī was asked, “What is the hidden desire?”

He replied, “Love of leadership.”

It is hidden: concealed from others and often even from the person who harbours it. The same is true of love of wealth and physical form: a person may love such things without knowing it. His soul remains at ease as long as what he loves is present; but when he loses it, what emerges from

his soul’s anguish and devastation reveals the love that was already there. Love necessarily entails awareness; thus, the soul necessarily has an awareness of certain things. Yet a person may be unaware of this within himself, especially since Satan conceals things from him. His sins, too, remain as a stain upon his heart. Allah Most High says:

“No! Rather, their hearts have been stained by what they used to earn.”

“No! Indeed, that Day they will be veiled from their Lord.”

Al-Tirmidhī and others relate, through al-Qa‘qā‘ ibn Hakīm, from Abū Sālih, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a servant sins, a black mark is placed upon his heart. If he repents, desists, and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished clean. But if he sins further, the mark grows until it covers his heart. That is the stain of which Allah says: ‘No! Rather, their hearts have been stained by what they used to earn.’”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “A good and authentic hadith.”

Another example is His saying, Most High:

“They say, ‘Our hearts are covered.’ Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little do they believe.”

He also says:

“Indeed, when those who fear Allah are touched by a suggestion from Satan, they remember, and at once they see clearly.”

When those who fear Allah are afflicted by this passing suggestion that circles about their hearts, they recall what they already knew. The suggestion then vanishes, and they see the truth that was already known to them, but which the suggestion had prevented them from seeing. Allah Most High says:

“But their brethren draw them further into error, and never desist.”

Thus, the brethren of

the devils are drawn further into their error by the devils. “And never desist”: the devils never desist from supporting and encouraging them, nor do those people desist from their error. In that state of error, they fail to perceive what they already know and what is firmly rooted in their innate disposition; instead, they forget it. Thus, the messengers come only to remind the innate disposition of what it already knows, to strengthen and reinforce that knowledge, and to remove whatever alters the innate disposition. The messengers were sent to affirm and perfect the innate disposition, not to change or transform it. Perfection is attained through the innate disposition perfected by the revealed law.

Section

This forgetfulness—a person’s forgetting himself and what lies within him—results from his forgetting his Lord and what He has revealed. Allah Most High says:

“And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. It is they who are defiantly disobedient.”

He also says concerning the hypocrites:

“They forgot Allah, so He abandoned them.”

And He says:

“Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; and so today you will be forgotten.”

His words, “And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves,” indicate that their forgetting Allah caused them to forget themselves, and that when they forgot Allah, He punished them by making them forget themselves.

translated_text:
Their forgetting themselves entails their turning away, their heedlessness, and their loss of awareness of what they previously knew about their own condition. It also entails their neglecting their own best interests. Thus, they do not remember themselves in a way that benefits and reforms them; had they remembered Allah, they would have remembered themselves. This is the reverse of the saying:

“Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.”

Some people attribute this to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Yet these are not the Prophet’s words, nor does this saying appear in any of the books of hadith, nor is any chain of transmission known for it. However, the following is reported in some earlier books—if the report is authentic:

“O human being, know yourself, and you will know your Lord.”

Whether the meaning of this statement is sound or unsound, its wording cannot be used as authoritative proof, for it has not been established as the statement of anyone protected from error. If, however, it is interpreted in a sound sense, the soundness of that meaning is known regardless of whether this wording conveys it or not. The statement that is firmly established is what appears in the Quran, namely His words:

“And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves.”

This indicates that forgetting the Lord necessarily leads to forgetting oneself. Accordingly, whoever remembers Allah and does not forget Him will remember himself. For if he

translated_text:
were to forget himself regardless of whether he remembered Allah or forgot Him, his forgetting himself would not be caused by his forgetting his Lord. Since the verse indicates that a person’s forgetting himself is caused by his forgetting his Lord, it follows that whoever remembers his Lord does not experience this forgetfulness of himself. Remembrance includes recalling what one already knows. Thus, whoever recalls what he knows of his Lord recalls what he knows of himself.

He was born with the innate disposition that entails knowing his Lord, loving Him, and affirming His oneness. If he does not forget his Lord, whom he has known, but instead remembers Him in a manner that entails loving Him, knowing Him, and affirming His oneness, he remembers himself. He then perceives the knowledge of Allah, love for Him, and affirmation of His oneness that were previously within him.

When the adherents of innovation—the Jahmiyyah and others like them—turned away from the prescribed remembrance of Allah, which was present in the innate disposition and brought by the revealed Law, and which includes knowing Him, loving Him, and affirming His oneness, they forgot Allah in this respect. He therefore made them forget themselves in this respect: they forgot the innate knowledge, innate love, and innate affirmation of His oneness that were within them.

A number of Quran commentators have said:

“They forgot Allah” means that they neglected Allah’s command; “so He made them forget themselves” means their own best interests, since they had sent ahead no good for themselves. This is the wording used by a number of them, including al-Baghawī.

The wording used by others, including Ibn al-Jawzī, is:

“When they failed to obey Him.”

Both said that “They forgot Allah” means that they neglected Allah’s command.

Such interpretations also occur frequently in the words of those who offer a general statement conveying a meaning indicated by the verse, without explaining it as fully as it deserves. Their statement, “They neglected Allah’s command,” means that they neglected to obey Him; the first is thus made identical to the second. Yet Allah, glorified is He, said:

“And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves.”

Here there are two things: their forgetting Allah, and then their forgetting themselves, which was their punishment.

If it is said, “The second is identical to the first, but merely elaborates on what was stated generally, as in His words, ‘How many towns We have destroyed! Our punishment came upon them by night or while they were taking their midday rest.’ Here, the two describe the same thing,” the answer is:

He did not say, “They forgot Allah, so they forgot their own best interests,” such that one could say that the two are identical. Rather, He said:

“They forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves.”

Thus, He caused them to forget themselves. If this were identical to the first, He would have mentioned something that excused them, rather than something by which He punished them.

If the second were identical to the first, then “They forgot Allah” would mean that they neglected to obey Him, and He was the One who made them forget to do so. The unsoundness of this interpretation, both in wording and in meaning, is evident.

If, however, it were said that “They forgot Allah” means that they forgot His command, and “so He made them forget” means that He made them forget to act in obedience to Him—that is, to call that obedience to mind—this would be closer to the meaning, and the first instance of forgetting would retain its literal sense. For whoever forgets Allah’s command itself does not obey Him.

But they interpreted forgetting Allah as abandoning His command. His command, which is His speech, is not within their power such that they could abandon it; what they abandon is acting upon it. Thus, “command” here means what is commanded.

Unless it is said that by abandoning His command they mean abandoning faith in it: when they abandoned faith, He consequently caused them to abandon acting upon it. This, too, is a weak interpretation. If abandoning faith means only abandoning affirmation of its truth, that alone suffices as disbelief and sin. Abandoning action upon it should not then be regarded as the punishment; rather, the former is more grievous. If abandoning faith means abandoning both affirmation and action, then this is abandoning obedience, as discussed above.

Their error arose from seeking to interpret the servant’s forgetting in light of what has been said about the Lord’s forgetting. Since the latter was interpreted as abandonment, they interpreted the former in the same way. This is unsound, for forgetting, as the opposite of remembering, can undoubtedly occur in a servant. A person turns away from what he has been commanded to do until he forgets it and no longer remembers it. There is therefore no need to interpret his forgetting as abandonment while remaining mindful and aware.

As for the Lord, exalted is He, nothing that contradicts His attributes of perfection can apply to Him—glorified and exalted is He. Yet interpreting His forgetting the disbelievers as mere abandonment is open to question. Moreover, this interpretation was offered concerning His words, exalted is He:

“Thus did Our signs come to you, but you forgot them.”

that is, you abandoned acting upon them. Here, however, He says, “They forgot Allah,” and one does not say of Allah, “They abandoned Him.”

Section

His words, “Who created” and “Created man from a clinging substance,” explain how He is made known through what is already known of creation in general and the creation of man in particular. This is among the ways in which the innate disposition recognizes Him, as explained earlier.

Once a person recognizes that He is the Creator, it is necessarily known that the Creator must possess power. Indeed, every action performed by an agent requires strength and power—even the actions of inanimate things. The falling of stones and water, and the movement of fire, occur through a force within them. Likewise, plants move through a force within them, and every living creature, whether an animal or otherwise, acts through a power within it. The same applies to human beings and others.

Creation is the greatest of all acts, for none but Allah has the power to create. Thus, the power to create is greater than every other power and has no equal among the powers of created beings. Teaching by the pen also necessarily entails power. Thus, both creation and teaching necessarily entail power.

Likewise, both necessarily entail knowledge. Anyone who teaches another must himself know what he teaches; otherwise, it would be impossible for him to teach someone else what he himself does not know. Thus, He who taught all things—human beings and others—what they did not know must all the more know what He taught them. Creation also necessarily entails knowledge, as the Most High says:

“Does He who created not know, while He is the Subtle, the All-Aware?”

This is because creation necessarily entails will. Bringing something into being with particular characteristics and a particular measure, rather than otherwise, can only occur through a will that selects one possibility over another. Will, in turn, necessarily entails knowledge: one wills only what one is aware of and conceives in one’s mind. Will without awareness is impossible.

Moreover, the very act of creating man brings into being this human being, one of the wonders of creation. His creation displays such precision and perfection as to astound the mind. An act performed with precision and perfection can proceed only from one who knows what he has done. This is self-evident. Creation thus indicates knowledge in both these ways.

In Surah al-Mulk, He says:

“And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.”

This explains the subtle wisdom found in created things, which involves bringing matters to their intended ends by the subtlest means. As Joseph, peace be upon him, said: “Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what

Once it is established that He is powerful and knowing, this necessarily entails that He is living. Likewise, will necessarily entails life. A living being who does not hear, see, or speak would be characterized by the opposite attributes: blindness, deafness, and muteness. This is impossible with respect to the Lord Most High. He must therefore possess hearing, sight, and speech.

Will either serves a wise purpose or does not. If it does not serve a wise purpose, it is foolishness, and He is far exalted above that. He must therefore be wise. Furthermore, He either intends to benefit His creatures and show them kindness, intends merely to harm and torment them, or intends neither, but wills whatever He wills, regardless of whether it brings benefit or harm. The second possibility would entail evil and injustice, from which the Lord is far exalted; the third would entail foolishness and frivolity. It follows necessarily that He, Most High, is merciful just as He is wise, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

There are several ways of establishing His attributes of perfection. One is what we have already indicated: action necessarily entails power and other attributes. Some speculative thinkers begin by establishing power, others knowledge, and others will. These are the methods followed by many speculative theologians.

These attributes are inferred from action as such. This is the approach of those who do not distinguish between one effect and another, such as Jahm ibn Safwān and his followers. They affirm neither wisdom nor mercy, since action as such does not necessarily entail either. Yet they establish knowledge on the basis of well-ordered, perfectly executed acts. Likewise, mercy is established through beneficial acts, and wisdom through praiseworthy ends.

However, they contradict themselves when they infer knowledge from order and precision, since these indicate knowledge only if the agent acts for an intended end. They say that He acts without a wise purpose, yet then infer knowledge from the orderliness of His acts. This is a contradiction. {وَقَالُوا مَنْ أَشَدُّ مِنَّا قُوَّةً}

{أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّ اللَّهَ الَّذِي خَلَقَهُمْ هُوَ أَشَدُّ مِنْهُمْ قُوَّةً.}

translated_text:
on the basis of self-evident knowledge of this, or because their failure to demonstrate it would imply incapacity. Yet they demonstrate it only if the agent intends to manifest them as proof of the prophets’ truthfulness. Thus, when they say that He does nothing for any purpose, they contradict themselves.

Another method of establishing the attributes is to infer the cause from its effect: whoever produces something perfect has a greater claim to perfection. The third method is a fortiori reasoning, based on precedence and superiority: if perfection is established for a contingent, created being that has come into existence, then the necessarily existent, eternal Creator has a greater claim to it. The Quran employs all three methods.

An example of inferring from an effect the greater perfection of its cause is His statement, Most High:

“They said, ‘Who is greater than us in strength?’”

Allah, Most High, said:

“Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is greater than them in strength?”

Likewise, all the strength and might found in created beings indicate that Allah is greater in strength and might. Whatever knowledge they possess indicates that Allah is more knowledgeable, and whatever knowledge and life they possess indicate that Allah has a greater claim to knowledge and life.

And this is a method acknowledged by rational people generally. Even the philosophers say: “Every perfection in an effect comes from its cause.” As for a fortiori reasoning, examples include His statement:

“To Allah belongs the highest description,”

and His statement:

“He sets forth for you an example drawn from yourselves: do you have, among those whom your right hands possess, any partners in what We have provided for you, such that you are equal in it, fearing them as you fear one another?”

These and similar passages indicate that every perfection free of deficiency established for an originated, created, contingent being belongs with greater reason to the eternal, necessarily existent Creator, because He has a greater claim to perfection by virtue of His superiority. The earlier method, by contrast, rests on His being the One who made that being perfect and bestowed those attributes upon it.

His name “the Most High” is explained in these two senses. It is explained as meaning that He is higher than all others in rank, and thus has a greater claim to the attributes of perfection. It is also explained as meaning that He is high above them in subjugation and mastery: that is, He exercises power over them, while they are subject to His power. This entails His being their Creator and Lord. Both meanings entail that He Himself is above everything, with nothing above Him, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You are the First, and nothing is before You; You are the Last, and nothing is after You. You are the Manifest, and nothing is above You; You are the Inward, and nothing is nearer than You.”

translated_text:
Thus, nothing is before Him or after Him, above Him or nearer than Him, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, declared in praising his Lord. Otherwise, if He were supposed to be beneath any created thing, that would be an imperfection, and that thing would be higher than Him.

And if it were said that He is neither within the world nor outside it, that would amount to denying Him. He is exalted above this. This is what it means for Him to be the Most High, the Highest. Moreover, when used without qualification, the expressions “the Most High” and “highness” are used in the Quran only in this sense, which necessarily entails the other two senses. They are not used to signify mere power or mere superiority.

The term “highness” conveys being above. Other verbs, too, indicate being above when construed with the preposition denoting elevation, as in His statement:

“Then He rose over the Throne.”

This indicates His being high above the Throne. The early generations explained “rising” in terms that convey ascending above the Throne, as al-Bukhārī records in his Sahīh from Abū al-Āliyah concerning His words, “Then He rose”: he said, “He ascended.”

Ibn Abī Hātim and others likewise transmitted this through their chains of narration. He transmitted it through Ādam ibn Abī Iyās, from Abū Ja‘far, from Abū al-Rabī‘, from Abū al-Āliyah: concerning “Then He rose,” he said, “He ascended.”

translated_text:
Al-Bukhārī also said:

“Mujāhid said concerning His words, ‘Then He rose over the Throne’: ‘He rose above the Throne.’”

Yet one may speak of being “high above something” (‘alā ‘alā) or “exalted beyond something” (‘alā ‘an). The latter occurs in several places in the Quran, though with the verb ta‘ālā (“He is exalted”), as in His words:

“Glorified and exalted is He, far above what they say!”

“Knower of the unseen and the seen; exalted is He above what they associate with Him.”

A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere. The point here is that each statement—that He created, and that He is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen—indicates these two ways of affirming the attributes, just as it directed us to the first way: inferring them from His acts.

His words, “the Most Generous,” entail that He surpasses all others in generosity. Generosity is a comprehensive term encompassing every excellent quality. This therefore entails that He has a greater claim to every praiseworthy quality, and praiseworthy qualities are attributes of perfection. Thus, He is more deserving of being described as beneficent towards creation and merciful, and of being attributed with wisdom, power, knowledge, life, and all such perfections.

The same applies to His words, “He created.” The Creator is eternal, without beginning, self-sufficient, necessarily existent in Himself, and the Self-Subsisting Sustainer. It is known that He has a greater claim to the attributes of perfection than a created, originated, contingent being. This is from the standpoint of a fortiori reasoning. As for reasoning from the effect, the Creator of another being

 هُوَ نَاطِقٌ.
translated_text:
that He has made living, knowing, capable, hearing and seeing has a greater claim to be living, knowing, powerful, hearing and seeing.

And “the Most Generous,” “who taught by the pen,” “taught man what he did not know.” He thus made man knowledgeable, and one who possesses knowledge must be alive. He also honoured him by granting him power, hearing and sight. The Most Generous, who made another knowledgeable, has a greater claim to possess knowledge Himself. The same applies to all other attributes of perfection and praiseworthy qualities.

This is reasoning from a particular created being, whereas the first argument reasons from creation in general. Thus, this establishes the attributes as a matter of necessary knowledge, without strained argumentation. The same applies to reasoning from superiority and a greater claim to perfection: the Lord has a greater claim to perfection than the created being.

These methods are so evident that non-Muslims, whether followers of religious traditions or otherwise, also employ them. Christians, for example, used this method to affirm that Allah subsists in Himself so that He may speak. However, they called Him a “substance” and went astray by making the attributes three—the hypostases.

They said:

“We found that things are divided into substances and things that are not substances. Since substance is the higher of the two kinds, we said: ‘He is a substance.’ Then we found that substances are divided into living and non-living, and that the living is more perfect, so we said: ‘He is living.’ We found that living beings are divided into the nātiq (endowed with reason or speech) and the non-nātiq, so we said: ‘He is nātiq.’”

{عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسَانَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ}
 فَإِنَّ الْأَنْبِيَاءَ مِنْ النَّاسِ. فَقَدْ دَلَّتْ هَذِهِ الْآيَاتُ عَلَى جَمِيعِ الْأُصُولِ الْعَقْلِيَّةِ فَإِنَّ إمْكَانَ النُّبُوَّاتِ هُوَ آخِرُ مَا يُعْلَمُ بِالْعَقْلِ. وَأَمَّا وُجُودُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَآيَاتِهِمْ فَيُعْلَمُ بِالسَّمْعِ الْمُتَوَاتِرِ مَعَ أَنَّ قَوْلَهُ 
{عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسَانَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ}
 يَدْخُلُ فِيهِ إثْبَاتُ تَعْلِيمِهِ لِلْأَنْبِيَاءِ مَا عَلَّمَهُمْ فَهِيَ تَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِمْكَانِ وَالْوُقُوعِ.
translated_text:
Likewise, it may be said to them regarding the other attributes of perfection: things are divided into those that possess power and those that do not, and those that possess power are more perfect. We have discussed at length what is correct and what is mistaken in their statements in the book we entitled The Correct Response to Those Who Altered the Religion of the Messiah. The purpose here is to draw attention to how this verse, and these verses—which were the first to be revealed—point to the foundations of religion.

His saying, “Taught man what he did not know,” indicates His power to teach man what He has taught him, despite the various deficiencies found in humankind. If He is able to impart such knowledge, then all the more is He able to teach the prophets what He has taught them. This is included in His saying, “Taught man what he did not know,” for the prophets are human beings.

These verses thus indicate all the rational foundations, for the possibility of prophethood is the furthest point that reason can establish. As for the existence of the prophets and their signs, this is known through mass-transmitted reports. Moreover, His saying, “Taught man what he did not know,” includes the affirmation that He taught the prophets what He taught them. These verses therefore indicate both the possibility and the actual occurrence of prophethood.

translated_text:
We have mentioned elsewhere that affirming His transcendence rests on two principles. The first is that He is free from any imperfection that contradicts His perfection. Whatever establishes His perfection also establishes His freedom from any imperfection that contradicts it. This makes clear that His freedom from imperfection is known through reason, contrary to the claim of a group of speculative theologians that it can be known only through revelation.

We have explained elsewhere that the rational methods they have followed—inferring the temporal origination of bodies from accidents—establish neither His existence, nor any of His attributes of perfection, nor His freedom from any imperfection. Thus, they have no basis for ruling out any imperfection in His case. They themselves acknowledge that, unlike attributes, any action is possible for Him. Yet their approach to the attributes is unsound and contradictory, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The second principle is that nothing is like Him in His attributes of perfection. The Quran is replete with affirmations of these two principles: it affirms the attributes of perfection in detail and declares Him free from any likeness to others. Glory be to Him! Exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers say.

Section

His words, “In the name of your Lord who created,” and His words, “Who taught by the pen,” “taught man what he did not know,” establish His actions and His speech. Creation is His action, and teaching includes teaching what He has revealed, as He says:

“The Most Merciful taught the Quran, created man, and taught him articulate speech.”

His words, “by the pen,” include teaching His speech, which is written with the pen. The fact that this was revealed in the opening of the surah in which He sent down His speech and taught His Prophet His speech, which is written with the pen, shows that the verse encompasses this. For the occasion prompting unrestricted and general wording must necessarily fall within its scope.

If, then, this indicates that He created and spoke—and He has said, “He created man”—it is known both through reason and through the wording that the created human being is distinct from the Lord’s act of creating him. The same applies to His creation of anything else. Those who disputed this did so only because of a misconception that occurred to them, as discussed later and elsewhere. Otherwise, they do not dispute that khalaqa (“he created”) is a verb with a verbal noun, as in: khalaqa (“he created”), yakhluqu (“he creates”), khalqan (“creation”). The human being is the object of the action denoted by the verbal noun—the “created being”—not the action itself.

translated_text:
A verbal noun may, however, be used to denote the object of the action, as in “a dirham of the ruler’s minting.” An example is His statement, “This is Allah’s creation,” meaning here: this is what Allah has created. The discussion is not about khalq (“creation”) in the sense of “a created thing,” but about khalq in the sense of the action itself, expressed by the verbal noun, as in khalaqa (“he created”), yakhluqu (“he creates”), khalqan (“creation”). Likewise, He says:

“Your creation and resurrection are only like those of a single soul.”

“He creates you in your mothers’ wombs, stage after stage of creation.”

“I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to their own creation.”

Since creation is His action, it occurs by His will, for it is impossible for His action to occur without His will. Whatever occurs by His will cannot be beginningless in its individual instance, although its kind may be beginningless. Since the creation of anything that comes into being must have a complete cause necessitating its occurrence, it follows that He has always been characterized by voluntary acts subsisting in Him. Yet if it is established that another created thing existed before this one, it is thereby established that He is characterized by one act of creation after another. Likewise with speech: He speaks by His will.

It is impossible for Him to lack the attribute of speech and then acquire it, for two reasons:

First, this would deny His perfection, and speech is an attribute of perfection.

Second, it is impossible for this to come about. For one who lacks speech cannot

translated_text:
make himself capable of speech. One who lacks knowledge cannot make himself knowledgeable, and one who is not alive cannot make himself alive. These attributes are thus inseparable from His essence.

Likewise, one who is not a creator cannot make himself a creator. For if He were unable to create, making Himself a creator would be an even greater act, and would therefore be impossible all the more certainly: making Himself a creator entails the existence of something created. For this reason, since He is able to make a human being an agent, He is the Creator of what that human being does. Thus, if He were to make Himself a creator, He would be the Creator of whatever He made Himself create. If, then, it is supposed that His being a creator in beginningless eternity is impossible, it would be impossible for Him to make Himself a creator in any way whatsoever. The assertion that action was impossible for Him in beginningless eternity entails its being impossible for Him always.

Yet the verse establishes that He created. It is therefore known that He has always been able to create, that creation has always been possible for Him, and that creation has always been possible and within His power. This invalidates the foundational premise of the Jahmiyyah. Moreover, if He has the power to do so, that which necessitates it is not something separate and external to Him; rather, it is from Himself. It is therefore impossible for Him to make Himself willing after not having been so. It follows that He has always possessed will and power. When power and will are present, the object of that power must necessarily exist.

And the speculative theologians who dispute this say, “He has always had power over what will come to be.”

They are told: “Power can exist only if its object is possible. If His power is everlasting, has it always been possible for Him to bring about what lies within His power?”

They say: “No; rather, possibility—the possibility of action—came into being.”

This contradicts their affirmation of power. If, instead, they say, “Rather, the possibility exists,” it becomes clear that action has always been possible. This establishes the possibility of infinitely many things within the Lord’s power existing.

Thus, if He has always possessed power, action has always been possible, and this possible action has actually occurred in the time that continues without end, then consider what necessitates the existence of things within His power as a class—His will, for example. Either its existence in beginningless eternity is impossible, in which case action must also be impossible, although we have already shown that it is possible. Moreover, if its existence were impossible, it would always remain impossible, since there is nothing there to make it possible, let alone bring it into existence. It is well known that its coming into existence after not existing must have something that necessitates it.

If, on the other hand, its existence in beginningless eternity is possible, then the existence of this possible thing depends on nothing other than His essence, and His essence is sufficient to bring it about. It follows that He has always possessed will. The same applies to all attributes of perfection: once their possibility in beginningless eternity is established, it follows that

they have existed from beginningless eternity. For if they did not exist, their existence would be impossible, since in beginningless eternity there is nothing besides Himself to necessitate their existence. If they are possible, and He Himself is their fully sufficient cause, their existence from beginningless eternity must be necessary.

This is among the things demonstrating that He has always been living, knowing, powerful, willing, speaking, and acting, since nothing but His essence necessitates these things, and His essence alone suffices for them. It follows that the kind has no beginning and that He has always spoken whenever He wills. Individual instances of the kind, however, occur successively, in accordance with possibility and wisdom.

For this reason, it has been explained elsewhere that, in reality, no possible thing has its existence and nonexistence equally balanced. Rather, either what necessitates its existence is present, making its existence necessary, or it is absent, making its existence impossible. Whatever attributes the Lord possesses, His possession of them is necessary; whatever attributes He does not possess, His possession of them is impossible. Whatever He wills comes to be, and its existence is necessary; whatever He does not will does not come to be, and its existence is impossible. Thus, a possible thing necessarily exists when the fully sufficient determining factor is present, and its existence is impossible without it.

and His words,

“Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen,”

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said:
“Allah has always possessed knowledge and speech and has always been forgiving.”

He also said:
“Allah has always been One who speaks whenever He wills.”

Section

Just as the first verse revealed of the Quran indicates this, so does the greatest verse in the Quran, but more expansively and fully. This is the Verse of the Throne, as established in the Sahīh:

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, “Abū al-Mundhir, do you know which verse of Allah’s Book that you know is the greatest?”

He replied, “Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.”

He said, “May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!”

Here He begins the verse with the word “Allah,” which is greater than His words “and your Lord.” For this reason, He also begins the greatest surah in the Quran with it, saying:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

And He said:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.”

This is because the polytheists had taken a god other than Him, even though they acknowledged that He is the Creator. In His words “created,” He did not explicitly deny the existence of another creator, since that was already understood. No one has ever affirmed another creator in the unrestricted sense—one who created everything, mankind and all else. Divinity, however, is a different matter. Allah Most High said:

“They said, ‘Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act.’”

And He Most High said:

“The leaders among them went off, saying, ‘Carry on, and remain steadfast in worshipping your gods. Indeed, this is something intended.’”

And He Most High said:

“Do you truly testify that there are other gods besides Allah? Say, ‘I do not testify.’ Say, ‘He is but One God.’”

And He Most High said:

“Say, ‘If there were gods alongside Him, as they claim, they would surely have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.’”

Thus, they sought other gods alongside Him, but did not affirm another creator alongside Him. He therefore said in the greatest of verses:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.”

He mentions this in three places in the Quran, each of which contains one of the three foundations of religion: Allah’s oneness, the messengers, and the Hereafter. These are the foundations with which He sent all the messengers. He tells us that the polytheists disbelieve in them, as in His words:

“And do not follow the desires of those who deny Our signs, who do not believe in the Hereafter, and who set up equals to their Lord.”

So here He said:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.”

He coupled this with the affirmation that there is no deity except Him. In Āl ‘Imrān, He added:

“He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, and He revealed the Torah and the Gospel previously, as guidance for mankind, and He revealed the Criterion.”

This is belief in the scriptures and the messengers.

And He said in Tā Hā:

“On that Day, intercession will be of no benefit except from one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and whose words He approves. He knows what is before them and what is behind them, but they do not encompass Him in knowledge. And all faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence. Whoever bears wrongdoing will have failed.”

Section

Among the greatest foundations is a person’s knowledge of how Allah has described Himself. This includes the attributes pertaining to His actions, as in His words in this surah:

“Who created.”

“Created man from clinging clots.”

Creation is mentioned in many places, as are His other actions. These are of two kinds. One is an action that takes a direct object, such as “created,” which necessarily implies something created. The same applies to “provided,” as in His words:

“Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then will bring you to life

—can any of those you associate with Him do any of these things?”

The same applies to guiding, leading astray, teaching, raising up, sending, and addressing. Likewise, He tells us:

“He completed them as seven heavens in two days.”

“He fashioned them into seven heavens.”

And He says:

“We built the heaven with might.”

“He who made the earth a resting place for you and the sky a canopy, and sent down water from the sky, bringing forth fruits thereby as provision for you.”

And in another verse:

“He who made the earth a settled abode for you and the sky a canopy, formed you and perfected your forms, and provided you with good things.”

Such passages are very numerous in the Quran.

Examples of intransitive actions include His words:

“Then He rose towards the heaven.”

“Then He rose over the Throne.”

“Are they waiting for anything but for Allah to come to them in canopies of clouds?”

“Are they waiting for anything but for the angels to come to them, or for your Lord to come, or for some of your Lord’s signs to come?”

And His words:

“And your Lord comes, with the angels, rank upon rank.”

As for the first kind, Muslims agree that it is attributed to Allah and that He is the One who creates and provides; this is not an attribute of any of His creatures. But does an act—namely, creation—subsist in Him, or is the act identical with what is done, and creation identical with what is created? The second view is that acts subsist in Him. This is the position of the early Muslim generations and the majority of those who affirm the attributes. “takwīn” (bringing into being).

This is also the position of the Karrāmiyyah, the Hishāmiyyah, and similar groups, as well as the early followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. It is also the later of al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā’s two positions.

Now, if it is said that the act of creation is distinct from the created thing and subsists in the Lord, is it a beginningless act of creation inseparable from the Lord’s essence, even though created things have a beginning, as the followers of Abū Hanīfah and others maintain? Or is it an act of creation that originated in His essence when the genus of created things originated? Or is it one act of creation after another? There are three views. One or the other of these views is held by the imams of the Sunnah and hadith and the majority of their scholars. It is also the position of groups among the speculative theologians, including the Karrāmiyyah, the Hishāmiyyah, and others. Thus, whoever says, “He speaks by His will and choice, with speech that subsists in His essence,” can say, “He acts by His choice and will, with an act that subsists in His essence.”

Among those who affirm that matters subject to His choice subsist in His essence, some accept the argument from accidents as valid, along with its use to establish that bodies have a beginning. These include the Karrāmiyyah and later Hanafi, Māliki, Hanbali, and Shāfiʿī scholars. Others do not accept it as valid, such as the imams of the early Muslim generations and the imams of the Sunnah and hadith, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Bukhārī, and others.

 يَقُومُ بِنَفْسِهِ.

 وَإِذَا قَامَ بِمَحَلِّ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَقُومَ بِالْخَالِقِ أَوْ بِغَيْرِهِ وَالثَّانِي بَاطِلٌ لِأَنَّهُ لَوْ قَامَ بِغَيْرِهِ لَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الْغَيْرُ هُوَ الْخَالِقَ لَا هُوَ.
 وَهَذَا رَدٌّ عَلَى طَائِفَةٍ ثَانِيَةٍ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّهُ يَقُومُ بِالْمَخْلُوقِ. وَإِذَا قَامَ بِالْخَالِقِ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ قَدِيمًا أَوْ مُحْدَثًا وَلَوْ كَانَ قَدِيمًا لَلَزِمَ قِدَمُ الْمَخْلُوقِ فَإِنَّ الْخَلْقَ وَالْمَخْلُوقَ مُتَلَازِمَانِ. فَوُجُودُ خَلْقٍ بِلَا مَخْلُوقٍ مُمْتَنِعٌ وَكَذَلِكَ وُجُودُ تَأْثِيرٍ بِلَا أَثَرٍ. وَإِنْ كَانَ مُحْدِثًا فَهُوَ بَاطِلٌ لِوَجْهَيْنِ. أَحَدُهُمَا أَنَّهُ يَلْزَمُ قِيَامُ الْحَوَادِثِ بِهِ. وَالثَّانِي أَنَّ ذَلِكَ الْخَلْقَ الْحَادِثَ يَفْتَقِرُ إلَى خَلْقٍ آخَرَ وَيَلْزَمُ التَّسَلْسُلُ وَمَعْمَرُ بْنُ عَبَّادٍ الْتَزَمَ التَّسَلْسُلَ وَجَعَلَ لِلْخَلْقِ خَلْقًا وَلِلْخَلْقِ خَلْقًا
translated_text:
This issue is referred to as “the question of causation”: does it have real existence or not? Is causation distinct from both the cause and the effect, or not? Al-Rāzī’s statements on this differ, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The principal argument of those who say that the act of creation is identical with the created thing, and that causation is simply the existence of the effect—affirming nothing beyond this—is as follows: if creation and causation were something distinct from the created thing itself and the effect, they would either subsist in a substrate or not. The latter is invalid, since qualities cannot subsist independently.

This is a reply to a group among the Muʿtazilah who said that it subsists independently.

They continue: if it subsists in a substrate, it must subsist either in the Creator or in something else. The latter is invalid, because if it subsisted in something else, that other thing would be the creator, rather than Him.

This is a reply to a second group, who say that it subsists in the created thing. If it subsists in the Creator, it must be either beginningless or originated. If it were beginningless, this would entail that the created thing is beginningless, since the act of creation and the created thing necessarily accompany one another. An act of creation without a created thing is impossible, as is causation without an effect. If it is originated, this is invalid for two reasons. First, it would entail that originated events subsist in Him. Second, that originated act of creation would require another act of creation, entailing an infinite regress. Muʿammar ibn ʿAbbād accepted the infinite regress and posited an act of creation for the act of creation, and another act of creation for that act of creation

translated_text:
but not within Allah’s essence, and held that all this occurred at one and the same time. This, then, is their principal argument. Each group that disagreed with them rejected one of its premises. Those who allowed creation to subsist independently or in the created thing rejected those two premises. As for the majority, each answered according to his own position.

Some said:

Rather, creation and bringing into being are beginningless, just as, according to you, will is beginningless. Affirming that will is beginningless does not entail the prior existence of what is willed. Likewise, creation and bringing into being are beginningless without this entailing the prior existence of the created thing.

This objection is binding upon the Kullābiyyah, whether Ashʿarīs or others, and they have no answer to it. It does not, however, bind those who deny that a particular act of willing is beginningless—indeed, deny that will is beginningless, as the Jahmiyyah and Muʿtazilah maintain—or who affirm that will as a kind is beginningless, as maintained by the leading scholars of Ahl al-Hadīth and those philosophers, theologians, and others who agree with them.

But the proponent of this view is told:

This beginningless bringing into being must either occur by His will or not occur by His will. If it occurs without His will, it follows that He created the creation without willing it. If it occurs by His will, it follows that something beginningless is willed, which is false. Were this valid, it would be possible for the world to be beginningless while also being created

 الْإِرَادَةُ مُسْتَلْزِمَةٌ لِلْمُرَادِ وَالْخَلْقُ مُسْتَلْزِمٌ لِلْمَخْلُوقِ. وَمَا ذُكِرَ حُجَّةٌ عَلَى هَؤُلَاءِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ. فَإِنَّ الْإِرَادَةَ وَالْخَلْقَ مِنْ الْأُمُورِ الْإِضَافِيَّةِ وَثُبُوتُ إرَادَةٍ بِلَا مُرَادٍ وَخَلْقٌ بِلَا مَخْلُوقٍ مُمْتَنِعٌ.
 لَكِنَّ الْمُنَازِعَ يَقُولُ:
 تُوجَدُ الْإِرَادَةُ وَالْخَلْقُ وَيَتَأَخَّرُ الْمُرَادُ الْمَخْلُوقُ فَيُقَالُ لِهَؤُلَاءِ تَقُولُونَ: تُوجَدُ الْإِرَادَةُ أَوْ الْخَلْقُ مَعَ الْإِرَادَةِ وَلَا يُوجَدُ لَا الْمُرَادُ وَلَا الْمَخْلُوقُ. ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ بِمَا لَا يَتَنَاهَى مِنْ تَقْدِيرِ الْأَوْقَاتِ يُوجَدُ الْمُرَادُ الْمَخْلُوقُ مِنْ غَيْرِ سَبَبٍ. وَهَذَا مَعْلُومُ الْبُطْلَانِ فِي بِدَايَةِ الْعُقُولِ. فَإِنَّ الْإِرَادَةَ أَوْ الْخَلْقَ كَانَ مَوْجُودًا مَعَ الْقُدْرَةِ. فَإِنْ كَانَ هَذَا مُؤَثِّرًا تَامًّا اسْتَلْزَمَ وُجُودَ الْأَثَرِ وَلَزِمَ وُجُودُ الْأَثَرِ عِنْدَ وُجُودِ الْمُؤَثِّرِ التَّامِّ. فَإِنَّ الْأَثَرَ 
" مُمْكِنٌ "
 وَالْمُمْكِنُ يَجِبُ وُجُودُهُ عِنْدَ وُجُودِ الْمُرَجِّحِ
translated_text:
through a beginningless act of creation, by a beginningless will. It is known that this is false. Hence, all those who say, “The Quran is beginningless,” say that He spoke independently of His will and power. A willed effect must therefore have a beginning, and likewise a willed act must have a beginning.

Moreover, those who dispute with them say:

Will entails what is willed, and creation entails what is created. The foregoing argument applies against both groups, for will and creation are relational in nature: the existence of will without something willed, or creation without something created, is impossible.

But the disputant says:

Will and creation exist, while the willed, created thing comes later.

These people are then told: You say that will exists—or that creation exists together with will—while neither what is willed nor what is created exists. Then, after an infinite span of hypothetical time, the willed, created thing comes into existence without any cause. This is false by the most elementary dictates of reason. For will or creation already existed together with power. If this constituted a complete cause, it would entail the existence of the effect, and the effect would necessarily exist when the complete cause existed. For the effect is “contingent,” and a contingent thing must exist upon the existence of the determining factor

original_text:

وَهُنَا تَنَازَعَ النَّاسُ فَقَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ مِثْلُ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ الْهَيْصَمِ الكرامي وَمَحْمُودٍ الْخَوَارِزْمِيّ يَكُونُ الْمُمْكِنُ أَوْلَى بِالْوُقُوعِ لَكِنْ لَا يَنْتَهِي إلَى حَدِّ الْوُجُوبِ.
 وَقَالَ أَكْثَرُ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَالْأَشْعَرِيَّةِ:
 بَلْ لَا يَصِيرُ أَوْلَى وَلَكِنَّ الْقَادِرَ أَوْ الْقَادِرَ الْمُرِيدَ يُرَجِّحُ أَحَدَ الْمُتَمَاثِلَيْنِ بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ. وَآخَرُونَ عَرَفُوا أَنَّ هَذَا لَازِمٌ فَاعْتَرَفُوا بِأَنَّهُ عِنْدَ وُجُودِ الْمُرَجِّحِ التَّامِّ يَجِبُ وُجُودُ الْأَثَرِ وَعِنْدَ الدَّاعِي التَّامِّ مَعَ الْقُدْرَةِ يَجِبُ وُجُودُ الْفِعْلِ كَمَا اعْتَرَفَ بِذَلِكَ أَبُو الْحُسَيْنِ الْبَصْرِيُّ وَالرَّازِي والطوسي وَغَيْرُهُمْ. وَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ قُدَمَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ يَقُولُونَ بِالْإِرَادَةِ الْمُوجِبَةِ وَأَنَّ الْإِرَادَةَ تَسْتَلْزِمُ وُجُودَ الْمُرَادِ. والمتفلسفة أَوْرَدُوا هَذَا عَلَى الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ لَكِنْ بِأَنَّ الْأَثَرَ يُقَارِنُ وُجُودَ التَّأْثِيرِ فَيَكُونُ مَعَهُ بِالزَّمَنِ. وَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ لَا يَعْرِفُ إلَّا هَذَا الْقَوْلَ وَذَاكَ الْقَوْلُ
translated_text:
in its complete form. For otherwise, the thing would remain contingent even after the determining factor existed, admitting either existence or nonexistence, and would then require a further determining factor. This entails an infinite regress, which ends only when there exists a complete determining factor that necessitates the outcome.

Here people disagreed. One group, including Muhammad ibn al-Haysam al-Karrāmī and Mahmūd al-Khwārizmī, held that a contingent thing becomes more likely to occur, but its occurrence does not become necessary.

Most of the Muʿtazilah and Ashʿarīs said:

Rather, its occurrence does not become more likely. Instead, an agent possessing power—or possessing both power and will—gives preference to one of two equivalent alternatives without a determining factor.

Others recognized that this consequence was unavoidable. They therefore acknowledged that, when the complete determining factor exists, the effect must exist, and that, when the complete motive is present together with power, the act must occur. Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī, al-Rāzī, al-Tūsī and others acknowledged this. Many of the earlier speculative theologians affirmed a necessitating will, holding that will entails the existence of what is willed.

The philosophers raised this objection against the speculative theologians, but maintained that the effect accompanies the exercise of causal influence, so that the two exist together in time. Many people know only this view and that view

. فَالْعِتْقُ وَالطَّلَاقُ يَقَعَانِ عَقِبَ الْإِعْتَاقِ وَالتَّطْلِيقِ لَا يَتَرَاخَى الْأَثَرُ وَلَا يُقَارَنُ. وَكَذَلِكَ الِانْكِسَارُ وَالِانْقِطَاعُ مَعَ الْقَطْعِ وَالْكَسْرِ.

translated_text:
—al-Rāzī and others, for example—and thus remain bewildered over this fundamental principle, one of the greatest foundations of knowledge, religion, and speculative theology. We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained that a third view is correct: the view held by the leading scholars. It is that the complete exercise of causal influence necessarily entails the existence of its effect immediately afterward, neither simultaneously with it nor after a delay. Those speculative theologians who maintain that there is a delay are mistaken, while those who maintain simultaneity, such as the philosophers, are even more mistaken. Their position entails impossibilities that we have explained elsewhere.

This third view is supported by both revelation and reason. Allah Most High says:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

People of sound reason say, “I cut it, and it was severed; I broke it, and it broke,” and, “He divorced the woman, and she became divorced; he emancipated the slave, and he became free.” Thus, emancipation and divorce take effect immediately after the acts of emancipation and divorce: the effect is neither delayed nor simultaneous. The same applies to becoming broken or severed in relation to the acts of breaking and cutting.

This helps explain that, when the act of creation occurs, the created thing must exist immediately afterward. Thus one says, “Allah brought the thing into being, and it came into being.” Its coming into being follows immediately upon Allah’s bringing it into being, neither simultaneously with that act nor after a delay.

translated_text:
Likewise, complete will, together with power, necessarily entails the existence of what is willed and lies within that power. He wills to create, and the act of creation occurs through His will and power. The act of creation then necessarily entails the existence of the created thing, even if that act of creation comes about through another cause and follows immediately upon it. This involves only the effect’s existence immediately after its fully operative cause, and an infinite succession of effects. Both are true, and Allah knows best.

As for the created thing, it can only be separate from Him; nothing created subsists in Him. Rather, will itself, together with power, entails the act of creation, just as it entails speech. The act of creation does not require another act of creation; rather, it requires that through which it occurs, namely, the preceding will. When He creates one thing, He wills to create another. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.

Those who say that the act of creation comes into being—such as the Hishāmiyyah and the Karrāmiyyah—say:

We affirm that temporally originated events subsist in Him. There is no evidence that this is invalid. Rather, reason and transmitted revelation—the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations—establish its reality, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

translated_text:
Nor is it possible to affirm that Allah governs this world without accepting this, as those philosophers closest to the truth, such as Abū al-Barakāt, author of al-Muʿtabar, and others, have acknowledged.

As for their statement, “It follows that the act of creation requires another act of creation,” those who accept this, such as the Karrāmiyyah and others, have answered them: “You maintain that created things separate from Him come into being without any cause coming into being at all. In that case, to maintain that the act of creation through which created things come into being itself comes into being without any cause coming into being is closer to reason and transmitted revelation.” This is a reply they must accept on this assumption—the assumption that voluntary acts subsist in Him.

The Karrāmiyyah call what subsists in Him hādith (“temporally occurring”), but do not call it muhdath (“brought into being”). For example, concerning the speech He utters, whether the Quran or otherwise, they say, “It occurs in time,” but do not permit saying, “It is brought into being.” For what “occurs in time” occurs through His power and will, like an “act.” What is “brought into being,” however, requires an act of bringing it into being. It would therefore follow that an act of bringing into being, distinct from what is brought into being, subsists in His Essence. That act would itself require another act of bringing into being, thus entailing an infinite regress.

Those other than the Karrāmiyyah among the leading authorities in hadith, the Sunnah, and theology do, however, call it “brought into being,” as He says:

“No reminder comes to them anew from their Lord.”

And in the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah introduces whatever commands He wills, and among what He has newly introduced is that you must not speak during prayer.”

What He newly introduced was the prohibition against their speaking during prayer. As for their statement, “What is brought into being requires an act of bringing it into being, and so on,” this entails an infinite succession of effects, such as His speaking one utterance after another—for Allah’s words have no end—and His having always spoken whenever He wills. This is the position of the leading authorities of the Sunnah, and it is the truth supported by revelation and reason.

The same applies to His actions, for acting and speaking are attributes of perfection. One who speaks is more perfect than one who does not speak, and one who creates is more perfect than one who does not create. The Most High says:

“Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then take heed?”

Thus, He has always possessed the attributes of perfection and been characterized by honor and majesty. This resolves the various difficulties and makes it clear that what the messengers have conveyed about Allah is among the truest of statements, and that rational proofs point only to what accords with the Messenger’s teachings. Yet error arose because many people were ignorant of what the Messenger conveyed

This is impossible for several reasons. One is the existence of an infinite number of things at a single instant, which is absolutely impossible. Another is that everything mentioned would be “brought into being,” not “contingent,” with nothing among them existing through itself to terminate the regress. In that case, it is all the more impossible.

This differs from saying, “Before this speech there was speech, and before this act there was an act.” This is possible according to most rational thinkers, including the leading authorities of the Sunnah, the leading philosophers, and others. Thus, to say, “He brought this newly occurring speech into being within Himself,” is intelligible. It is equivalent to our saying, “He spoke it.” This is the meaning of His words:

“Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Quran.”

That is, We spoke it in Arabic and sent it down in Arabic.

on the authority of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from al-Ashja‘ī, from Sufyān al-Thawrī, who explained His words, “We have made it an Arabic Quran,” as: “We have made it clear as an Arabic Quran.” A person distinguishes between his own speech and movement and his causing something else to move.

Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah and others among the early generations argued that the Quran is uncreated on the grounds that Allah created things by saying “Be!” If “Be!” were created, it would follow that He created one created thing by means of another, entailing an invalid infinite regress. For if He creates only by saying “Be!”, and “Be!” were created, it would follow that He could create nothing. This is an impossible circular dependence: He creates nothing until He says “Be!”, yet He does not say “Be!” until He creates it. Thus He could create nothing.

This is an infinite regress in the very basis of causation and action. It is like saying, “He does not act until He acts,” which entails that He does not act; or, “He does not create until He creates,” which entails that He does not create.

But if it is said, “He said ‘Be!’; before that ‘Be!’ there was another ‘Be!’, and before that ‘Be!’ there was another ‘Be!’,” this is not impossible. Such a regress concerns individual instances of causation, not causation as such. Likewise, in the future He will say “Be!” after “Be!” and create one thing after another without end.

Thus He creates fully realized created things through His act of creation. His act of creation is His act that subsists in Him, and this occurs only through His power and will.

translated_text:
If it is said that this act subsisting in Him requires another act, distinct from power and will, to bring it into existence—for if power and will alone were sufficient, they would suffice to bring the created thing into existence; yet since an act of creation is indispensable, this act of creation comes into existence after not having existed and subsists in Him—then its fully sufficient cause necessarily entails it and is followed by it, just like the fully sufficient cause of speech arising in His essence.

When a human being speaks, his speech, both its wording and its meaning, is preceded by another act. There must be a movement followed by the production of the letters that constitute speech. That movement is what makes the speech Arabic or non-Arabic, and it is an act subsisting in the agent. This newly occurring act of making likewise comes about through a fully sufficient cause preceding it.

The Lord’s essence is what necessitates all of this. It necessitates the second act on condition that the first has ended, not while the first is occurring. Its necessitating the second is an act subsisting in Him after the first. His essence necessitates this causal act, then another, then another. Every causal act is caused by what precedes it and is a condition for what follows it. None of these acts is created, even though they are “temporally originated.”

If someone says, “I call this ‘creation,’” his disagreement is merely verbal. He is told: Those who said, “The Quran is created,” did not mean this, nor was this what the early generations and the imams rejected. translated_text:
Imam Ahmad:

“Allah’s speech is from Allah; it is not separate from Him.”

They also said:

“The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated; it originated from Him.”

Ahmad said:

“‘It originated from Him’: He is the One who spoke it. It did not originate from a created being, as those who say it is created maintain.”

Allah Most High said:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

For this reason, no one says that He created His descent, His rising over the Throne, or His coming. The same applies to His speaking to Moses and calling him: He called him and spoke to him by His will and power. Speaking is an act subsisting in His essence; it is not creation. Likewise, when a human being speaks, he performs an act of speech and brings speech into being, but within himself, not separate from him. Thus, according to the early generations and the imams, speech is an attribute of action and also an attribute of essence.

Those who say that it is created say that it is an attribute of action, and regard both the act and the speech as separate from Him.

Those who say that it is an attribute of essence say that He speaks independently of His will and power. The position of the early generations is that He speaks by His will and power, and that His speech subsists in Him. Thus, it is an attribute of
