Here, however, action does not mean creation. Rather, as Imam Ahmad said:

“Making is of two kinds: making that is creation and making that is not creation.”

All of this entails that acts subsist in His essence and fall into two categories: transitive acts, such as creation, and intransitive acts, such as speaking and descending. The early generations affirm both this kind and the other.

As for making the Quran Arabic, although this is transitive in Arabic grammar, in the sense that it takes an object in the accusative, in the case of speech the act—“speaking”—is connected to its object—“speech”—and both subsist in the speaker. Thus, the object may refer to the act denoted by a verbal noun. When you say qāla qawlan hasanan (“he spoke fine words”), qawl (“saying”) may refer solely to the act of saying, or solely to the speech itself, in which case it is the object. It may also refer to both together, in which case it is both a direct object and a verbal noun.

Likewise, “Quran” is originally a verbal noun, as in qara'a qur'ānan (“he recited a recitation”), denoting the act and movement. The speech recited was then called “Quran.” Concerning the first meaning, Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.”

“So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.”

Concerning the second, He said:

“Indeed, this Quran”.

In that case, reading is what is read, and recitation is what is recited.

Recitation and reading may instead mean the verbal noun denoting the act. In that case, reading and recitation are not what is read and recited, but necessarily entail it. They may also mean both together. In that case, recitation is not identical to what is recited, because it includes the act; nor is it separate and distinct from what is recited, because what is recited forms part of it.

This applies when reading and what is read concern a single, specific instance, such as the Lord’s reading and what He reads, or the servant’s reading and what he reads. But if “reading” means the servant’s reading—that is, his movement—while “what is read” means the Lord’s attribute, then undoubtedly the servant’s movement is not the Lord’s attribute. Yet this is a strained distinction. Rather, the servant’s reading is what he reads, like his recited text. If his reading of the Quran means the Quran itself, then it is what he reads. If it means his movement, then it is not what he reads. If both are intended, neither statement may be made without qualification.

Al-Bukhārī affirms only that the servants’ acts—their movements and voices—are created. Reading in this sense is the servant’s act, subject to commands and prohibitions. As for the speech itself, it is Allah’s speech. Al-Bukhārī did not say that the servant’s utterance is either created or uncreated, just as Ahmad prohibited both formulations. Those acts and attributes of the servants that al-Bukhārī declared created were not declared uncreated by Ahmad or any other scholar of the early generations, even if they remained silent on the matter because it was self-evident and their aim was to refute the Jahmiyyah. What Ahmad declared uncreated was Allah’s speech, not an attribute of the servants; al-Bukhārī did not declare this created.

Ahmad’s aim, however, was to refute those who considered Allah’s speech created when it is conveyed from Him, whereas al-Bukhārī’s aim was to refute those who said, “The servants’ acts and voices are uncreated.” Both aims are sound, and there is no contradiction between them. Section

As for intransitive acts, such as rising over the Throne and coming, people disagree over whether to affirm them at all. These acts involve no existing object known to them from whose existence as a created thing they could infer the act of creation. Rather, these acts are known only through revelation. Their basis, therefore, is revelation, not reason. Thus, those who deny the attributes known through revelation also deny these acts, whether they say, “The act of creation is distinct from the created thing,” or, “The act of creation is the created thing.” Those in either group who affirm the attributes known through revelation also affirm these acts.

Those who affirm the attributes known through revelation hold two views concerning these acts:

Some classify them as transitive acts by regarding them as events that arise in something else. This is the view of al-Ash‘arī, the leading scholars among his followers, and those who agreed with them, such as al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn al-Zāghūnī, and Ibn Aqīl in many of his statements.

He says: “These acts are not exclusive to bodies; rather, both bodies and accidents can be described in these terms. Thus one says, ‘The fever has come,’ ‘The cold has come,’ and ‘The heat has come,’ and similar expressions.” This is also the position of al-Qādī Abū Bakr, al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, and others.

They likewise interpreted in this way what was reported from the early generations, such as al-Awzā‘ī and others, who said concerning the descent: “Allah Himself acts above the Throne.” This was related by al-Qādī ‘Abd al-Wahhāb from al-Qādī Abū Bakr, and was also related from al-Ash‘arī and others, as mentioned in several places in his books. They regard this, however, as belonging to the attributes known through revelation. This is the position of al-Bayhaqī and a group of others, and it is the first of al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā’s two views.

Everyone who maintains that attributes subject to the Lord’s will do not subsist in Him denies that an act He wills can subsist in Him, whether intransitive or transitive. Those among them who nevertheless affirm a pre-eternal act—such as those who affirm bringing into being and hold this view—say that this pre-eternal act subsists in Him, but not by His will, just as they say concerning His pre-eternal will.

The second view is that these are, as the evidence indicates, acts that subsist in His very essence by His will

and choice, just as they say concerning transitive acts. This is the position of the leading authorities in Sunnah, hadith, jurisprudence, and Sufism, as well as many among the various schools of speculative theology, as previously explained.

Their disagreement over the interpretation of His words rests on this distinction:

“Then He turned to the heaven,”

“Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds?”

and:

“Then He established Himself over the Throne,”

and similar passages. Those who deny these acts interpret His coming as the coming of His command or His punishment. They interpret His establishment over the Throne as power and dominion, or as exalted rank.

There are two views concerning establishment over the Throne: whether it is an attribute of action or an attribute of essence. Those who hold that it is an attribute of essence interpret it to mean that He has power over the Throne. Yet He has always possessed power and has always been exalted in rank. The weakness of this view thus becomes apparent in several respects. One is His statement:

“Then He established Himself over the Throne.”

He thus speaks of His establishment over the Throne using the conjunction “then.”

Another is that He joined one verb to another, saying: “He created, then established Himself.” Another is that their interpretation makes no distinction between the Throne and anything else. If it is said that the Throne is the greatest of created things, this does not preclude affirming the same of other things, as in His words:

Although He mentions His lordship over the Throne because of its greatness, His lordship encompasses everything. Thus, one may say:

Establishment, however, pertains specifically to the Throne, by the agreement of the Muslims, even though He has dominion and power over everything in heaven and earth and whatever is between them. If His establishment over the Throne meant His power over it, it would be permissible to say that He established Himself over heaven and earth and whatever is between them. Various groups have used this argument, including al-Ashʿarī, who said: “The Muslims’ consensus that establishment pertains specifically to the Throne demonstrates the invalidity of this view.” Furthermore, He has had power over it ever since He created it.

Another is that they dispute the claim that the word istiwā (establishment) is used in Arabic to mean power or exalted rank. Its actual usage in the Quran, the Sunnah, and Arab speech rules out this interpretation, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

 الِاسْتِوَاءُ صِفَةُ فِعْلٍ فَهَؤُلَاءِ لَهُمْ قَوْلَانِ هُنَا عَلَى مَا تَقَدَّمَ هَلْ هُوَ فِعْلٌ بَائِنٌ عَنْهُ لِأَنَّ الْفِعْلَ بِمَعْنَى الْمَفْعُولِ أَمْ فِعْلٌ قَائِمٌ بِهِ يَحْصُلُ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ. الْأَوَّلُ قَوْلُ ابْنِ كِلَابٍ وَمَنْ اتَّبَعَهُ كَالْأَشْعَرِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ. وَهُوَ قَوْلُ الْقَاضِي وَابْنِ عَقِيلٍ وَابْنِ الزَّاغُونِي وَغَيْرِهِمْ.
translated_text:
“Then Bishr established himself over Iraq … without a sword or blood being shed.”

He explained that, even if authentic, this verse would provide no evidence. For they did not say, “Umar established himself over Iraq” when he conquered it, nor “Uthmān established himself over Khurāsān,” nor “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, established himself over Yemen.” Rather, this verse—if authentic—was said about Bishr ibn Marwān when he entered Iraq and established himself upon its royal throne. This expression was used just as one says, “He sat on the royal throne,” or “under royal authority.” One also says, “He took his seat as king,” intending this meaning.

Moreover, numerous Quranic verses and hadiths, together with the consensus of the early generations, indicate that Allah is above the Throne, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

As for those who say that establishment is an attribute of action, they hold two views here, corresponding to the distinction discussed earlier: Is it an act separate from Him, because “act” means the result of the act, or an act subsisting in Him that occurs through His will and power? The first is the view of Ibn Kullāb and those who followed him, such as al-Ashʿarī and others. It is also the view of al-Qādī, Ibn ʿAqīl, Ibn al-Zāghūnī, and others.

وَالثَّانِي قَوْلُ أَئِمَّةِ أَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَكَثِيرٍ مِنْ طَوَائِفِ الْكَلَامِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ. وَلِهَذَا صَارَ لِلنَّاسِ فِيمَا ذَكَرَ اللَّهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ الِاسْتِوَاءِ وَالْمَجِيءِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ سِتَّةُ أَقْوَالٍ.

{لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ}

 وَهُوَ عِنْدُهُمْ يَنْزِلُ وَيَأْتِي وَلَمْ يَزَلْ عَالِيًا وَهُوَ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ كَمَا قَالَ حَمَّادُ بْنُ زَيْدٍ:
 هُوَ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ يَقْرُبُ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ كَيْفَ شَاءَ.
 وَقَالَ إسْحَاقُ بْنُ رَاهَوَيْه:
 يَنْزِلُ وَلَا يَخْلُو مِنْهُ الْعَرْشُ وَنُقِلَ ذَلِكَ عَنْ أَحْمَد بْنِ حَنْبَلٍ فِي رِسَالَتِهِ إلَى مُسَدَّدٍ. وَتَفْسِيرُ النُّزُولِ بِفِعْلِ يَقُومُ بِذَاتِهِ هُوَ قَوْلُ عُلَمَاءِ أَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ وَهُوَ الَّذِي حَكَاهُ أَبُو عُمَرَ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْبَرِّ عَنْهُمْ وَهُوَ قَوْلُ عَامَّةِ الْقُدَمَاءِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد وَقَدْ صَرَّحَ بِهِ ابْنُ حَامِدٍ وَغَيْرُهُ.
translated_text:
The second is the view of the leading scholars of hadith and the Sunnah, and of many groups of speculative theologians, as discussed earlier. Thus, people have adopted six positions concerning what Allah mentions in the Quran about His establishment, coming, and similar matters.

One group says that these texts are to be understood according to their apparent meaning, and regards His coming as being of the same kind as the coming of created beings, and His descent as being of the same kind as theirs. These are those who liken Allah to His creation and equate Him with it. Some of them say: “When He descends, He leaves the Throne vacant and no longer remains above it.”

Another group says that, rather, the texts retain their apparent meaning in a manner befitting Him, as with all the other attributes with which He is described:

“There is nothing like Him”

—neither in His essence, nor in His attributes, nor in His acts. They say: “He descends in a manner befitting His majesty, and likewise comes in a manner befitting His majesty.” In their view, He descends and comes while remaining on high, above the Throne. As Hammād ibn Zayd said: “He is above the Throne and draws near to His creation however He wills.”

Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh said: “He descends without leaving the Throne vacant.” This was also transmitted from Ahmad ibn Hanbal in his letter to Musaddad. Explaining the descent as an act subsisting in His essence is the position of the scholars of hadith, and it is the position that Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr reported from them. It is also the position of the great majority of the early followers of Ahmad, and Ibn Hāmid and others explicitly affirmed it.

 مَا أَعِرْفُ مُرَادَ اللَّهِ بِهَذَا.

 هَذَا مِمَّا نُهِيَ عَنْ تَفْسِيرِهِ أَوْ مِمَّا يُكْتَمُ تَفْسِيرُهُ. وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يُقَرِّرُهُ كَمَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ الْأَحَادِيثُ الصَّحِيحَةُ وَالْآثَارُ الْكَثِيرَةُ عَنْ السَّلَفِ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ.

{ثُمَّ اسْتَوَى إلَى السَّمَاءِ}
 قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ وَأَكْثَرُ مُفَسِّرِي السَّلَفِ: أَيْ ارْتَفَعَ إلَى السَّمَاءِ. وَقَالَ الْفَرَّاءُ وَابْنُ كيسان
translated_text:
The first position—denying that matters dependent on His will subsist in Him—is that of al-Tamīmī, who agreed with Ibn Kullāb in this, and of al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā and his followers.

Two other groups say: “Rather, He neither descends nor comes,” as discussed earlier. Some interpret these expressions figuratively, while others entrust their meaning to Allah.

Two further groups suspend judgment. Some say: “We do not know what Allah intended by this,” while others go no further than reciting the Quran.

The great majority of those who identify with the Sunnah and follow the early generations reject interpretations that deny that He Himself is the One who is established and who comes. Yet many of them reject false interpretations while saying: “I do not know what Allah intended by this.” Some say: “This is among the things we have been forbidden to explain, or whose explanation is to be withheld.” Others affirm it as conveyed in the authentic hadiths and the numerous reports from the early generations—the Companions and their successors.

Abū Muhammad al-Baghawī, al-Husayn ibn Masʿūd al-Farrāʾ, known as Muhyī al-Sunnah (Reviver of the Sunnah), said in his Quran commentary:

“Then He rose towards heaven.”

Ibn ʿAbbās and most Quran commentators among the early generations said: “That is, He rose towards heaven.” And al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Kaysān

{الرَّحْمَنُ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ اسْتَوَى}

translated_text:
and a group of grammarians said: “That is, He turned to creating heaven.” It was also said: “He intended to do so.” This is what Ibn al-Jawzī mentioned in his Quran commentary. He said:

“Then He rose towards heaven”—that is, He set about creating it.

Likewise, he favours the interpretation that His coming means the coming of His command, and the view of those who interpret His rising figuratively. He also mentioned this in other books and agreed with some of Ibn ʿAqīl’s views. He said: “Ibn ʿAqīl held differing views on this subject, and his opinions and scholarly judgments vary across his writings.”

In his commentary on the words, “Then He rose over the Throne,” al-Baghawī said:

“Al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: ‘He settled.’ Abū ʿUbaydah said: ‘He ascended.’ The Muʿtazilah interpreted His rising as taking dominion. As for Ahl al-Sunnah, they say: ‘Rising over the Throne is an attribute of Allah, without specifying how. One must believe in it and entrust knowledge concerning it to Allah.’

“A man asked Mālik ibn Anas about His words, ‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne’: ‘How did He rise?’ Mālik bowed his head for a long while and began to sweat profusely. Then he said: ‘His rising is not unknown, but how is beyond comprehension. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation. I can only regard you as misguided.’ Then he ordered that the man be removed, and he was taken out.”

translated_text:
He said:

“It is reported from Sufyān al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak and other scholars of the Sunnah that, concerning these verses about the ambiguous attributes, they said: ‘Let them stand as they have come, without specifying how.’”

Concerning His words,

“Are they waiting for anything but for Allah to come to them in canopies of clouds?”

he said:

“The preferable course concerning this verse and others like it is to believe in their apparent meaning, entrust knowledge concerning them to Allah, and believe that Allah is free of the characteristics of created things. This was the path followed by the leading scholars of the early generations and the scholars of the Sunnah.”

Al-Kalbī said:

“This belongs to the concealed matters that are not to be explained.”

(I say: It has also been related from him that, in explaining His words, “Then He rose,” he said: “He settled.” Thus, he explained that passage but regarded this one as belonging to the concealed matters that are not to be explained. For that passage describes Him as being above the Throne, whereas this one describes His coming in canopies of clouds.

Al-Baghawī said:

“Makhūl, al-Zuhrī, al-Awzāʿī, Mālik, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Sufyān al-Thawrī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Ahmad and Ishāq used to say concerning this and similar passages: ‘Let them stand as they have come, without specifying how.’”

Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said:

“Whatever Allah has used to describe Himself in His Book, its explanation consists in reciting it and remaining silent about it. No one has the right to explain it except Allah and His Messenger.”

original_text:
وَهَذِهِ الْآيَةُ أغمض مِنْ آيَةِ الِاسْتِوَاءِ. وَلِهَذَا كَانَ أَبُو الْفَرَجِ يَمِيلُ إلَى تَأْوِيلِ هَذَا وَيُنْكِرُ قَوْلَ مَنْ تَأَوَّلَ الِاسْتِوَاءَ بِالِاسْتِيلَاءِ.
 قَالَ فِي تَفْسِيرِهِ قَالَ الْخَلِيلُ بْنُ أَحْمَد:
 
" الْعَرْشُ "
 السَّرِيرُ وَكُلُّ سَرِيرٍ لِلْمُلْكِ يُسَمَّى 
" عَرْشًا "
 وَقَلَّمَا يُجْمَعُ الْعَرْشُ إلَّا فِي الِاضْطِرَارِ.
 قُلْت:
 وَقَدْ رَوَى ابْنُ أَبِي حَاتِمٍ عَنْ أَبِي رَوْقٍ عَنْ الضَّحَّاكِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ قَالَ: يُسَمَّى 
" عَرْشًا "
 لِارْتِفَاعِهِ.
 قُلْت:
 وَالِاشْتِقَاقُ يَشْهَدُ لِهَذَا كَقَوْلِهِ 
{وَمَا كَانُوا يَعْرِشُونَ}
 وَقَوْلِهِ 
{مَعْرُوشَاتٍ وَغَيْرَ مَعْرُوشَاتٍ}
 .
 وَقَوْلُ سَعْدٍ:
 وَهَذَا كَافِرٌ بِالْعَرْشِ. وَمَقْعَدُ الْمَلِكِ يَكُونُ أَعْلَى مِنْ غَيْرِهِ. فَهَذَا بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى غَيْرِهِ عَالٍ عَلَيْهِ وَبِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى مَا فَوْقَهُ هُوَ دُونَهُ.
 وَفِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{إذَا سَأَلْتُمْ اللَّهَ فَاسْأَلُوهُ الْفِرْدَوْسَ فَإِنَّهُ أَعْلَى الْجَنَّةِ وَأَوْسَطُ الْجَنَّةِ وَسَقْفُهُ عَرْشُ الرَّحْمَنِ}
 . فَدَلَّ عَلَى أَنَّ الْعَرْشَ أَعْلَى الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ كَمَا بُسِطَ فِي مَوَاضِعَ أُخَرٍ.
 قَالَ أَبُو الْفَرَجِ:
 وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ ذِكْرَ الْعَرْشِ مَشْهُورٌ عِنْدَ الْعَرَبِ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ وَالْإِسْلَامِ.
 قَالَ أُمَيَّةُ بْنُ أَبِي الصَّلْتِ:
مَجِّدُوا اللَّهَ فَهُوَ لِلْمَجْدِ أَهْلٌ … رَبُّنَا فِي السَّمَاءِ أَمْسَى كَبِيرًا
translated_text:
And this verse is more obscure than the verse concerning rising over the Throne. Hence Abū al-Faraj inclined towards interpreting this passage figuratively, while rejecting the interpretation of rising over the Throne as gaining dominion.

He said in his commentary:

“Al-Khalīl ibn Ahmad said: ‘ʿArsh means a throne, and every royal seat is called an ʿarsh. The word ʿarsh is rarely used in the plural except out of necessity.’”

I say: Ibn Abī Hātim narrated from Abū Rawq, from al-Dahhāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: “It is called an ʿarsh because of its elevation.”

I say: Its derivation supports this, as in His words, “and what they used to build,” and His words, “trellised and untrellised,” as well as Saʿd’s statement: “This man was an unbeliever among the dwellings of Mecca (al-ʿurush).” A king’s seat is higher than other seats. Thus, relative to what is below it, it is high above it; relative to what is above it, it is beneath it.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“When you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the highest and most central part of Paradise, and its roof is the Throne of the Most Merciful.”

This indicates that the Throne is the highest of all created things, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Abū al-Faraj said:

Know that mention of the Throne was well known among the Arabs, both before Islam and after its advent. Umayyah ibn Abī al-Salt said:

> Glorify Allah, for He is worthy of glory;
> Our Lord in heaven is great.

original_text:
بِالْبِنَاءِ الْأَعْلَى الَّذِي سَبَقَ النَّا … س وَسَوَّى فَوْقَ السَّمَاءِ سَرِيرًا
شَرْجَعًا لَا يَنَالُهُ بَصَرُ الْعَيْـ … نِ تَرَى دُونَهُ الْمَلَائِكُ صُوَرًا
قُلْت:
 يُرِيدُ أَنَّهُ ذَكَرَهُ مِنْ الْعَرَبِ مَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُسْلِمًا أَخَذَهُ عَنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ. فَإِنَّ أُمِّيَّةَ وَنَحْوَهُ إنَّمَا أَخَذَ هَذَا عَنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَإِلَّا فَالْمُشْرِكُونَ لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَ هَذَا.
 قَالَ أَبُو الْفَرَجِ ابْنُ الْجَوْزِيِّ وَقَالَ كَعْبٌ:
 إنَّ السَّمَوَاتِ فِي الْعَرْشِ كَقِنْدِيلِ مُعَلَّقٍ بَيْنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ.
 قَالَ:
 وَإِجْمَاعُ السَّلَفِ مُنْعَقِدٌ عَلَى أَنْ لَا يَزِيدُوا عَلَى قِرَاءَةِ الْآيَةِ.
 وَقَدْ شَذَّ قَوْمٌ فَقَالُوا:
 الْعَرْشُ بِمَعْنَى الْمُلْكِ وَهُوَ عُدُولٌ عَنْ الْحَقِيقَةِ إلَى التَّجَوُّزِ مَعَ مُخَالَفَةِ الْأَثَرِ. أَلَمْ يَسْمَعُوا قَوْلَهُ 
{وَكَانَ عَرْشُهُ عَلَى الْمَاءِ}
 أَفَتُرَاهُ كَانَ الْمُلْكُ عَلَى الْمَاءِ؟ .
 قَالَ وَبَعْضُهُمْ يَقُولُ:
 اسْتَوَى بِمَعْنَى اسْتَوْلَى وَيَسْتَدِلُّ بِقَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ:
حَتَّى اسْتَوَى بِشْرٌ عَلَى الْعِرَاقِ … مِنْ غَيْرِ سَيْفٍ وَدَمٍ مِهْرَاقِ
وَقَالَ الشَّاعِرُ أَيْضًا:
translated_text:
in the highest edifice—He who existed before mankind
and fashioned a throne above the heaven,
a spacious throne beyond the reach of human sight;
beneath it you see the angels as forms.

I say: He means that those Arabs who mentioned it without being Muslims had taken this from the People of the Book. Umayyah and others like him only took this from the People of the Book; otherwise, the polytheists had no knowledge of it.

Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī said:

“Kaʿb said: ‘The heavens in relation to the Throne are like a lamp suspended between heaven and earth.’”

He said:

“The early generations unanimously agreed not to go beyond reciting the verse. Some, however, departed from this and said that the Throne means dominion. This abandons the literal meaning for a figurative one, while also contradicting the transmitted reports. Have they not heard His words:

‘And His Throne was upon the water’?

Would you then suppose that dominion was upon the water?”

He said:

“Some of them say that istawā (‘rose over’) means istawlā (‘gained dominion over’), citing the poet’s words:

Until Bishr established himself over Iraq,
without a sword or any blood being shed.

The poet also said:

original_text:
قَدْ قَلَّمَا اسْتَوَيَا بِفَضْلِهِمَا جَمِيعًا … عَلَى عَرْشِ الْمُلُوكِ بِغَيْرِ زُورِ
قَالَ:
 وَهُوَ مُنْكَرٌ عِنْدَ اللُّغَوِيِّينَ.
 قَالَ ابْنُ الْأَعْرَابِيِّ:
 إنَّ الْعَرَبَ لَا تَعْلَمُ اسْتَوَى بِمَعْنَى اسْتَوْلَى وَمَنْ قَالَ ذَلِكَ فَقَدْ أَعْظَمَ.
 قَالَ:
 وَإِنَّمَا يُقَالُ 
" اسْتَوْلَى فُلَانٌ عَلَى كَذَا "
 إذَا كَانَ بَعِيدًا عَنْهُ غَيْرَ مُتَمَكِّنٍ ثُمَّ تَمَكَّنَ مِنْهُ وَاَللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى لَمْ يَزَلْ مُسْتَوْلِيًا عَلَى الْأَشْيَاءِ. وَالْبَيْتَانِ لَا يُعْرَفُ قَائِلَهُمَا كَذَا قَالَ ابْنُ فَارِسٍ اللُّغَوِيُّ. وَلَوْ صَحَّا لَمْ يَكُنْ حُجَّةً فِيهِمَا لِمَا بَيَّنَّا مِنْ اسْتِيلَاءِ مَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُسْتَوْلِيًا نَعُوذُ بِاَللَّهِ مِنْ تَعْطِيلِ الْمُلْحِدَةِ وَتَشْبِيهِ الْمُجَسِّمَةِ.
 قُلْت:
 فَقَدْ تَأَوَّلَ قَوْلَهُ 
{ثُمَّ اسْتَوَى إلَى السَّمَاءِ}
 . وَأَنْكَرَ تَأْوِيلَ 
{ثُمَّ اسْتَوَى عَلَى الْعَرْشِ}
 . وَهُوَ فِي لَفْظِ 
" الْإِتْيَانِ "
 قَدْ ذَكَرَ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فَقَالَ: قَوْلُهُ 
{أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ فِي ظُلَلٍ}
 كَانَ جَمَاعَةٌ مِنْ السَّلَفِ يُمْسِكُونَ عَنْ مِثْلِ هَذَا.
 وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى عَنْ أَحْمَد أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 الْمُرَادُ بِهِ قُدْرَتُهُ وَأَمْرُهُ.
 قَالَ:
 وَقَدْ بَيَّنَهُ فِي قَوْلِهِ 
{أَوْ يَأْتِيَ أَمْرُ رَبِّكَ}
 .
 قُلْت:
 هَذَا الَّذِي ذَكَرَهُ الْقَاضِي وَغَيْرُهُ أَنَّ حَنْبَلًا نَقَلَهُ عَنْ
translated_text:
Rarely indeed have the two, through their merit, together
ascended the throne of kings, without falsehood.”

He said:

“This is rejected by the lexicographers.”

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said:

“The Arabs do not know istawā (‘rose over’) to mean istawlā (‘gained dominion over’). Whoever claims this has committed a grave error.”

He said:

“One only says, ‘So-and-so gained dominion over such-and-such,’ when it had been beyond his reach and control, and he subsequently gained control over it. But Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has always held dominion over all things. It is not known who composed these two lines; this is what Ibn Fāris the lexicographer stated. Even if their authenticity were established, they would offer no proof, given our explanation that gaining dominion implies not having possessed it before. We seek refuge in Allah from the heretics’ denial of His attributes and the corporealists’ likening Him to His creation.”

I say: Thus, he interpreted His words figuratively:

“Then He turned to the heaven,”

yet rejected a figurative interpretation of:

“Then He rose over the Throne.”

Regarding the expression “coming,” however, he mentioned both views, saying:

“Concerning His words, ‘that Allah should come to them in canopies,’ a number of the early generations would refrain from speaking about such matters. Al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā reported that Ahmad said: ‘What is meant is His power and His command.’”

He said:

“This is clarified in His words: ‘or your Lord’s command should come.’”

I say: This account mentioned by al-Qādī and others was transmitted by Hanbal from

original_text:
أَحْمَد فِي كِتَابِ 
" الْمِحْنَةِ "
 أَنَّهُ قَالَ ذَلِكَ فِي الْمُنَاظَرَةِ لَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْمِحْنَةِ لَمَّا احْتَجُّوا عَلَيْهِ بِقَوْلِهِ 
" تَجِيءُ الْبَقَرَةُ وَآلُ عِمْرَانَ "
 قَالُوا: وَالْمَجِيءُ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا لِمَخْلُوقِ. فَعَارَضَهُمْ أَحْمَد بِقَوْلِهِ 
{وَجَاءَ رَبُّكَ}
 
{أَوْ يَأْتِيَ رَبُّكَ}
 وَقَالَ: الْمُرَادُ بِقَوْلِهِ 
" تَجِيءُ الْبَقَرَةُ وَآلُ عِمْرَانَ "
: ثَوَابُهُمَا كَمَا فِي قَوْلِهِ 
{وَجَاءَ رَبُّكَ}
 أَمْرُهُ وَقُدْرَتُهُ. وَقَدْ اخْتَلَفَ أَصْحَابُ أَحْمَد فِيمَا نَقَلَهُ حَنْبَلٌ. فَإِنَّهُ لَا رَيْبَ أَنَّهُ خِلَافُ النُّصُوصِ الْمُتَوَاتِرَةِ عَنْ أَحْمَد فِي مَنْعِهِ مِنْ تَأْوِيلِ هَذَا وَتَأْوِيلِ النُّزُولِ وَالِاسْتِوَاءِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَفْعَالِ. وَلَهُمْ ثَلَاثَةُ أَقْوَالٍ.
 قِيلَ:
 إنَّ هَذَا غَلَطٌ مِنْ حَنْبَلٍ انْفَرَدَ بِهِ دُونَ الَّذِينَ ذَكَرُوا عَنْهُ الْمُنَاظَرَةَ مِثْلَ صَالِحٍ وَعَبْدِ اللَّهِ والمروذي وَغَيْرِهِمْ. فَإِنَّهُمْ لَمْ يَذْكُرُوا هَذَا وَحَنْبَلٌ يَنْفَرِدُ بِرِوَايَاتِ يُغَلِّطُهُ فِيهَا طَائِفَةٌ كَالْخَلَّالِ وَصَاحِبِهِ.
 قَالَ أَبُو إسْحَاقَ ابْنُ شاقلا:
 هَذَا غَلَطٌ مِنْ حَنْبَلٍ لَا شَكَّ فِيهِ. وَكَذَلِكَ نُقِلَ عَنْ مَالِكٍ رِوَايَةٌ أَنَّهُ تَأَوَّلَ 
" يَنْزِلُ إلَى السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا "
 أَنَّهُ يَنْزِلُ أَمْرُهُ. لَكِنَّ هَذَا مِنْ رِوَايَةِ حَبِيبٍ كَاتِبِهِ وَهُوَ كَذَّابٌ بِاتِّفَاقِهِمْ. وَقَدْ رُوِيَتْ مِنْ وَجْهٍ آخَرَ لَكِنَّ الْإِسْنَادَ مَجْهُولٌ.
 وَالْقَوْلُ الثَّانِي:
 قَالَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد: هَذَا قَالَهُ إلْزَامًا لِلْخَصْمِ
translated_text:
Ahmad in The Book of the Ordeal: he said this while debating them during the ordeal, when they argued against him by citing the statement, “Al-Baqarah and Āl Imrān will come.” They said, “Only something created can come.” Ahmad countered them with Allah’s words:

“And your Lord comes,”

and:

“Or your Lord should come.”

He said that “Al-Baqarah and Āl Imrān will come” means their reward, just as “And your Lord comes” means His command and His power.

Ahmad’s followers differed over what Hanbal transmitted. There is no doubt that it contradicts the statements transmitted from Ahmad through numerous independent chains, in which he prohibited figurative interpretation of this, of the descent, of rising over the Throne, and of other such actions. They held three views.

The first was that this was an error unique to Hanbal, not shared by those who recounted Ahmad’s debate, such as Sālih, Abd Allāh, al-Marwadhī, and others. They did not mention this. Hanbal does transmit certain reports alone in which a number of scholars, such as al-Khallāl and his associate, judge him to have erred.

Abū Ishāq Ibn Shāqlā said: “This is undoubtedly an error on Hanbal’s part.”

Similarly, a report was transmitted from Mālik that he interpreted “He descends to the lowest heaven” as meaning that His command descends. However, this was transmitted by his scribe Habīb, whom they unanimously considered a liar. It has also been transmitted through another route, but that chain of transmission is unknown.

The second view: a group of Ahmad’s followers said that he stated this in order to bind his opponent

original_text:
عَلَى مَذْهَبِهِ لِأَنَّهُمْ فِي يَوْمِ الْمِحْنَةِ لَمَّا احْتَجُّوا عَلَيْهِ بِقَوْلِهِ 
" تَأْتِي الْبَقَرَةُ وَآلُ عِمْرَانَ "
 أَجَابَهُمْ بِأَنَّ مَعْنَاهُ: يَأْتِي ثَوَابُ الْبَقَرَةِ وَآلِ عِمْرَانَ كَقَوْلِهِ 
{أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ}
 أَيْ أَمْرُهُ وَقُدْرَتُهُ عَلَى تَأْوِيلِهِمْ لَا أَنَّهُ يَقُولُ بِذَلِكَ. فَإِنَّ مَذْهَبَهُ تَرْكُ التَّأْوِيلِ.
 وَالْقَوْلُ الثَّالِثُ:
 أَنَّهُمْ جَعَلُوا هَذَا رِوَايَةً عَنْ أَحْمَد وَقَدْ يَخْتَلِفُ كَلَامُ الْأَئِمَّةِ فِي مَسَائِلَ مِثْلِ هَذِهِ لَكِنَّ الصَّحِيحَ الْمَشْهُورَ عَنْهُ رِدُّ التَّأْوِيلِ. وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ ابْنُ الزَّاغُونِي وَغَيْرُهُ وَذَكَرَ أَنَّ تَرْكَ التَّأْوِيلِ هِيَ الرِّوَايَةُ الْمَشْهُورَةُ الْمَعْمُولُ عَلَيْهَا عِنْدَ عَامَّةِ الْمَشَايِخِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِنَا. وَرِوَايَةُ التَّأْوِيلِ فَسَّرَ ذَلِكَ بِالْعَمْدِ وَالْقَصْدِ لَمْ يُفَسِّرْهُ بِالْأَمْرِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ كَمَا فَسَّرُوا 
{ثُمَّ اسْتَوَى إلَى السَّمَاءِ}
 . فَعَلَى هَذَا فِي تَأْوِيلِ ذَلِكَ إذَا قِيلَ بِهِ وَجْهَانِ. وَابْنُ الزَّاغُونِي وَالْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى وَنَحْوُهُمَا وَإِنْ كَانُوا يَقُولُونَ بِإِمْرَارِ الْمَجِيءِ وَالْإِتْيَانِ عَلَى ظَاهِرِهِ فَقَوْلُهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ جِنْسِ قَوْلِ ابْنِ كِلَابٍ وَالْأَشْعَرِيِّ.
 فَإِنَّهُ أَيْضًا يَمْنَعُ تَأْوِيلَ النُّزُولِ وَالْإِتْيَانِ وَالْمَجِيءِ وَيَجْعَلُهُ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ الْخَبَرِيَّةِ وَيَقُولُ:
 إنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَفْعَالَ لَا تَسْتَلْزِمُ الْأَجْسَامَ بَلْ يُوصَفُ بِهَا غَيْرُ الْأَجْسَامِ. وَكَلَامُ ابْنِ الزَّاغُونِي فِي هَذَا
translated_text:
on the basis of the opponent’s own doctrine. For during the ordeal, when they argued against him by citing the saying, “Al-Baqarah and Āl Imrān will come,” he answered that it meant that the reward of Al-Baqarah and Āl Imrān would come, just as Allah’s words, “that Allah should come to them,” meant His command and His power according to their figurative interpretation—not that he himself held this view. His position was to refrain from figurative interpretation.

The third view was that they accepted this as a position reported from Ahmad. The imams’ statements may vary on such questions, but the sound, well-known position transmitted from him is the rejection of figurative interpretation. Ibn al-Zāghūnī and others mentioned both reports, noting that refraining from figurative interpretation was the well-known report followed by most of the scholars of our school. In the report allowing figurative interpretation, he explained this as deliberate intent and purpose, not as command and power, just as they interpreted, “Then He turned toward heaven.” Accordingly, if figurative interpretation is adopted, there are two ways of interpreting this.

Although Ibn al-Zāghūnī, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, and others like them hold that coming and arrival should be accepted in their apparent sense, their position on this is of the same kind as that of Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash‘arī. For he too rejects figurative interpretation of descent, arrival, and coming, and regards these as attributes known through revelation. He says: “These actions do not necessarily imply bodies; rather, things other than bodies may be described by them.” Ibn al-Zāghūnī’s discussion of this

As for the Lord Himself being high above the universe, Ibn Kullāb holds that this is known through reason, as do most of those who affirm the divine attributes, as al-Khattābī, Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, and others have mentioned.

This is also Ibn al-Zāghūnī’s position and the later of Judge Abū Ya‘lā’s two positions. Initially, the judge followed al-Ash‘arī’s view that this was an attribute known through revelation. This is also the position of Judge Abū Bakr, al-Bayhaqī, and others like them.

As for Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī and his followers, they differed from al-Ash‘arī and his early followers concerning the attributes known through revelation and did not affirm them. Some, however, denied them, interpreting rising over the Throne as exercising dominion over it. This was the earlier of Abū al-Ma‘ālī’s two positions. Others, such as al-Rāzī and al-Āmidī, suspended judgment, neither affirming nor denying them.

Abū al-Ma‘ālī’s later position was that figurative interpretation of the attributes known through revelation was forbidden. He stated that this was the consensus of the early generations, and that, had figurative interpretation been permissible or obligatory, they would have devoted greater attention to it than to other matters. translated_text:
His words, “And none knows its interpretation except Allah.” He mentioned this in al-Nizāmiyya fī al-Arkān al-Islāmiyya (The Nizāmiyya Treatise on the Pillars of Islam). This is the approach of most of those who identify with the Sunnah: they regard figurative interpretation as contrary to the way of the early generations.

This matter has been discussed at length elsewhere, including the ambiguity of the term ta’wīl (interpretation), the discussion of His words, “And none knows its interpretation except Allah,” and the fact that both views are correct. Those who say that none knows its ta’wīl except Allah mean the realities to which the words ultimately refer, which Allah alone knows. Those who say that people firmly grounded in knowledge know its ta’wīl mean the explanation of the Quran conveyed by the Messenger and the Companions.

The disagreement concerns only the use of the term ta’wīl for adopting the less likely meaning—that is, construing an expression in its less likely sense rather than its more likely sense, with accompanying evidence. This is a later terminological usage. It is this kind of interpretation that the early generations and the leading scholars rejected: the interpretations advanced by the people of innovation.

Likewise, Ahmad says in his Refutation of the Jahmiyya: “Those who interpreted the Quran contrary to its proper interpretation.” Ahmad discussed the Quran’s ambiguous passages and explained them all.

translated_text:
And some of these explanations are agreed upon among the early generations, while others are disputed.

Abū ‘Abd Allāh, the grandfather, mentioned in his commentary something similar to what al-Baghawī mentioned, rather than what Ibn al-Jawzī mentioned. He said:

As for the coming attributed to Allah, the leading scholars of the early generations—such as Makhūl, al-Zuhrī, al-Awzā‘ī, Ibn al-Mubārak, Sufyān al-Thawrī, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, Mālik ibn Anas, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and their followers—agree that it is to be left as it has been transmitted. The same applies to similar accounts found in the Quran or transmitted in the Sunnah, such as the hadiths concerning the descent and the like. This is the safe course and the way of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah: they believe in their apparent meaning, entrust knowledge of them to Allah, and believe that Allah is free of the marks of createdness. The leading scholars have followed this course, generation after generation, as Allah Most High says:

“None knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, ‘We believe in it.’”

Regarding His words, “that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds,” Ibn al-Sā’ib said: “This belongs to what is kept hidden and is not to be explained.” He also mentioned something resembling al-Khattābī’s discussion of this matter.

If it is asked, “How can someone believe in something when they do not fully comprehend its true reality?” the answer is: Just as it is possible to believe in Allah

The heretics say: “Then it must be obtained through someone else.”

If these people tell them, “This is impossible for anyone,” they reject that claim and say: “The Quran only states that no one but Allah knows the meaning of that discourse. But on what basis do you claim that divine matters cannot be known through rational proofs that mere verbal exposition and reports cannot adequately convey?”

The heretics say that the messengers addressed people through imaginative representations; the speculative theologians say through expressions requiring figurative interpretation; and these literalists say through words whose meanings were left unknown. The errors of these three groups have been discussed at length. It has been explained that the Messenger brought the utmost knowledge and clarity, such that no human being could bring anything more perfect than what he brought—may Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon him. The most perfect thing he brought is the Quran, and people differ enormously in their understanding of it.

Ibn al-Sāʾib’s statement, “This belongs to what is concealed and is not explained,” implies that it has an explanation which the scholars know but conceal.

And this may be understood in two ways. Either he means that some of what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—explained is concealed from everyone. This is outright concealment, which Allah has condemned. Such is the condition of the People of the Book. He censured those who conceal the clear proofs and guidance He explained to people, after making them clear to people in the Book. He said:

“And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah?”

Such is the condition of the People of the Book in concealing passages in their scripture: some interpret them figuratively, while others declare their meanings indeterminate. These passages contain proofs of Muhammad’s prophethood—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and other matters. For they cannot deny the wording of the Torah, the Gospel, and the other books of the prophets—which, among the People of the Book, number twenty-odd books. Rather, they distort it through false interpretation and conceal its correct meanings from their ordinary people, as Allah Most High said:

“And among them are unlettered people who know nothing of the Scripture except its recitation.”

Whoever treats the people of the Quran in the same way, instructing them to remain unlettered concerning it, knowing nothing of the Book except its recitation, has instructed them to do the very thing for which Allah condemned the People of the Book.

 وَفِي الصَّحِيحِ عَنْ عَائِشَةَ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ:
 
{إذَا رَأَيْتُمْ الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ مَا تَشَابَهَ مِنْهُ فَأُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ سَمَّاهُمْ اللَّهُ فَاحْذَرُوهُمْ}
 . فَهَذَا فِعْلُ مَنْ يُعَارِضُ النُّصُوصَ بَعْضَهَا بِبَعْضِ لِيُوقِعَ الْفِتْنَةَ وَهِيَ الشَّكُّ وَالرَّيْبُ فِي الْقُلُوبِ كَمَا رُوِيَ أَنَّهُ 
{خَرَجَ عَلَى الْقَوْمِ وَهُمْ يَتَجَادَلُونَ فِي الْقَدَرِ هَؤُلَاءِ يَقُولُونَ: أَلَمْ يَقُلْ اللَّهُ كَذَا؟
 وَهَؤُلَاءِ يَقُولُونَ:
 أَلَمْ يَقُلْ اللَّهُ كَذَا؟
 فَكَأَنَّمَا فُقِئَ فِي وَجْهِهِ حَبُّ الرُّمَّانِ ثُمَّ قَالَ:
 أَبِهَذَا أُمِرْتُمْ أَنْ تَضْرِبُوا كِتَابَ اللَّهِ بَعْضَهُ بِبَعْضِ؟ اُنْظُرُوا مَا أُمِرْتُمْ بِهِ فَافْعَلُوهُ}
 . فَكُلُّ مَنْ اتَّبَعَ الْمُتَشَابِهَ عَلَى هَذَا الْوَجْهِ فَهُوَ مَذْمُومٌ. وَهُوَ حَالُ مَنْ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يُشَكِّكَ النَّاسَ فِيمَا عَلِمُوهُ لِكَوْنِهِ وَإِيَّاهُمْ لَمْ يَفْهَمُوا مَا تَوَهَّمُوا أَنَّهُ يُعَارِضُهُ. هَذَا أَصْلُ الْفِتْنَةِ أَنْ يُتْرَكَ الْمَعْلُومُ لِغَيْرِ مَعْلُومٍ كَالسَّفْسَطَةِ الَّتِي تُورِثُ شُبَهًا يَقْدَحُ بِهَا فِيمَا عُلِمَ وَتُيُقِّنَ. فَهَذِهِ حَالُ مَنْ يُفْسِدُ قُلُوبَ النَّاسِ وَعُقُولَهُمْ بِإِفْسَادِ مَا فِيهَا مِنْ الْعِلْمِ وَالْعَمَلِ أَصْلَ الْهُدَى فَإِذَا شَكَّكَهُمْ فِيمَا عَلِمُوهُ بَقُوا حَيَارَى.
وَالرَّسُولُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَدْ أَتَى بِالْآيَاتِ الْبَيِّنَاتِ الدَّالَّةِ عَلَى
translated_text:
combined two things: evil intent and ignorance. They do not understand its meaning, yet seek to set parts of Allah’s Book against one another, thereby sowing confusion and doubt.

It is authentically reported from ‘Ā’ishah that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“When you see those who pursue its ambiguous passages, they are the ones Allah has named, so beware of them.”

This is what those who set scriptural texts against one another do to stir up discord—that is, doubt and uncertainty in people’s hearts. Thus, it is reported that:

“He came out to some people who were disputing about divine decree. Some were saying, ‘Did Allah not say such-and-such?’ while others were saying, ‘Did Allah not say such-and-such?’ His face looked as though pomegranate seeds had been burst upon it. Then he said, ‘Is this what you were commanded to do—to set parts of Allah’s Book against one another? Look to what you have been commanded, and do it.’”

Everyone who pursues the ambiguous passages in this manner is blameworthy. Such is the case of someone who seeks to make people doubt what they know because neither he nor they have understood what they imagine contradicts it. This is the root of discord: abandoning what is known for what is unknown, like the sophistry that generates doubts used to undermine established, certain knowledge. Such is the condition of those who corrupt people’s hearts and minds by undermining the knowledge and practice within them—the foundation of guidance. Once they make people doubt what they know, they are left bewildered.

{إذَا جَاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ وَالْفَتْحُ}
 فَذَكَرُوا ظَاهِرَ لَفْظِهَا.
 وَلَمَّا فَسَّرَهَا ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ بِأَنَّهَا إعْلَامُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِقُرْبِ وَفَاتِهِ قَالَ:
 مَا أَعْلَمُ مِنْهَا إلَّا مَا تَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
his truthfulness. The Quran contains clear verses that form the foundation of the Book. Their meaning is known, and they are known to be true; through them, people find guidance and benefit.

Whoever pursues the ambiguous passages seeks discord and seeks their interpretation. In the first, their intention is corrupt; as for the second, they are not qualified for it. Rather, they interpret these passages in ways that distort their meaning, since they are not firmly grounded in knowledge. One firmly grounded in knowledge is someone whose understanding of the clear passages is firmly established and unwavering. He does not doubt or become uncertain about them because of ambiguous passages that appear to contradict them; rather, he believes in them. Those firmly grounded in knowledge may know the interpretation of the ambiguous passages.

As for someone who is not firmly grounded in this understanding, but doubts the clear passages whenever an ambiguous passage appears to contradict them, he considers it possible that the ambiguous passage means something that contradicts the clear one. He therefore does not know the meaning of the ambiguous passage, since he is not firmly grounded in understanding the clear passages. He seeks discord through both. Such a person is to receive a punishment that deters him, as ‘Umar did with Sabīgh. But someone whose aim is guidance and truth is not one of these people.

‘Umar himself used to ask questions, and be asked, about the subtle meanings of verses. He asked his companions about Allah’s words:

“When Allah’s help and victory come.”

They explained the apparent meaning of its wording. But when Ibn ‘Abbās explained that it informed the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that his death was near, ‘Umar said:

“I understand nothing from it beyond what you understand.”

وَهَذَا بَاطِنُ الْآيَةِ الْمُوَافِقُ لِظَاهِرِهَا. فَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا أُمِرَ بِالِاسْتِغْفَارِ عِنْدَ ظُهُورِ الدِّينِ وَالِاسْتِغْفَارُ يُؤْمَرُ بِهِ عِنْدَ خِتَامِ الْأَعْمَالِ وَبِظُهُورِ الدِّينِ حَصَلَ مَقْصُودُ الرِّسَالَةِ عَلِمُوا أَنَّهُ إعْلَامٌ بِقُرْبِ الْأَجَلِ مَعَ أُمُورٍ أُخَرٍ وَفَوْقَ كُلِّ ذِي عِلْمٍ عَلِيمٌ. وَالِاسْتِدْلَالُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ بِمَلْزُومَاتِهِ. وَالشَّيْءُ قَدْ يَكُونُ لَهُ لَازِمٌ وَلِلَازِمِهِ لَازِمٌ وَهَلُمَّ جَرَّا. فَمِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَكُونُ أَفْطَنَ بِمَعْرِفَةِ اللَّوَازِمِ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ يَسْتَدِلُّ بِالْمَلْزُومِ عَلَى اللَّازِمِ.
 وَمِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ لَا يَتَصَوَّرُ اللَّازِمَ وَلَوْ تَصَوَّرَهُ لَمْ يَعْرِفْ الْمَلْزُومَ بَلْ يَقُولُ:
 يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَلْزَمَ وَيَجُوزَ أَنْ لَا يَلْزَمَ؛ وَيُحْتَمَلُ وَيُحْتَمَلُ. وَتَرَدُّدُ الِاحْتِمَالِ هُوَ مِنْ عَدَمِ الْعِلْمِ وَإِلَّا فَالْوَاقِعُ هُوَ أَحَدُ أَمْرَيْنِ. فَحَيْثُ كَانَ احْتِمَالٌ بِلَا تَرْجِيحٍ كَانَ لِعَدَمِ الْعِلْمِ بِالْوَاقِعِ وَخَفَاءِ دَلِيلِهِ وَغَيْرِهِ قَدْ يَعْلَمُ ذَلِكَ وَيَعْلَمُ دَلِيلَهُ. وَمَنْ ظَنَّ أَنَّ مَا لَا يَعْلَمُهُ هُوَ لَا يَعْلَمُهُ غَيْرُهُ كَانَ مِنْ جَهْلِهِ. فَلَا يَنْفِي عَنْ النَّاسِ إلَّا مَا عَلِمَ انْتِفَاؤُهُ عَنْهُمْ وَفَوْقَ كُلِّ ذِي عِلْمٍ عَلِيمٌ أَعْلَمُ مِنْهُ حَتَّى يَنْتَهِيَ الْأَمْرُ إلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى. وَهَذَا قَدْ بُسِطَ فِي مَوَاضِعَ.
 ثُمَّ إنَّهُمْ يَقُولُونَ:
 الْمَأْثُورُ عَنْ السَّلَفِ هُوَ السُّكُوتُ عَنْ الْخَوْضِ فِي
translated_text:
And this is the verse’s inner meaning, which accords with its apparent meaning. When he was commanded to seek forgiveness upon the religion’s triumph—seeking forgiveness being enjoined at the completion of deeds, and the religion’s triumph marking the fulfilment of the purpose of his mission—they understood, together with other considerations, that this announced the approach of his death. “Above everyone endowed with knowledge is one more knowledgeable.”

A thing is inferred from what entails it. Something may have an implication, and that implication may have a further implication, and so on. Some people are more perceptive than others in recognizing these implications, inferring what is entailed from what entails it.

Others do not conceive of the implication; even if they did, they would not recognize what entails it. Instead, they say: “It may follow, or it may not; this is possible, and so is that.” Such indecision between possibilities arises from a lack of knowledge; in reality, one of the two is the case. Wherever possibilities are entertained without grounds for preferring one over another, this is due to ignorance of what is actually the case and to its evidence being hidden from the person concerned. Someone else may know both the reality and its evidence. Whoever imagines that what he does not know is also unknown to others does so out of ignorance. One should therefore deny knowledge to others only where one knows that they lack it. Above everyone endowed with knowledge is one more knowledgeable, who knows more than he does, until ultimately the matter reaches Allah Most High. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Then they say:

“What is transmitted from the early generations is that one should refrain from delving into

تَأْوِيلِ ذَلِكَ وَالْمَصِيرُ إلَى الْإِيمَانِ بِظَاهِرِهِ وَالْوُقُوفُ عَنْ تَفْسِيرِهِ لِأَنَّا قَدْ نُهِينَا أَنْ نَقُولَ فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ بِرَأْيِنَا وَلَمْ يُنَبِّهْنَا اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ عَلَى حَقِيقَةِ مَعْنَى ذَلِكَ.

 فَإِذَا قَالُوا مَعَ ذَلِكَ:
 
{وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ إِلَّا اللَّهُ}
 أَثْبَتُوا تَأْوِيلًا لَا يَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَهُمْ يَنْفُونَ جِنْسَ التَّأْوِيلِ. وَنَقُولُ مَا الْحَامِلُ عَلَى هَذَا التَّأْوِيلِ الْبَعِيدِ؟ وَقَدْ أَمْكَنَ بِدُونِهِ أَنْ نُثْبِتَ إتْيَانًا وَمَجِيئًا لَا يُعْقَلُ كَمَا يَلِيقُ بِهِ كَمَا أَثْبَتْنَا ذَاتًا لَهَا حَقِيقَةً لَا تُعْقَلُ وَصِفَاتٍ مِنْ سَمْعٍ وَبَصَرٍ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ لَا تُعْقَلُ. وَلِأَنَّهُ إذَا جَازَ تَأْوِيلُ هَذَا وَأَنْ نُقَدِّرَ مُضْمَرًا مَحْذُوفًا مِنْ قُدْرَةٍ أَوْ عَذَابٍ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ فَمَا مَنَعَكُمْ مِنْ تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ 
" تَرَوْنَ رَبَّكُمْ "
 كَذَلِكَ؟ .
translated_text:
its interpretation, believe in its apparent meaning, and refrain from explaining it, for we have been forbidden to speak about the Book of Allah on the basis of our own opinions, and Allah and His Messenger have not made its true meaning known to us.”

The response is:

Everyone is indeed commanded to remain silent about what they do not know. However, this statement implies that they did not know the verse’s meaning, explanation or interpretation. If it was not clear to them, this amounts to acknowledging their lack of knowledge of it. These are the words of someone in doubt, who does not know what is intended by the verse. Yet when certain interpretations are mentioned to them—such as interpreting it as the coming of His command and His power—they reject this on the grounds that it renders the specification meaningless. This is a denial and rejection of such interpretation.

If, despite this, they say:

“And no one knows its interpretation except Allah,”

they affirm an interpretation known only to Allah, while denying interpretation of this kind altogether.

And we say: What calls for this far-fetched interpretation? Without it, we can affirm a coming and an arrival beyond comprehension, in a manner befitting Him, just as we affirm an essence whose reality is beyond comprehension, and attributes—hearing, sight and others—that are beyond comprehension. For if it is permissible to interpret this and posit an implicit, omitted term, such as power, punishment or the like, what has prevented you from interpreting the words “You will see your Lord” in the same way?

original_text:
وَهَذَا كَلَامٌ فِي إبْطَالِ التَّأْوِيلِ وَحَمْلٌ لِلَّفْظِ عَلَى مَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ ظَاهِرُهُ عَلَى مَا يَلِيقُ بِجَلَالِ اللَّهِ.
 فَإِذَا قِيلَ مَعَ هَذَا:

 فَعُلِمَ أَنَّ التَّأْوِيلَ الَّذِي لَا يَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ لَا يُنَاقِضُ حَمْلَهُ عَلَى مَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّفْظُ بَلْ هُوَ أَمْرٌ آخَرُ يُحَقِّقُ هَذَا وَيُوَافِقُهُ لَا يُنَاقِضُهُ وَيُخَالِفُهُ كَمَا قَالَ مَالِكٌ:
 الِاسْتِوَاءُ مَعْلُومٌ وَالْكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ. وَإِذَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ أَمْكَنَ أَنَّ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ مَنْ يَعْلَمُ مِنْ مَعْنَى الْآيَةِ مَا يُوَافِقُ الْقُرْآنَ لَمْ يَعْلَمْهُ غَيْرُهُ وَيَكُونُ ذَلِكَ مِنْ تَفْسِيرِهَا. وَهُوَ مِنْ التَّأْوِيلِ الَّذِي يَعْلَمُهُ الرَّاسِخُونَ فِي الْعِلْمِ كَمَنْ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّ الْمُرَادَ بِالْآيَةِ مَجِيءُ اللَّهِ قَطْعًا لَا شَكَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لِكَثْرَةِ مَا دَلَّ عِنْدَهُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ. وَيَعْلَمُ مَعَ ذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ الْعَلِيُّ الْأَعْلَى يَأْتِي إتْيَانًا تَكُونُ الْمَخْلُوقَاتُ مُحِيطَةً بِهِ وَهُوَ تَحْتُهَا. فَإِنَّ هَذَا مُنَاقِضٌ لِكَوْنِهِ الْعَلِيَّ الْأَعْلَى. وَالْجَدُّ الْأَعْلَى أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ قَدْ جَرَى فِي تَفْسِيرِهِ عَلَى مَا ذَكَرَ مِنْ الطَّرِيقَةِ. وَهَذِهِ عَادَتُهُ وَعَادَاتُ غَيْرِهِ.
translated_text:
This argument invalidates such interpretation and takes the wording in its apparent sense, in a manner befitting Allah’s majesty.

If, alongside this, it is said that it has an interpretation known only to Allah, and “interpretation” means this same kind of interpretation, that would be a contradiction. How can someone deny this kind of interpretation while affirming an interpretation known only to Allah?

It is thus clear that the interpretation known only to Allah does not contradict understanding the passage according to what its wording indicates. Rather, it is something else that substantiates and agrees with this understanding, rather than contradicting or opposing it. As Mālik said:

“The rising is known, but its manner is unknown.”

That being so, one scholar may understand something of the verse’s meaning that accords with the Quran but is unknown to another. This would constitute an explanation of the verse and belong to the interpretation known to those firmly grounded in knowledge. For example, someone may know with absolute certainty that the verse refers to Allah’s coming, without any doubt, because of the abundant evidence available to him. At the same time, he knows that He is the Most High, the Highest, and comes in such a way that created things surround Him while He is beneath them. This contradicts His being the Most High, the Highest.

The forebear Abū ʿAbd Allāh—may Allah have mercy on him—followed the method he mentioned in his commentary. This is his usual practice, and that of others.

He also cited Ibn al-Zāghūnī, saying: Shaykh Alī ibn Ubayd Allāh al-Zāghūnī said:

“Our imam Ahmad’s statements concerning this coming differ, with two reports regarding whether it is understood in its apparent sense or admits of figurative interpretation. According to one report, it is understood in its apparent sense: that He Himself comes.

On this basis, he says:

Figurative interpretation does not apply. Nevertheless, His own coming must be understood only in a manner befitting Him. It has been established that affirming His coming is not to be understood as affirming a departure and movement that entail vacating one place and occupying another. Such coming is characteristic of created beings, which cannot encompass places and locations because these are larger and greater than they are. Their coming to those places requires moving from what is near to what is distant. This is impossible in the case of the Creator, Most High, because nothing is greater than Him. His coming does not require movement or departure, since neither the need for this nor what necessitates it exists in His case.

We therefore affirm coming as an attribute of His, while rejecting the supposition that what necessarily applies to created beings applies to Him, since they differ in their need for such movement. Another example is His saying:

‘And your Lord comes, with the angels in row upon row.’

He said:

(I say:

That His coming, arrival and descent are unlike the coming, arrival and descent of created beings is self-evident and agreed upon by the scholars of the Sunnah and all people of reason. Attributes and actions correspond to the essence that possesses those attributes and performs those actions. Since His essence is distinct from all other essences and unlike them, it necessarily follows that His attributes are distinct from all other attributes and unlike them. His attributes relate to His essence as the attributes of anything relate to its essence.

There is no doubt that He is the Most High, the Most Exalted, the Magnificent. He is higher than everything and greater than everything. His descent and coming therefore cannot be such that created things encompass Him or are greater and larger than Him. That is impossible.

Uthmān ibn Saīd explained that, even if authentic, this report would not support their position, because it concerns the explanation of His words, “the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all.” They related from Thābit: “Everlasting and enduring, never departing from what is His due,” just as Ibn Ishāq said: “He does not depart from His station.”

I say:

Al-Kalbī himself, who transmitted this report, explains “He rose over the Throne” as “He settled,” and “Then He rose towards the heaven” as “He ascended to the heaven.”

As for “movement,” Ibn Hāmid and a group of scholars say: “He descends with motion and movement.” Others among the scholars of the Sunnah, such as al-Tamīmī, one of Ahmad’s followers, rejected this and said: “Rather, He descends without motion or movement.” A third group, including Ibn Battah and others, suspend judgment on this matter. Al-Qādī Abū Yalā mentioned these three positions in his book “Differences between the Two Transmissions and the Two Views, and the Negation of the Expression as a Whole.”

 يَنْزِلُ نُزُولًا لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ نَزَلَ نُزُولًا لَا يُمَاثِلُ نُزُولَ الْمَخْلُوقِينَ نُزُولًا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ كَمَا أَنَّهُ فِي ذَلِكَ وَفِي سَائِرِ مَا وَصَفَ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ فِي ذَلِكَ. وَهُوَ مُنَزَّهٌ أَنْ يَكُونَ نُزُولُهُ كَنُزُولِ الْمَخْلُوقِينَ وَحَرَكَتِهِمْ وَانْتِقَالِهِمْ وَزَوَالِهِمْ مُطْلَقًا لَا نُزُولَ الْآدَمِيِّينَ وَلَا غَيْرِهِمْ. فَالْمَخْلُوقُ إذَا نَزَلَ مِنْ عُلْوٍ إلَى سُفْلٍ زَالَ وَصْفُهُ بِالْعُلُوِّ وَتَبَدَّلَ إلَى وَصْفِهِ بِالسُّفُولِ وَصَارَ غَيْرُهُ أَعْلَى مِنْهُ. وَالرَّبُّ تَعَالَى لَا يَكُونُ شَيْءٌ أَعْلَى مِنْهُ قَطُّ بَلْ هُوَ الْعَلِيُّ الْأَعْلَى وَلَا يَزَالُ هُوَ الْعَلِيُّ الْأَعْلَى مَعَ أَنَّهُ يَقْرُبُ إلَى عِبَادِهِ وَيَدْنُو مِنْهُمْ وَيَنْزِلُ إلَى حَيْثُ شَاءَ وَيَأْتِي كَمَا شَاءَ. وَهُوَ فِي ذَلِكَ الْعَلِيُّ الْأَعْلَى الْكَبِيرُ الْمُتَعَالِي عَلِيٌّ فِي دُنُوِّهِ قَرِيبٌ فِي عُلُوِّهِ. فَهَذَا وَإِنْ لَمْ يَتَّصِفْ بِهِ غَيْرُهُ فَلِعَجْزِ الْمَخْلُوقِ أَنْ يَجْمَعَ بَيْنَ هَذَا وَهَذَا. كَمَا يَعْجِزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ هُوَ الْأَوَّلُ وَالْآخِرُ وَالظَّاهِرُ وَالْبَاطِنُ.
translated_text:
Allah and His Messenger have affirmed, using the wording in which it was affirmed, and denying what Allah and His Messenger have denied, just as they denied it. This means affirming His descent, approach, and coming, while denying that He has any likeness, peer, equal, or rival. This is the reasoning al-Bukhārī and others use to deny that anything is like Him.

It is said:

He descends in a manner in which nothing is like Him. He has descended in a manner unlike the descent of created beings—a descent unique to Him—just as nothing is like Him in this or in any other attribute with which He has described Himself. He is far exalted above His descent resembling the descent, motion, movement from place to place, or departure of created beings in any respect, whether human or otherwise.

When a created being descends from above to below, it ceases to be described as being above and becomes described as being below, while something else becomes higher than it. But nothing can ever be higher than the Lord, exalted is He. Rather, He is the All-High, the Most High, and He remains the All-High, the Most High, even as He draws close to His servants, comes near them, descends wherever He wills, and comes however He wills. Throughout this, He is the All-High, the Most High, the Most Great, the Supremely Exalted: exalted in His nearness and near in His exaltedness.

Although none other than Him possesses these attributes together, this is because created beings are incapable of combining the two, just as they are incapable of being the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden.

" إنَّهُ يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ كَمَا يَلِيقُ بِشَأْنِهِ "

translated_text:
For this reason, Abū Saʿīd al-Kharrāz was asked, “How did you come to know Allah?” He replied:

“By combining opposites.”

He meant that what would be contradictory in the case of created beings is combined in His case. Thus, He is the Creator of everything—the deeds of His servants and all other entities and actions, with whatever evil they contain—while also being just, wise, and merciful. He enables those of His servants whom He so enables to commit sins, although He has the power to prevent them, yet in this He is wise and just. He is the most knowledgeable of all who know, the wisest of judges, and the best of arbiters. He knows what is before them and what is behind them. It is therefore all the more fitting and certain that their knowledge cannot encompass what is greater than that. They asked about the spirit and were told:

“The spirit is of my Lord’s command, and you have been given only a little knowledge.”

It is related in the two Sahīh collections that, when a sparrow dipped its beak into the sea, al-Khidr said to Moses:

“My knowledge and yours have diminished Allah’s knowledge no more than this sparrow has diminished this sea.”

As for what is denied of Him and from which He is declared free, one category consists of whatever contradicts His known perfect attributes. Anything of this kind is denied of Him, as He says:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.”

And He says:

“And put your trust in the Ever-Living, who does not die.”

Drowsiness, sleep, and death of any kind are therefore impossible for Him. It is impermissible to say of any of these, “It may apply to Him in a manner befitting Him,” because anything of this kind entails a deficiency in His perfection.

translated_text:
Likewise, it is impermissible to say:

“He is below rather than above, with a lowness befitting His majesty.”

For He—glory be to Him—is the Exalted, the Most High; He is never anything but high above. Lowness is a deficiency from which He is far removed. The statement,

“You are the Inward, and nothing is nearer than You,”

implies lowness only to an ignorant person who does not understand the true nature of height and lowness, and therefore imagines that the heavens and whatever they contain may be beneath the earth, whether by night or by day. This is an error, like imagining that what lies in the eastern sky is beneath what lies in the western sky. This too is an error. Rather, the sky is always above the earth. Even though the celestial sphere is round and surrounds the earth, it is truly above the earth in every direction. This has been explained at length elsewhere.

The second category is that He is far exalted above any created thing resembling Him in any of His attributes. Accordingly, what is affirmed by the wording of the Quran and Sunnah is to be affirmed, and what is denied by their wording is to be denied. As for terms that admit more than one meaning, such as “motion,” “descent,” and “change of place,” one must say concerning them that He is far exalted above resembling created beings in any respect. He does not resemble any created being in descent, motion, change of place, departure, or anything else. As for affirming this category, as with the term “descent,” or denying it

Those who affirm these say: “We affirm motion, or motion and change of place, or motion and departure, in a manner befitting Him, just as His descent and coming befit Him.”

Those who deny them say: “Rather, this entire category must be denied.” Some of them deny this category with respect to Him in every sense, holding that no newly arising states can subsist in Him.  إنَّ قِيَامَ الصِّفَاتِ بِهِ. أَوْ قِيَامَ الصِّفَاتِ الِاخْتِيَارِيَّةِ هُوَ مِنْ سِمَاتِ الْحَدَثِ. وَهَذَا بَاطِلٌ عِنْدَ السَّلَفِ وَأَئِمَّةِ السُّنَّةِ بَلْ وَجُمْهُورُ الْعُقَلَاءِ بَلْ مَا ذَكَرُوهُ يَقْتَضِي حُدُوثَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ. فَإِنَّهُ مَا مِنْ مَوْجُودٍ إلَّا وَلَهُ صِفَاتٌ تَقُومُ بِهِ وَتَقُومُ بِهِ أَحْوَالٌ تَحْصُلُ بِالْمَشِيئَةِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ. فَإِنْ كَانَ هَذَا مُسْتَلْزِمًا لِلْحُدُوثِ لَزِمَ حُدُوثُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَأَنْ لَا يَكُونَ فِي الْعَالَمِ شَيْءٌ قَدِيمٌ. وَهَذَا قَدْ بُسِطَ فِي مَوَاضِعَ أَيْضًا. وَسِمَاتُ الْحَدَثِ الَّتِي تَسْتَلْزِمُ الْحُدُوثَ مِثْلُ افْتِقَارٍ إلَى الْغَيْرِ. فَكُلُّ مَا افْتَقَرَ إلَى غَيْرِهِ فَإِنَّهُ مُحْدَثٌ كَائِنٌ بَعْدَ أَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ. وَالرَّبُّ مُنَزَّهٌ عَنْ الْحَاجَةِ إلَى مَا سِوَاهُ بِكُلِّ وَجْهٍ. وَمَنْ ظَنَّ أَنَّهُ مُحْتَاجٌ إلَى الْعَرْشِ أَوْ حَمَلَةِ الْعَرْشِ فَهُوَ جَاهِلٌ ضَالٌّ. بَلْ هُوَ الْغَنِيُّ بِنَفْسِهِ وَكُلُّ مَا سِوَاهُ فَقِيرٌ إلَيْهِ مِنْ كُلِّ وَجْهٍ. وَهُوَ الصَّمَدُ الْغَنِيُّ عَنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَكُلُّ مَا سِوَاهُ يَصْمُدُ إلَيْهِ مُحْتَاجًا إلَيْهِ 
{يَسْأَلُهُ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ هُوَ فِي شَأْنٍ}
translated_text:
the signs of temporal origination, or anything that entails imperfection and temporal origination—the Lord is free of all such things,” this is a true, well-known statement upon which there is agreement. The issue, however, concerns what those who negate the attributes claim to be marks of temporal origination, while others dispute their claim—especially since the Quran and Sunnah contradict their position.

The Jahmiyyah say: “The subsistence of attributes in Him, or of attributes pertaining to His will, is among the marks of temporal origination.” This is false according to the early generations, the leading scholars of the Sunnah, and indeed the majority of rational people. In fact, their claim entails that everything has a temporal beginning. For every existing being has attributes subsisting in it, as well as states that arise through will and power. If this necessarily entails temporal origination, it follows that everything has a temporal beginning and that nothing in all existence is eternal. This too has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The marks of temporal origination that necessarily entail it include dependence upon another. Whatever depends upon another has a temporal beginning, coming into existence after not having existed. The Lord is entirely free of any need for anything besides Himself. Whoever thinks that He needs the Throne or the bearers of the Throne is ignorant and astray. Rather, He is self-sufficient, while everything besides Him depends upon Him in every respect. He is the One upon whom all depend, needing nothing, while everything besides Him turns to Him in need:

“All who are in the heavens and the earth ask of Him; every day He is engaged in a matter.”

" مَا اسْتَلْزَمَ نَقْصًا أَوْ حُدُوثًا فَالرَّبُّ مُنَزَّهٌ عَنْهُ "

translated_text:
And among the marks of temporal origination are imperfections such as ignorance, blindness, deafness, and muteness. Anything possessing such qualities can only have a temporal beginning, for the Eternal, who has no beginning, is free of them. He possesses the opposites of these qualities, and the attributes of perfection are inseparable from Him. An inseparable attribute cannot cease to exist unless that which possesses it ceases to exist. His Essence is eternal, without beginning, necessarily existent in itself, and independent of everything besides itself. Nonexistence and cessation are utterly impossible for it. Its inseparable attributes therefore cannot cease to exist, nor can it possess their opposites. Only a temporally originated being can possess those opposites. They are thus marks of temporal origination, necessarily entailing that whatever possesses them has a temporal beginning. This falls within the statement:

“The Lord is free of anything that entails temporal origination or imperfection.”

An imperfection contrary to His attributes of perfection necessarily entails that whatever possesses it has a temporal beginning. Temporal origination, in turn, necessarily entails the imperfection inherent in created beings. Every created being depends upon another, comes into existence after not having existed, knows only what it has been taught, and can do only what it has been enabled to do. It is encompassed and subject to another’s power.

These imperfections, inherent in every created being, necessarily accompany temporal origination: wherever there is temporal origination, they are present. Temporal origination likewise necessarily accompanies them: wherever there is a temporally originated being, these imperfections are present. Thus, our statement is true:

“The Lord is free of anything that entails imperfection or temporal origination.”

translated_text:
Temporal origination and the imperfection inherent in created beings necessarily accompany one another. The Lord is free of each on two grounds: each is intrinsically impossible for Him, and each necessarily entails the other, which is likewise intrinsically impossible for Him. Thus each, considered in two respects, is both evidence and something established by evidence, showing that the Lord is free of it and of what it implies—its necessary concomitant.

Need of another and dependence upon another necessarily entail temporal origination and the imperfection inherent in created beings. I use the qualification “inherent” to encompass all created beings. Otherwise, some imperfections characterize certain created beings but not others, and are therefore not inherent in every created being. The Lord is free of these as well. Yet if He is free of the imperfection inherent in every created being, He is all the more certainly free of imperfections peculiar to some created beings. For if a created being is held to be free of an imperfection, the Creator is all the more deserving of being declared free of it. This is the method of arguing “with greater reason,” as indicated by the Quran in several places.

In our response to “The Tadmur Questions,” entitled “Establishing the Affirmation of the Names and Attributes and Explaining the True Reconciliation of Divine Decree and Revealed Law,” we explained that, when declaring the Lord free of something, it is not permissible to rely merely on its absence from revelation and transmitted reports, saying: “Whatever is mentioned in the reports, we affirm; whatever is not mentioned, we do not affirm—rather, we deny it,” and basing our denial on the absence of a report.

translated_text:
Rather, this is mistaken for two reasons:

First: the absence of a transmitted report is merely the absence of one particular proof, and the implication of a proof does not hold in reverse. Thus, if He has not informed us of something, it does not follow that it is nonexistent in reality. Allah has names by which He has named Himself and which He has reserved for Himself in His knowledge of the unseen. Just as affirmation requires evidence, so too does negation. But when no report has been transmitted concerning something and it is not known to be established, one must remain silent about it and not speak about Allah without knowledge.

Second: there are things which no transmitted report excludes from Him or declares Him free of, yet transmitted reports establish that He possesses their opposites, thereby establishing their absence from Him. The governing principle is that He is free of everything that contradicts His attributes of perfection. Both revelation and reason establish this. Whatever is not mentioned in a transmitted report, we deny if we know it to be absent; otherwise, we remain silent about it. We therefore neither affirm nor deny anything without knowledge.

Treating the negation of something—whether an attribute or anything else—as equivalent to negating the evidence for it is a method followed by some scholars of rational inquiry and transmitted reports. It is mistaken unless that evidence is a necessary concomitant of the thing in question. If the necessary concomitant is absent, that which necessarily entails it is also absent. Evidence in general, however, must imply what it establishes, whereas the converse is not required. Thus, the existence of evidence entails the existence of what it establishes, but the implication does not hold in reverse.

translated_text:
Thus, there are three categories: whatever is known to be established is affirmed; whatever is known to be absent is denied; and whatever is not known to be either absent or established is left unaddressed. This is what is required. Remaining silent about something is not the same as asserting definitively that it is absent or established. Whoever makes affirmations only in the terms established by revelation, seeks clarification and further detail when other terms are used, and, if the meaning accords with what revelation affirms, affirms it using the scriptural wording, has held fast to revelation in both wording and meaning. This is the path of those who hold fast to the firmest handhold.

However, one must understand the scriptural evidence, both its chains of transmission and its texts. The authenticity of the Quran’s wording is known; one must therefore understand the ways in which it conveys meaning. As for the Sunnah, one must know what has been authentically established and what is known to be fabricated. For some who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah, revered the Sunnah and revelation, and believed that they had held fast to the Book and the Sunnah in this matter, collected hadiths concerning the divine attributes. Among these were reports known to be fabricated, reports more likely to be fabricated, reports more likely to be authentic, and reports whose status was uncertain. They made these hadiths articles of belief and compiled works on them. Some of them declare those who disagree with what these hadiths indicate to be unbelievers.

Others go further, saying: “The Quran conveys meaning through transmitted words, and evidence conveyed through transmitted words does not yield certainty.” They instead place their reliance on what they claim to be rational arguments, although these are false and unsound; some are demonstrably invalid and untrue. These people, too, may declare those who disagree with them unbelievers, just as the former group does. Both approaches are false, even if their adherents do not declare their opponents unbelievers. If someone does declare his opponent an unbeliever, he becomes one of those people of innovation who introduce an innovation and declare anyone who disagrees with them concerning it an unbeliever, as the Khawārij and others have done.

It has been explained at length elsewhere that proofs yielding certain knowledge can never contradict one another. Rational evidence yielding certain knowledge never contradicts revealed evidence yielding certain knowledge, as we have explained in the book *Averting Conflict between Reason and Revelation*.

He is quick to declare anyone who disagrees with him an unbeliever over what he claims to be the Sunnah, although he may himself be mistaken, either because he relies on weak hadiths or because he relies on authentic hadiths that do not support his contention. Even where he is correct concerning the Sunnah, it is not permissible to declare everyone who disagrees with him an unbeliever. Not everyone who errs is an unbeliever, especially in subtle questions over which the Muslim community has disagreed extensively, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Likewise, Abū ʿAlī al-Ahwāzī compiled a work on the divine attributes in which he brought together both sound and unsound material. The same applies to the material collected by ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Mandah. Although he is among the most prolific transmitters of hadith, he narrates many weak hadiths without distinguishing the authentic from the weak. He sometimes compiles an entire chapter whose hadiths are all weak, such as those concerning eating clay and other subjects. He also narrates from Abū ʿAlī al-Ahwāzī.

Some of the unusual, fabricated reports he narrated reached Hasan ibn ʿAdī, who based false beliefs upon them and claimed that Allah can be seen directly with one’s own eyes in this world. Those of his followers who hold this view then declare anyone who disagrees with them an unbeliever. As noted above, this is the practice of the people of innovation, as exemplified by the Khawārij.

The expression “creaking” also occurs in other reports.

translated_text:
al-Zāghūnī and others like them, that this wording was authentic. They therefore accepted it as transmitted and explained its meaning by saying that His rising over the Throne does not extend to that portion.

It is reported that Ibn al-‘Āyidh said: “It is the place where Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, will sit.”

Ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī transmitted the hadith in his Tafsīr, as did others, with the wording:

“He indeed sits upon it, and not even four fingers’ breadth of it remains to spare.”

This wording is negative. Even if the only difficulty in the hadith were the discrepancy between its two versions—one denying what the other affirms—it would still be impossible to state categorically that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, intended the affirmative meaning: that four fingers’ breadth of the Throne remains to spare, over which the Lord does not rise. This is a peculiar interpretation, with no corroboration whatsoever in any of the narrations. Rather, it implies that the Throne is greater and larger than the Lord. This is false and contrary to the Quran, the Sunnah and reason.

It also implies that one recognizes the Lord’s greatness only by magnifying the created Throne, while making the Throne greater than Him. Thus, the Lord would be deemed great only by comparison with a created thing that is greater than the Lord. This is an unsound meaning, contrary to what is known from the Quran, the Sunnah and reason. The Quran’s approach in this regard is to demonstrate the Lord’s greatness: He is greater than everything whose greatness one recognizes. It therefore mentions the greatness of created things and explains that the Lord is greater than they are.

as in the other hadith recorded in the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere—the hadith concerning the creaking of the Throne—when the Bedouin said:

“‘We seek Allah’s intercession with you, and your intercession with Allah Most High.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, glorified Allah until its effect could be seen on his Companions’ faces. Then he said: ‘Woe to you! Do you know what you are saying? Do you know who Allah is? Allah’s majesty is far greater than that. His Throne is above His heavens like this’—and he gestured with his hand to indicate a dome—‘and indeed it creaks under Him as a new saddle creaks under its rider.’”

He thus explained the greatness of the Throne and that it is above the heavens like a dome. He then explained how small it is before Allah’s greatness, and that it creaks under Him as a new saddle creaks under its rider. This affirms the greatness of the Throne while showing that the Lord is greater still.

Likewise, it is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Are you astonished at Saʿd’s jealousy? I am more jealous than he, and Allah is more jealous than I.”

He also said:

“No one is more jealous than Allah. For that reason, He has forbidden indecencies, both open and secret.”

There are many such examples. This and other evidence indicate that the correct version of the report is the negative one: it mentions the greatness of the Throne, yet despite that greatness, the Lord has risen over all of it, with not even four fingers’ breadth remaining to spare.

This is the lower limit of the bodily measures used to measure area, just as a corresponding measure is used in weighing. Thus one says: “There is not a palm-sized patch of cloud in the sky.” People measure dimensions by the armspan and the cubit, and the smallest measure they have is
