translated_text:
the palm. Thus, when they wish to deny the presence of any amount, small or great, they use this measure, saying: “There is not a palm-sized patch of cloud in the sky.” This is like expressions of comprehensive negation such as:

“Indeed, Allah does not wrong even an atom’s weight,”

and:

“They do not possess even the thin membrane of a date stone,”

and similar expressions. The Messenger thus explained that none of the Throne remains to spare—not even this slight amount, four fingers’ breadth, which is the smallest measure used. This is a sound meaning, consistent with the Arabic language, with what the Book and the Sunnah indicate, and with the Messenger’s manner of explaining things; it also has supporting evidence. It can therefore be affirmed with certainty that this is what the hadith says.

Those who said, “Nothing remains to spare except four fingers’ breadth,” did not understand this meaning. They thought that he had made an exception, so they introduced an exception and were mistaken. Rather, it reinforces the negation and confirms that it is comprehensive. Otherwise, what wisdom would there be in leaving four fingers’ breadth of the Throne unoccupied? These fingers are human fingers, for that is what the expression is understood to mean. Why, then, would the Lord not have risen over this slight portion, when the Throne is small before the greatness of Allah Most High?

There is also a hadith narrated by Ibn Abī Hātim concerning His words, “Vision cannot encompass Him.” Its meaning has supporting evidence that points to this. We should therefore examine the hadith and establish the agreement between the Book and the Sunnah. Such is the matter, and Allah knows best.

He said: Abū Zur‘ah narrated to us: Minjāb ibn al-Hārith narrated to us: Bishr ibn ‘Umārah informed us, from Abū Rawq, from ‘Atiyyah al-‘Awfī, from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning His words, Most High:

“Vision cannot encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision”:

“If the jinn, humankind, devils and angels, from the time they were created until they ceased to exist, were arranged in a single row, they would never encompass Allah.”

This has supporting evidence, such as the reports in the authentic collections explaining His words, Most High:

“The whole earth will be in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “The seven heavens, the seven earths and all who are in them are, in the hand of the Most Merciful, no more than a mustard seed in the hand of one of you.”

It is known that the Throne does not reach this degree, for it has bearers and there is space around it. Allah Most High says:

“Those who bear the Throne and those around it.”

This has been discussed at length elsewhere, in “The Question of Encompassing” and other discussions. And Allah knows best.

Section

Thus, the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained the principles that lead to the truth

translated_text:
in the best possible manner, and explained most clearly the signs pointing to the Creator—glory be to Him—His most beautiful names, His sublime attributes, and His oneness, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

As for the innovators among the speculative theologians, philosophers, and others like them, they did not establish the truth. Rather, they laid down principles that contradict it. They not only failed to find guidance themselves or direct others to the truth; they also established principles contrary to the truth. Recognizing that these principles contradicted what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had brought, they gave them precedence over his message.

At times they say, “The Messenger brought imaginative representations”; at others, “He brought teachings requiring figurative interpretation”; and at others, “He brought teachings that leave people in ignorance.”

The philosophers and those who agree with them sometimes say: “He addressed the general public through imaginative representations. He did not intend to tell them things as they really were; rather, he told them the opposite, so that they would imagine what would benefit them.”

This is the position of those who acknowledge that he knew the truth, such as Ibn Sīnā and his like. They say: “What he accomplished through imaginative representations was the utmost that could be achieved.”

Others among them say: “He did not know the truth; rather, he imagined things and made others imagine them,” as al-Fārābī and his like maintain. They regard the philosopher as superior to the prophet and consider prophethood to be a kind of dreaming.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا أَكْثَرُ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ فَيَقُولُونَ:
 بَلْ لَمْ يَقْصِدْ أَنْ يُخْبِرَ إلَّا بِالْحَقِّ لَكِنْ بِعِبَارَاتِ لَا تَدُلُّ وَحْدَهَا عَلَيْهِ بَلْ تَحْتَاجُ إلَى التَّأْوِيلِ لِيَبْعَثَ الْهِمَمَ عَلَى مَعْرِفَتِهِ بِالنَّظَرِ وَالْعَقْلِ وَيَبْعَثَهَا عَلَى تَأْوِيلِ كَلَامِهِ لِيُعَظِّمَ أَجْرَهَا. وَالْمَلَاحِدَةُ يَسْلُكُونَ مَسْلَكَ التَّأْوِيلِ وَيَفْتَحُونَ بَابَ الْقَرْمَطَةِ. وَهَؤُلَاءِ يُجَوِّزُونَ التَّأْوِيلَ مَعَ الْخَاصَّةِ.
 وَأَمَّا أَهْلُ التَّخْيِيلِ فَيَقُولُونَ:
 الْخَاصَّةُ قَدْ عَرَفُوا أَنَّ مُرَادَهُ التَّخْيِيلُ لِلْعَامَّةِ فَالتَّأْوِيلُ مُمْتَنِعٌ.
 وَالْفَرِيقَانِ يَسْلُكُونَ مَسْلَكَ إلْجَامِ الْعَوَامِّ عَنْ التَّأْوِيلِ لَكِنَّ أُولَئِكَ يَقُولُونَ:
 لَهَا تَأْوِيلٌ يَفْهَمُهُ الْخَاصَّةُ. وَهِيَ طَرِيقَةُ الْغَزَالِيِّ فِي 
" الْإِلْجَامِ "
.
 اسْتَقْبَحَ أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 كَذَّبُوا لِلْمَصْلَحَةِ. وَهُوَ أَيْضًا لَا يَرَى تَأْوِيلَ الْأَعْمَالِ كَالْقَرَامِطَةِ بَلْ تَأْوِيلَ الْخَبَرِ عَنْ الْمَلَائِكَةِ وَعَنْ الْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ. وَكَذَلِكَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ تَرَى التَّأْوِيلَ فِي ذَلِكَ. وَهَذَا مُخَالِفٌ لِطَرِيقَةِ أَهْلِ التَّخْيِيلِ. وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ الْغَزَالِيُّ هَذَا عَنْهُمْ فِي 
" الْإِحْيَاءِ "
 لَمَّا ذَكَرَ إسْرَافَهُمْ فِي التَّأْوِيلِ وَذَكَرَهُ فِي مَوَاضِعَ كَمَا حَكَى كَلَامَهُ فِي 
" السَّبْعِينِيَّةِ "
 وَغَيْرِهَا.
translated_text:
As for most speculative theologians, they say:

“Rather, he intended to convey nothing but the truth, yet used expressions that do not indicate it on their own, but require figurative interpretation. This was to spur people to discover the truth through reflection and reason, and to interpret his words, thereby increasing their reward.”

The heretics follow the path of figurative interpretation and open the door to Qarmatianism. These people permit figurative interpretation among the elite.

As for those who advocate imaginative representations, they say:

“The elite already know that his intention was to provide imaginative representations for the common people, so figurative interpretation is impossible.”

Both groups follow the approach of restraining the common people from figurative interpretation. The former, however, say: “There is a figurative interpretation that the elite understand.” This is al-Ghazālī’s approach in al-Iljām. He found it objectionable to say: “They lied to serve a beneficial purpose.” Nor does he endorse interpreting actions figuratively, as the Qarmatians do, but rather accounts concerning the angels and the Last Day. A group of philosophers likewise advocates figurative interpretation in these matters. This differs from the approach of those who advocate imaginative representations.

Al-Ghazālī mentioned this position of theirs in al-Ihyā’ when discussing their excesses in figurative interpretation. He also mentioned it in several other places, as quoted from his writings in al-Sab‘īniyya and elsewhere.

original_text:
وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّالِثُ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ:
 هَذَا لَا يَعْلَمُ مَعْنَاهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ أَوْ لَهُ تَأْوِيلٌ يُخَالِفُ ظَاهِرَهُ لَا يَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ. فَهَؤُلَاءِ يَجْعَلُونَ الرَّسُولَ وَغَيْرَهُ غَيْرَ عَالِمِينَ بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ. فَلَا يُسَوِّغُونَ التَّأْوِيلَ لِأَنَّ الْعِلْمَ بِالْمُرَادِ عِنْدَهُمْ مُمْتَنِعٌ. وَلَا يستجيزون الْقَوْلَ بِطَرِيقَةِ التَّخْيِيلِ لِمَا فِيهَا مِنْ التَّصْرِيحِ بِكَذِبِ الرَّسُولِ.
 بَلْ يَقُولُونَ:
 خُوطِبُوا بِمَا لَا يَفْهَمُونَهُ لِيُثَابُوا عَلَى تِلَاوَتِهِ وَالْإِيمَانِ بِأَلْفَاظِهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَفْهَمُوا مَعْنَاهُ. يَجْعَلُونَ ذَلِكَ تَعَبُّدًا مَحْضًا عَلَى رَأْيِ الْمُجْبِرَةِ الَّذِينَ يُجَوِّزُونَ التَّعَبُّدَ بِمَا لَا نَفْعَ فِيهِ لِلْعَامِلِ بَلْ يُؤْجَرُ عَلَيْهِ. وَالْكَلَامُ عَلَى هَؤُلَاءِ وَفَسَادِ قَوْلِهِمْ مَذْكُورٌ فِي مَوَاضِعَ. وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا أَنَّ الَّذِي دَعَاهُمْ إلَى ذَلِكَ ظَنُّهُمْ أَنَّ الْمَعْقُولَ يُنَاقِضُ مَا أَخْبَرَ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَوْ ظَاهِرُ مَا أَخْبَرَ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ. وَقَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَى رَدِّ هَذَا فِي مَوَاضِعَ وَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ الْعَقْلَ لَا يُنَاقِضُ السَّمْعَ وَأَنَّ مَا نَاقَضَهُ فَهُوَ فَاسِدٌ. وَبَيَّنَ بَعْدِ هَذَا أَنَّ الْعَقْلَ مُوَافِقٌ لِمَا جَاءَ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ شَاهِدٌ لَهُ وَمُصَدِّقٌ لَهُ.
 لَا يُقَالُ:
 إنَّهُ غَيْرُ مُعَارِضٍ فَقَطْ بَلْ هُوَ مُوَافِقٌ مُصَدِّقٌ فَأُولَئِكَ كَانُوا يَقُولُونَ: هُوَ مُكَذِّبٌ مُنَاقِضٌ. بَيَّنَ أَوَّلًا أَنَّهُ لَا يُكَذِّبُ وَلَا يُنَاقِضُ ثُمَّ بَيَّنَ ثَانِيًا أَنَّهُ مُصَدِّقٌ مُوَافِقٌ.
translated_text:
The third group consists of those who say:

“Only Allah knows the meaning of this, or it has an interpretation contrary to its apparent meaning that only Allah knows.”

These people thus regard the Messenger and everyone else as not knowing what Allah revealed. They do not permit figurative interpretation because, in their view, knowledge of the intended meaning is impossible. Nor do they consider it permissible to adopt the approach of imaginative representations, since it explicitly attributes lying to the Messenger.

Rather, they say:

“They were addressed in words they did not understand so that they might be rewarded for reciting them and believing in their wording, even without understanding their meaning.”

They regard this as purely an act of worship, following the view of the determinists, who hold that a person may be required to perform acts of worship that bring him no benefit, yet be rewarded for them. These people and the unsoundness of their position have been discussed elsewhere.

The point here is that what led them to this was their assumption that what is known through reason contradicts what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—conveyed, or the apparent meaning of what he conveyed. This claim has been refuted at length elsewhere, where it has been shown that reason does not contradict revelation and that whatever contradicts revelation is unsound. Beyond this, it has been shown that reason agrees with what the Messenger brought, bears witness to it, and confirms its truth.

It is not merely said that reason does not oppose it; rather, reason agrees with it and confirms its truth. Those people used to say that reason disproves and contradicts it. It was first shown that reason neither disproves nor contradicts it; then, secondly, that reason confirms its truth and agrees with it.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا هَؤُلَاءِ فَيُبَيَّنُ أَنَّ كَلَامَهُمْ الَّذِي يُعَارِضُونَ بِهِ الرَّسُولَ بَاطِلٌ لَا تَعَارُضَ فِيهِ. وَلَا يَكْفِي كَوْنُهُ بَاطِلًا لَا يُعَارَضُ بَلْ هُوَ أَيْضًا مُخَالِفٌ لِصَرِيحِ الْعَقْلِ. فَهُمْ كَانُوا يَدَّعُونَ أَنَّ الْعَقْلَ يُنَاقِضُ النَّقْلَ.
 فَيُبَيِّنُ أَرْبَعَ مَقَامَاتٍ:
 أَنَّ الْعَقْلَ لَا يُنَاقِضُهُ. ثُمَّ يُبَيِّنُ أَنَّ الْعَقْلَ يُوَافِقُهُ. وَيُبَيِّنُ أَنَّ عَقْلِيَّاتِهِمْ الَّتِي عَارَضُوا بِهَا النَّقْلَ بَاطِلَةٌ. وَيُبَيِّنُ أَيْضًا أَنَّ الْعَقْلَ الصَّرِيحَ يُخَالِفُهُمْ. ثُمَّ لَا يَكْفِي أَنَّ الْعَقْلَ يُبْطِلُ مَا عَارَضُوا بِهِ الرَّسُولَ بَلْ يُبَيِّنُ أَنَّ مَا جَعَلُوهُ دَلِيلًا عَلَى إثْبَاتِ الصَّانِعِ إنَّمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَفْيِهِ. فَهُمْ أَقَامُوا حُجَّةً تَسْتَلْزِمُ نَفْيَ الصَّانِعِ وَإِنْ كَانُوا يَظُنُّونَ أَنَّهُمْ يُثْبِتُونَ بِهَا الصَّانِعَ. وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا أَنَّ كَلَامَهُمْ الَّذِي زَعَمُوا أَنَّهُمْ أَثْبَتُوا بِهِ الصَّانِعَ إنَّمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَفْيِ الصَّانِعِ وَتَعْطِيلِهِ. فَلَا يَكْفِي فِيهِ أَنَّهُ بَاطِلٌ لَمْ يَدُلَّ عَلَى الْحَقِّ؛ بَلْ دَلَّ عَلَى الْبَاطِلِ الَّذِي يَعْلَمُونَ هُمْ وَسَائِرُ الْعُقَلَاءِ أَنَّهُ بَاطِلٌ. وَلِهَذَا كَانَ يُقَالُ فِي أُصُولِهِمْ 
" تَرْتِيبُ الْأُصُولِ فِي تَكْذِيبِ الرَّسُولِ "
 وَيُقَالُ أَيْضًا هِيَ 
" تَرْتِيبُ الْأُصُولِ فِي مُخَالَفَةِ الرَّسُولِ وَالْمَعْقُولِ "
. جَعَلُوهَا أُصُولًا لِلْعِلْمِ بِالْخَالِقِ وَهِيَ أُصُولٌ تُنَاقِضُ الْعِلْمَ بِهِ. فَلَا يَتِمُّ الْعِلْمُ بِالْخَالِقِ إلَّا مَعَ اعْتِقَادِ نَقِيضهَا. وَفَرْقٌ بَيْنَ الْأَصْلِ وَالدَّلِيلِ الْمُسْتَلْزِمِ لِلْعِلْمِ بِالرَّبِّ وَبَيْنَ الْمُنَاقِضِ الْمُعَارِضِ لِلْعِلْمِ بِالرَّبِّ.
translated_text:
As for these people, it is shown that the arguments with which they oppose the Messenger are invalid and offer no valid counterargument. It is not enough merely to show that their arguments are invalid and cannot counter his message; they also contradict plain reason. They claimed that reason contradicts revelation.

Four points are therefore demonstrated: that reason does not contradict revelation; that reason agrees with it; that the rational arguments they used to oppose revelation are invalid; and that plain reason itself contradicts their position.

Moreover, it is not enough to show that reason refutes the arguments with which they opposed the Messenger. It is also shown that what they presented as proof of the Maker’s existence actually points to His nonexistence. They have advanced an argument that necessarily entails denying the Maker, even though they think they are establishing His existence through it. The point here is that the arguments by which they claimed to establish the Maker’s existence point only to denying and negating Him. It is not merely that their reasoning is invalid and fails to establish the truth; rather, it points to a falsehood that they themselves, along with all other rational people, know to be false.

For this reason, their principles were described as:

“Arranging the principles to belie the Messenger.”

They were also described as:

“Arranging the principles to oppose the Messenger and reason.”

They made these principles foundations for knowledge of the Creator, yet they are principles that contradict knowledge of Him. Knowledge of the Creator cannot, therefore, be complete unless one believes the opposite of these principles. There is a difference between a foundation and proof that necessarily lead to knowledge of the Lord, and something that contradicts and opposes knowledge of Him.

original_text:
فالمتفلسفة يَقُولُونَ إنَّهُمْ أَثْبَتُوا وَاجِبَ الْوُجُودِ. وَهُمْ لَمْ يُثْبِتُوهُ بَلْ كَلَامُهُمْ يَقْتَضِي أَنَّهُ مُمْتَنِعُ الْوُجُودِ. وَالْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةُ وَنَحْوُهُمْ يَقُولُونَ إنَّهُمْ أَثْبَتُوا الْقَدِيمَ الْمُحْدِثَ لِلْحَوَادِثِ وَهُمْ لَمْ يُثْبِتُوهُ بَلْ كَلَامُهُمْ يَقْتَضِي أَنَّهُ مَا ثَمَّ قَدِيمٌ أَصْلًا. وَكَذَلِكَ الْأَشْعَرِيَّةُ والكَرَّامِيَة وَغَيْرُهُمْ مِمَّنْ يَقُولُ إنَّهُ أَثْبَتَ الْعِلْمَ بِالْخَالِقِ فَهُمْ لَمْ يُثْبِتُوهُ لَكِنَّ كَلَامَهُمْ يَقْتَضِي أَنَّهُ مَا ثَمَّ خَالِقٌ. وَهَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءُ الثَّلَاثَةُ هِيَ الَّتِي يُظْهِرُهَا هَؤُلَاءِ وَاجِبُ الْوُجُودِ وَالْقَدِيمُ وَالصَّانِعُ أَوْ الْخَالِقُ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ. ثُمَّ إنَّهُ مِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ بِضَرُورَةِ الْعَقْلِ أَنَّهُ لَا بُدَّ فِي الْوُجُودِ مِنْ مَوْجُودٍ وَاجِبٍ بِنَفْسِهِ قَدِيمٍ أَزَلِيٍّ مُحْدِثٍ لِلْحَوَادِثِ. فَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا مَعْلُومًا بِالْفِطْرَةِ وَالضَّرُورَةِ وَالْبَرَاهِينِ الْيَقِينِيَّةِ وَكَانَتْ أُصُولُهُمْ الَّتِي عَارَضُوا بِهَا الرَّسُولَ تُنَاقِضُ هَذَا دَلَّ عَلَى فَسَادِهَا جُمْلَةً وَتَفْصِيلًا. وَقَدْ ذَكَرْنَا فِي مَوَاضِعَ أَنَّ الْإِقْرَارَ بِالصَّانِعِ فِطْرِيٌّ ضَرُورِيٌّ مَعَ كَثْرَةِ دَلَائِلِهِ وَبَرَاهِينِهِ.
 وَنَقُولُ هُنَا:
 لَا رَيْبَ أَنَّا نَشْهَدُ الْحَوَادِثَ كَحُدُوثِ السَّحَابِ وَالْمَطَرِ وَالزَّرْعِ وَالشَّجَرِ وَالشَّمْسِ وَحُدُوثِ الْإِنْسَانِ وَغَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْحَيَوَانِ
translated_text:
Thus, the philosophers claim to have established the Necessary Existent. Yet they have not established His existence; rather, their arguments imply that His existence is impossible. The Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and others like them claim to have established the eternal One who originates all that comes into being. Yet they have not established His existence; rather, their arguments imply that nothing eternal exists at all. The same applies to the Ash'ariyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and others who claim to have established knowledge of the Creator: they have not done so; rather, their arguments imply that there is no Creator. These are the three designations they put forward: the Necessary Existent, the Eternal One, and the Maker or Creator, and similar names.

Now, it is self-evident to reason that there must exist a being whose existence is necessary in itself, who is beginningless and eternal, and who originates all that comes into being. Since this is known through our innate disposition, self-evident knowledge, and conclusive proofs, while the principles with which they opposed the Messenger contradict it, this demonstrates that those principles are invalid, both as a whole and in every detail. We have explained elsewhere that acknowledging the Maker is innate and self-evident, notwithstanding the abundance of evidence and proofs for His existence.

Here we say:

There is no doubt that we witness things coming into being, such as clouds, rain, crops, trees, and the sun, as well as the coming into being of human beings and other animals

and the coming into being of night and day, and other such things. It is self-evident to reason that whatever comes into being must have an originator, and that an infinite regress of originated things is impossible: an originated thing has an originator, which in turn has an originator, and so on without end. This is called an infinite regress of causal agents, causes, and efficient causation. It is impossible by the consensus of rational people, as has been explained at length elsewhere, where the objections raised against it were also discussed—including the statements of al-Āmidī and al-Abharī alongside those of al-Rāzī and others. Yet this is self-evident and necessarily known to reason, and those thoughts are Satan’s whisperings. Hence, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed a person who experiences such thoughts to seek refuge in Allah from Satan and to stop pursuing them. He said:

“Satan comes to one of you and asks, ‘Who created such-and-such? Who created such-and-such?’ He replies, ‘Allah.’ Then Satan asks, ‘Who, then, created Allah?’ If any of you experiences this, let him seek refuge in Allah and stop pursuing it.”

It is known that even a single thing cannot come into being without an originator. When things that come into being multiply and form a succession, their need for an originator is all the more evident. They are all originated, so they all need an originator. That dependence can end only with an originator who needs no other, but is eternal and beginningless in Himself—glorified and exalted is He.

If it is said, “Whatever exists is either eternal or originated, and whatever is originated must depend on something eternal; therefore, something eternal must exist in either case,” this is a sound demonstration.

Similarly, if it is said, “Either contingent or necessary,” and “contingent” is explained as meaning that which has come into being, this is an argument of the same kind. But if “contingent” is interpreted in a way that includes the eternal, as Ibn Sīnā and his followers, such as al-Rāzī, did, then this is invalid. For on this interpretation, one cannot establish at the outset the existence of a contingent being dependent on a necessary being, yet the proof cannot be completed without first establishing this. This can only be established on the basis that whatever comes into being must have an originator: its particular instances are witnessed, and its universal principles are known through reason.

As for affirming an eternal, beginningless being that is contingent, rational people unanimously agree that this is impossible. Ibn Sīnā and his followers also agreed that it is impossible, as they stated in their works on logic, following their predecessors. Yet they contradicted themselves at the outset. For both they and their predecessors say:

“What is possible, in the general and specific senses—that which can either exist or not exist—can only be originated; it cannot be necessary. Everything eternal and beginningless is necessary, in their view.”

Similarly, if it is said:

“Whatever exists is either created or uncreated, and whatever is created must depend on something existent that is uncreated; thus, the existence of something uncreated is established in either case.”

Similarly, if it is said:

“Whatever exists is either independent of anything else or dependent on something else, and that which depends on and needs something else can have its need and dependence met only by one who is independent of anything else

Similarly, if it is said:

“A living being either has life in its own right or derives its life from another. If its life comes from another, that other must all the more possess life and is therefore living in its own right. Thus, the existence of one who has life in its own right is established in either case.”

Similarly, if it is said:

“One who possesses knowledge either possesses it in his own right or has been taught by another. Whoever teaches another must all the more possess knowledge; and if he has not learned from another, he possesses knowledge in his own right. Thus, the existence of one who possesses knowledge in his own right is established under either of these two exhaustive alternatives, for no third possibility exists. Since one or the other must be the case, and under either alternative there exists one who possesses knowledge in his own right, one who has life in his own right, one who is independent in his own right, and one who is eternal and necessarily existent in his own right, it follows that such a being exists in reality and that his nonexistence is impossible in reality. This is what was to be proved.”

Similarly, if it is said:

“One who possesses power either possesses it in his own right or has been granted it by another. Whoever grants another power must all the more possess power. If his power does not come from another, it is inseparable from his very being. Thus, under every alternative, the existence of one who possesses power in his own right is established—one whose power is inseparable from his very being, whose knowledge is inseparable from his very being, and whose life is inseparable from his very being.”

Similarly, one who possesses wisdom either possesses it in his own right or derives it from another. Whoever makes another wise must all the more possess wisdom. Thus, the existence of one who possesses wisdom in his own right follows under either alternative.

Similarly, if it is said:

“One who is merciful either possesses mercy in his own right or has been made merciful by another. Whoever makes another merciful must all the more be merciful, and his mercy is inseparable from his very being. Thus, under either alternative, the existence of one who is merciful in his own right, whose mercy is inseparable from his very being, is established.”

Similarly, if it is said:

“One who is generous and beneficent either possesses generosity and beneficence in his own right or derives them from another. Whoever makes another generous and beneficent must all the more be generous and beneficent, with these qualities inseparable from his very being.”

An authentic report relates the following about the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“He saw a woman among the captives who, whenever she saw an infant, would nurse it out of compassion. He said, ‘Do you think this woman would throw her child into the Fire?’

“They replied, ‘No, O Messenger of Allah.’

“He said, ‘Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child.’”

He thus made clear that Allah is more merciful to His servants than even the most compassionate mother is to her child. For the One who made her merciful is more merciful than she is. This is also indicated by His words, “And your Lord is the Most Generous,” and by our saying, “Allah is greater.”

This entails that He deserves unqualified praise for these qualities, that He suffices whoever relies upon Him, and that He graciously protects His servant and grants him mighty support. This entails that He is superior to and more perfect than everything besides Him, as is also indicated by our saying, “Allah is greater.”

Similarly, it may be said:

One who speaks, hears, and sees either possesses speech, hearing, and sight in his own right, or has been made able to hear, see, and speak by another. Whoever makes another able to speak, hear, and see must all the more possess speech, hearing, and sight himself. Otherwise, the one acted upon would be more perfect than the one acting, for these are attributes of perfection.

Likewise, it may be said:

One who is just and truthful either possesses justice and truthfulness in his own right, or has been made truthful and just by another. Whoever makes another truthful and just must all the more be truthful and just himself. All these are sound and clear lines of reasoning.

This may be countered by saying: Whoever makes another unjust or untruthful must likewise be unjust and untruthful, and Ahl al-Sunnah say that He has made others so

The reply is: This is invalid on two grounds.

First, not everyone who causes another to possess a quality, whatever that quality may be, possesses it himself. Rather, whoever causes another to possess an attribute of perfection must all the more possess that attribute himself. As for attributes of deficiency, causing another to be deficient does not entail being deficient oneself. Someone with power can render another powerless without himself being powerless. Someone living can kill another and cause his death without himself being dead. Someone knowledgeable can render another ignorant without himself being ignorant. Someone who hears, sees, and speaks can render another blind, deaf, and mute without himself being so. Thus, causing another to be unjust and untruthful does not entail being untruthful and unjust oneself, for these are attributes of deficiency.

If it is objected that an untruthful and unjust person may sometimes compel another to be truthful and just, the reply is: He has not made him truthful and knowledgeable; he has merely commanded him to be so, and the other person has done so himself.

We did not say that everyone who commands another to do something himself possesses the quality he commands the other to have.

Had he acted on the other’s behalf, he would not have been unjust. If, however, he had some personal motive concerning the victim and killed him unjustly, the person giving the order was nevertheless entitled to have him killed.

The same applies when someone commands another to utter something that, as spoken by the latter, is false—as when Joseph instructed the herald to say:

“O caravan, you are indeed thieves!”

Joseph, peace be upon him, meant: “You indeed stole Joseph from his father,” and in this he was truthful. The person receiving the instruction meant: “You indeed stole the measuring cup.” He thought they had stolen it, so he was not deliberately lying, even though his statement was false.

The actions of the Lord, exalted be He, cannot be measured against those of His servants. Everything He creates serves a wise purpose and a benefit, even if some of what He creates contains evil. Thus, He creates foul entities, such as impure substances and devils, for an overriding wise purpose. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that the proofs establishing the Lord’s existence are exceedingly numerous. Those who claim that reason contradicts what the Messenger has reported, and who say they have established the existence of the Necessary Existent, the Eternal, or the Maker, have not established His existence. Rather, their arguments entail denying His existence and divesting Him of His attributes. They therefore deny Him rather than affirm Him. Their arguments are invalid

Even if they call them “the foundations of knowledge and religion,” they are “the foundations of ignorance and of Satan’s religion, not the religion of the Most Merciful.” Their discourse really amounts to “setting out principles in opposition to the Messenger and reason.” As the inhabitants of the Fire said:

Whoever opposes the Messenger therefore opposes both revelation and reason: he opposes both scriptural and rational proofs.

As for those who affirm the Necessary Existent, we have shown in several places that they have offered no proof of the Necessary Existent, and that when al-Rāzī followed Ibn Sīnā, his books contained no proof of the Necessary Existent. For they made establishing His existence dependent on establishing “the contingent,” a category in which they include the eternal. Thus, their method leaves no way to establish the Necessary Existent except by establishing an eternal contingent being. Yet this is impossible according to self-evident reason and the consensus of rational people. Their method therefore depends on a premise that clear reason shows to be false, and whose falsity rational people unanimously acknowledge. Their proof is consequently invalid.  إنَّهُ يَمْتَنِعُ اتِّصَافُهُ بِصِفَةِ ثُبُوتِيَّةٍ. وَهَذَا مُمْتَنِعُ الْوُجُوبِ لَا مُمْكِنُ الْوُجُوبِ فَضْلًا عَنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ وَاجِبَ الْوُجُودِ كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ هَذَا فِي مَوَاضِعَ وَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ الْوَاجِبَ الَّذِي يَدَّعُونَهُ يَقُولُونَ إنَّهُ لَا يَكُونُ لَا صِفَةً وَلَا مَوْصُوفًا أَلْبَتَّةَ. وَهَذَا إنَّمَا يَتَخَيَّلُ فِي الْأَذْهَانِ لَا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ فِي الْأَعْيَانِ. وَالْوَاجِبُ إذَا فُسِّرَ بِمُبْدِعِ الْمُمَكَّنَاتِ فَهُوَ حَقٌّ وَهُوَ اسْمٌ لِلَّذَّاتِ الْمُتَّصِفَةِ بِصِفَاتِهَا. وَإِذَا فُسِّرَ بِالْمَوْجُودِ بِنَفَسِهِ الَّذِي لَا فَاعِلَ لَهُ فَالذَّاتُ وَاجِبَةٌ وَالصِّفَاتُ وَاجِبَةٌ. وَإِذَا فُسِّرَ بِمَا لَا فَاعِلَ لَهُ وَلَا مُحْدِثَ فَالذَّاتُ وَاجِبَةٌ وَالصِّفَاتُ لَيْسَتْ وَاجِبَةً. وَإِذَا فُسِّرَ بِمَا لَيْسَ صِفَةً وَلَا مَوْصُوفًا فَهَذَا بَاطِلٌ لَا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ. بَلْ هُوَ مُمْتَنِعُ الْوُجُودِ لَا مُمْكِنَ الْوُجُودِ وَلَا وَاجِبَ الْوُجُودِ. وَكُلَّمَا أَمْعَنُوا فِي تَجْرِيدِهِ عَنْ الصِّفَاتِ كَانُوا أَشَدَّ إيغَالًا فِي التَّعْطِيلِ كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ فِي مَوَاضِعَ. وَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ قَالُوا إنَّهُمْ أَثْبَتُوا الْقَدِيمَ مِنْ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَمَنْ سَلَكَ سَبِيلَهُمْ مِنْ الْأَشْعَرِيَّةِ والكَرَّامِيَة الَّذِينَ اسْتَدَلُّوا بِحُدُوثِ الْأَعْرَاضِ
translated_text:
the Necessary Existent. Yet they have also affirmed something eternal that is not necessarily existent. What they affirmed concerning the eternal thus contradicts its being the Lord of all worlds, for they affirmed an eternal category comprising both the necessary and the non-necessary.

Moreover, they say that the Necessary Existent they have affirmed cannot possess any positive attribute. Such a being cannot possibly be necessary, let alone necessarily existent. This has been explained at length elsewhere, where it has been shown that they describe their supposed Necessary Existent as neither an attribute nor anything possessing attributes whatsoever. This can only be imagined in the mind; it has no reality outside it.

If “the Necessary Existent” is understood to mean the Originator of contingent beings, this is true, and the designation refers to the Essence possessing its attributes. If it is understood to mean the self-existent being that has no agent causing it, then both the Essence and the attributes are necessary. If it is understood to mean that which has neither an agent nor an originator, then the Essence is necessary, but the attributes are not necessary. If it is understood to mean that which is neither an attribute nor anything possessing attributes, this is false and has no reality. Indeed, its existence is impossible, neither contingent nor necessary. The further they go in stripping it of attributes, the more deeply they plunge into the denial of divine attributes, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

As for those who claim to have established the existence of the Eternal—the Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and those Ashʿarīs and Karrāmīs who followed their path, arguing from the coming into existence of accidents

 وَقَدْ أَقَمْنَا الدَّلِيلَ عَلَى حُدُوثِ كُلِّ جِسْمٍ. فَإِنَّ
translated_text:
and their inseparability from bodies, and from the impossibility of a beginningless succession of events, that bodies came into existence—they have not established the existence of the Maker, given the known invalidity of this argument. For they claim that the Lord cannot speak by His will or do whatever He wills. Indeed, their position ultimately implies that He cannot have always possessed power. Their arguments for this impossibility have been presented in full elsewhere, along with their own statements demonstrating the invalidity of those arguments.

As for their denial of the Creator, the implication of their position is that any being who has always spoken at will must have a beginning. It would therefore follow that the Lord has a beginning and is not eternal. Indeed, their fundamental principle implies that anything in which attributes and acts subsist must have come into existence. Every existent must possess attributes and acts, so it would follow that every existent came into existence.

For this reason, the leading proponents of this approach—the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah—explicitly denied the Lord’s attributes and denied that acts or any other matters subject to His will subsist in His Essence, since this is what their argument entails. Yet these attributes necessarily belong to Him, and denying a necessary concomitant entails denying that which it necessarily accompanies. Thus, their position ultimately amounts to negating the Lord and denying His existence.

They call attributes “accidents,” and acts and the like “events.” They therefore said, “The Lord must be held to transcend having accidents and events subsist in Him, for that would entail His being a body.”

They said:

“We have established a proof that every body came into existence. For

a body is never free of accidents that come into existence, nor does it precede them. Whatever is inseparable from events and does not precede them must itself have come into existence.”

Yet scriptural and rational proofs have established the position of the early generations: that the Lord has always spoken whenever He wills. Their position would therefore entail that He neither preceded events nor was ever separate from them. According to their position, He must consequently have come into existence. Thus, the very principle by which they established the existence of the Eternal entails that He is not eternal and that nothing eternal exists. Likewise, the others’ principle entails that He is not necessary in Himself and that nothing necessary in itself exists. The approach by which they claim to establish the Maker’s existence contradicts the affirmation of His existence.

If they say, “Knowledge of the Maker is possible only through this approach,” the correct response is: “Rather, complete knowledge of the Maker is possible only with knowledge of the invalidity of this approach.” Hence, everyone who accepts its validity has denied some of what the Messenger reported concerning matters that necessarily belong to the Lord. Denying a necessary concomitant entails denying that which it necessarily accompanies.

Those who claim to use this as proof that bodies came into existence argue along the same lines as those others who claim to use it as proof that bodies are contingent. Both arguments are invalid.

And the implication is that everything that exists came into existence and is contingent, and that nothing in existence is eternal or necessary in itself. Thus, their principles contradict the conclusion they seek to establish. This approach misleads rather than guides. But it is as Allah Most High says:

“And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil who becomes his companion.”

“And indeed, they turn them away from the path, while they think they are rightly guided.”

As for those who say, “We affirm the Maker and Creator,” and maintain that they follow another approach, such as inferring the Lord’s existence from attributes coming into existence—this does indeed point to Him without requiring the commitments made by the others. Al-Rāzī mentioned this approach. Al-Ashʿarī himself, however, did not use it. Rather, in al-Lumaʿ and his Epistle to al-Thaghr, he inferred from events that the things in which they inhere came into existence, as in his discussion of the sperm-drop, on the premise that a beginningless sequence of events is impossible. He then took the coming into existence of those substances—which he said he had demonstrated—as proof of the Maker’s existence. This approach is invalid, as has already been explained. It may then be said: These people affirm a Creator who performs no act of creation. Yet this is self-evidently impossible to reason. Thus, they have not affirmed a Creator.

Although the Karrāmiyyah say that the act of creation is distinct from the created thing, they maintain that the act of creation comes into existence without any cause necessitating its occurrence. This too is impossible. Thus, they have not affirmed a Creator.

Furthermore, both groups say: “What necessitates the selection of what comes into existence, rather than something else, is an eternal, beginningless will.”

The Karrāmiyyah say: “It is this will that determines what inheres in Him and what He creates.” According to the others, however, nothing willed inheres in Him. Rather, they say: “It is this will that determines what comes into existence.”

Both groups, and those who agree with them, say: “That will is eternal and beginningless, having always remained in one and the same state; then events came into existence without any cause whatsoever.”

They also say: “It is in its nature to select one of two equivalent alternatives over the other, and to precede what is willed from all eternity.” Thus, they ascribe to the will three invalid attributes, although sound reason plainly establishes that a will cannot be like this. Yet it is the will that brings about creation and coming into existence. If it is affirmed as they describe it, there can be neither creation nor coming into existence.

Likewise, they have described the power they affirm in terms that make it impossible for it to be power at all. Yet power is a condition of creation. If they negate a condition of creation, creation itself is negated, and He is no longer a Creator. Thus, what they attribute to the Creator contradicts His being a Creator; it is not a necessary consequence of His being a Creator. Yet they have made it a necessary consequence rather than a contradiction.

As for the will, they ascribe to it three necessary characteristics, all of which contradict its being a will. They say that it exists without anything willed by it existing—indeed, that this has always been the case—and then what it wills comes into existence without any change in the will itself. The invalidity of this is self-evident to reason. For when an agent wills to act, what preceded was a resolve to act and an intention to do so at a future time, not a will to perform the act immediately. Rather, when he acts, there must be a will to act at that moment.

Hence the saying:

“Prior volition is resolve; concurrent volition is intention.”

It is therefore impossible for an act to occur through resolve alone, without a fresh intention arising in the agent. Thus, created things could not come into being through such a will, even supposing that events could arise without a cause. How much more so when that too is inherently impossible? Thus, the impossibility arises both from the will and from its being determined by something that is inherently impossible.

The second is their claim that the will selects one of two equivalent alternatives over the other. This is a denial of the obvious. Rather, the will can only be directed towards something whose existence the agent prefers to its nonexistence, either because he knows it to be better or because his love for it is stronger. The third is their claim that a resolute will may fail to bring about what is willed despite the presence of power.

This too is false. Rather, whenever complete power and resolute will are present, what lies within that power must come into existence. Where this does not necessarily follow, it is only because of deficient power or the absence of complete will. As for the Lord, Exalted is He, whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. In several places, He declares that, had He willed, He would have done things that He has not done, as He says:

“Had We willed, We could have given every soul its guidance.”

“Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community.”

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another.”

He thus makes clear that, were He to will that, He would have the power to do it. Yet He does not do it because He has not willed it, since not willing it is more consonant with wisdom, even though He would have the power to do it were He to will it. What these people and others say about power and will has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Some of these people say that His power extends only to things distinct from Him, not to acts subsisting in Himself. This is the position of the Mu‘tazilah, the Jahmiyyah, and those among the Ash‘ariyyah and others who agree with them.

Others say that His power extends both to acts subsisting in Him and to things distinct from Him, as is reported of the Karrāmiyyah.

The correct view, as indicated by the Quran and reason, is that His power extends to both. The Most High says:

“Yes, We are able even to restore his fingertips.”

He also says:

“Is He not able to give life to the dead?”

“Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?”

“And We are certainly able to take it away.”

Such statements occur frequently in the Quran, more frequently than the other kind. What the Karrāmiyyah and Hishāmiyyah say is closer to reason and revelation than what the Jahmiyyah and those who agree with them say, although the position reported of them is mistaken insofar as they deny His power over things distinct from Him. Allah Most High has declared that He has power over all things.

It is related in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Abū Mas‘ūd when he saw him beating his slave: “Allah has greater power over you than you have over this slave.”

And in the Quran:

“Even if We take you away, We will surely exact retribution from them.”

“Or if We show you what We have promised them, We certainly have full power over them.”

This is discussed at length elsewhere. Everything the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has reported is necessarily true in reality. Every attribute he has affirmed of the Lord necessarily belongs to Him. If its absence is posited, the absence of that which entails it necessarily follows. Everything he has affirmed of the Lord necessarily belongs to Him, and whatever he has denied of Him is necessarily absent from Him. Thus, if the absence of a necessary consequence is posited, the absence of that which entails it necessarily follows.

All of this, however, is an implication of their position and demonstrates its falsity. Yet an implication of a position need not itself be a position held by its adherents. Indeed, most people make statements without accepting their implications. Thus, if someone says something that entails negation of the divine attributes, it does not follow that he believes in negating them. Rather, he may believe in affirming them without recognizing that implication.

Likewise, if the premises upon which they base their proof of the Creator are false, it does not follow that they themselves do not acknowledge the Creator, even if this is an implication of their position. If they say that He can be known only through this method, and its invalidity has become apparent, it follows that He cannot be known. Yet this implication demonstrates the falsity of their denial; it does not follow that they themselves do not acknowledge the Creator. For, as we have explained elsewhere, acknowledging the Creator, knowing Him, loving Him, and affirming His oneness are innate: they may be firmly established in a person’s heart while he thinks they are not there.

Some of them say that the method of rational inquiry they follow has increased their insight and knowledge. Ibn Hazm and others say this. He followed the argument based on accidents.

Many people say that this method has brought them nothing but doubt and uncertainty. These people have a sounder innate disposition, for such methods are unsound.

Others say: “I gained nothing from it—neither knowledge nor doubt.” This is because it yielded them no knowledge, nor did they accept it; thus neither its soundness nor its unsoundness became clear to them. Muslims may know that the Lord has power over all things and does whatever He wills, while remaining unaware of many necessary consequences of His power and will. Yet those who adhere to the right path do not deny these consequences simply because they do not know them, for denying them is an error. Not knowing them all, however, is inevitable for everyone. Glory be to Him whose knowledge encompasses all things and who has numbered everything precisely. As for all besides Him:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.”

And He, glorified be He,

“knows what is before them and what is behind them, but they cannot encompass Him in knowledge.”

The point, however, is to explain that those who oppose the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—even in a single word must have a corresponding measure of error in what they say. It is also to explain that the rational and revealed proofs transmitted from all the prophets agree with what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought, and contradict the claims of the people of innovation who oppose the Book and the Sunnah.

When they say that reason conflicts with revelation, they err on five fundamental points:

First: sound reason does not contradict revelation.

Second: it agrees with revelation.

Third: what they claim to be a rational argument opposing revelation is not sound.

Fourth: the purported rational argument they put forward against revelation is itself contrary to sound reason.

Fifth: the arguments by which they seek to establish the foundations, such as knowledge of the Creator and His attributes, do not establish them; rather, they contradict their establishment.

Section

This is because what the Messenger brought is from Allah’s knowledge. Whatever he reported from Allah was declared by Allah Himself. He, glorified be He, speaks with knowledge; it is impossible for Him to declare anything contrary to His knowledge. Whatever the Messenger commanded comes from Allah’s judgment, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise. Allah Most High says:

“But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you: He sent it down with His knowledge. The angels also bear witness, and sufficient is Allah as a witness.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Or do they say, ‘He has fabricated it’? Say, ‘Then bring ten fabricated surahs like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.’”

“But if they do not respond to you, then know that it was sent down with Allah’s knowledge and that there is no deity except Him. Will you then submit?”

Regarding His words, “He sent it down with His knowledge,” al-Zajjāj said: “He sent it down containing His knowledge.” Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī said: “He sent it down from His knowledge.” Others have given the same explanation.

This meaning is transmitted from the early generations, as Ibn Abī Hātim narrated from ‘Atā’ ibn al-Sā’ib, who said: “Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān taught me to recite the Quran. Whenever he taught one of us to recite the Quran, he would say, ‘You have received Allah’s knowledge, so no one today is better than you except by virtue of his deeds.’ Then he would recite:

‘He sent it down with His knowledge. The angels also bear witness, and sufficient is Allah as a witness.’”

Likewise, regarding the words of Allah Most High, “Then know that it was sent down with Allah’s knowledge,” they said: “He sent it down containing His knowledge.”

I say:

The preposition bā’ can indicate accompaniment, as when you say, “He came with his masters and children.” Thus, He sent it down containing and bearing His knowledge. Whatever reports it contains are given with Allah’s knowledge, and whatever commands it contains are issued with Allah’s knowledge. This is unlike speech sent down from someone other than Allah. Such speech may be false and unjust, like Musaylimah’s Quran. Or it may be true, yet contain only the knowledge of the created being who uttered it. It indicates Allah Most High’s knowledge only by implication: namely, that Allah knows whatever is true.

The Quran, however, contains Allah’s knowledge directly. He sent it down with His knowledge, not anyone else’s; nor is it speech devoid of knowledge. Since He sent it down with His knowledge, it follows that it is truth from Allah, and that the Messenger is indeed a messenger from Allah, who has made His knowledge clear within it.

Al-Zajjāj said:

A “witness” is one who makes clear what he testifies to. Allah makes that clear and also knows it to be true.

(I say:

Regarding His words, “But Allah bears witness,” His testimony consists in His clarification and disclosure, His demonstration and declaration. The clear signs through which He has demonstrated the Messenger’s truthfulness attest to it. Among them is the Quran, which is testimony in words. It is itself a sign and a miracle attesting to his truthfulness, just as the other signs do. All these signs are testimony from Allah, just like testimony in words, and may be even more compelling. This is why He mentioned this in Sūrat Hūd when He challenged them to produce its like, saying:

“Then bring ten fabricated surahs like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.”

“But if they do not respond to you, then know that it was sent down with Allah’s knowledge and that there is no god but Him. Will you then submit?”

Their inability to produce anything comparable demonstrates, all the more, the inability of others to do so. It thus becomes clear that all creation is incapable of producing anything comparable to it, and that it is a clear sign attesting to the Messenger’s mission and to Allah’s oneness.

Likewise, His words, “But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you,” follow the passage beginning, “We have revealed to you,” and ending, “so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers.” It has been reported that some of the disbelievers said, “We do not testify that Muhammad is a messenger,” whereupon Allah Most High said, “But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you.”

A better explanation, however, is that when He said, “so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers,” He denied that creation had any argument against the Creator. He then stated: Yet Allah’s proof against creation stands established through His testimony to the Messenger’s mission. He bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge. Thus, creation has no argument against Allah; rather, His is the conclusive proof. It is He who has guided His servants through what He sent down.

In light of the foregoing, His words, “He sent it down with His knowledge,” mean that it contains His knowledge of what has been, what will be, and what He has disclosed. This, too, is evidence that it is true. For if he reports matters of the unseen that none but Allah knows, this indicates that Allah informed him of them.

Al-Zajjāj mentioned two interpretations concerning the verse in Sūrat Hūd. The first is: “He sent it down knowing that He was sending it down and knowing that it is the truth from Him.” The second is: “He sent it down containing the unseen matters He disclosed in it, indicating what will happen and what has already happened.”

(I say: This latter interpretation is the one explained above. The first, however, is of the same kind as Ibn Jarīr’s explanation. For He knows it and the one to whom He sent it down; He knows that it is true and that its recipient is worthy of that for which Allah chose him. This would then resemble His words:

“And We certainly chose them, knowingly, above all other peoples,”

and the words of the one who said:

“I was only given it because of knowledge”—

meaning: because Allah knows that I deserve it.

(I say: This interpretation is included in the meaning of the first explanation. For when speech is sent down with the Lord’s knowledge, this entails that everything it contains comes from His knowledge, including its statements concerning itself and the Messenger. This is the correct interpretation, held by the majority; some of them mentioned no other.

The first interpretation, although correct in meaning, is only part of this explanation. As for taking the second to be what the verse means, that is mistaken, because the fact that the Lord—glorified is He—knows something does not indicate that it is either praiseworthy or blameworthy. He knows all things. No one would say that He sent it down without knowing it. Yet someone might suppose that He sent it down without His knowledge—meaning that it does not contain His knowledge—and that it was sent down by Satan, as the Most High says:

“Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every sinful liar.”

He Himself sends the devils forth and causes them to descend, but the speech they bring is not sent down from Him, nor is it sent down with Allah’s knowledge. Rather, it is sent down bearing the lies and other things the devils utter. This is why, whenever He—glorified is He—mentions the Quran being sent down, He specifies that it is sent down from Him, as in His words:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah.”

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

“Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.”

This is among the evidence used by Imam Ahmad and other leading scholars of the Sunnah to establish that the Quran is Allah’s speech, not something created that He brought into being in a locus other than Himself. Had that been the case, it would have been sent down from that locus, not from Allah. He also stated that it was sent down with Allah’s knowledge, that it is from Allah’s knowledge, and that Allah’s knowledge is uncreated.

" الرَّدِّ عَلَى الزَّنَادِقَةِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة فِيمَا شَكَّتْ فِيهِ مِنْ مُتَشَابِهِ الْقُرْآنِ وَتَأَوَّلَتْهُ عَلَى غَيْرِ تَأْوِيلِهِ "
. وَلِهَذَا كَانَ الْأَئِمَّةُ الْأَرْبَعَةُ وَغَيْرُهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ فِي التَّوْحِيدِ وَالصِّفَاتِ إلَى الْقُرْآنِ وَالرَّسُولِ لَا إلَى رَأْيِ أَحَدٍ وَلَا مَعْقُولِهِ وَلَا قِيَاسِهِ.
 قَالَ الأوزاعي:
 كُنَّا وَالتَّابِعُونَ مُتَوَافِرُونَ نَقُولُ: إنَّ اللَّهَ فَوْقَ عَرْشِهِ وَنُؤْمِنُ بِمَا وَرَدَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ مِنْ صِفَاتِهِ.
 وَقَالَ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ:
 لَا يُوصَفُ اللَّهُ إلَّا بِمَا وَصَفَ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ وَوَصَفَهُ بِهِ رَسُولُهُ لَا يَتَجَاوَزُ الْقُرْآنَ وَالْحَدِيثَ. وَقَالَ الشَّافِعِيُّ فِي خُطْبَةِ 
" الرِّسَالَةِ "
: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي هُوَ كَمَا وَصَفَ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ " وَفَوْقَ مَا يَصِفُهُ بِهِ خَلْقُهُ.
 وَقَالَ مَالِكٌ:
 الِاسْتِوَاءُ مَعْلُومٌ وَالْكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ وَالْإِيمَانُ بِهِ وَاجِبٌ
translated_text:
and its branches is the religion of Islam. This is the way of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the leading scholars of the Muslims. They never accepted anyone’s opposing the Quran with a rational argument or opinion to which he gave precedence over it. Rather, if someone encountered a difficulty, he would ask until the correct understanding became clear to him. For this reason, Imam Ahmad wrote Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning Their Doubts about Unclear Passages of the Quran and Their Misinterpretation of Them. Likewise, the four imams and others referred questions concerning Allah’s oneness and attributes to the Quran and the Messenger, not to anyone’s opinion, reasoning, or analogy.

Al-Awzāʿī said:
“When the Successors were still numerous, we used to say: Allah is above His Throne, and we believe in those attributes of His that are reported in the Sunnah.”

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal said:
“Allah is to be described only as He has described Himself and as His Messenger has described Him. One must not go beyond the Quran and hadith.”

Al-Shāfiʿī said in the introduction to al-Risālah (The Epistle):
“Praise be to Allah, who is as He has described Himself and above whatever descriptions His creatures give of Him.”

Mālik said:
“Istiwā (rising above) is known, its manner is unknown, and belief in it is obligatory

وَالسُّؤَالُ عَنْهُ بِدْعَةٌ. وَكَانَ يَكْرَهُ مَا أَحْدَثَ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ.
 وَرُوِيَ عَنْهُ وَعَنْ أَبِي يُوسُفَ:
 مَنْ طَلَبَ الدِّينَ بِالْكَلَامِ تَزَنْدَقَ.
 وَقَالَ الشَّافِعِيُّ:
 حُكْمِي فِي أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ أَنْ يُضْرَبُوا بِالْجَرِيدِ وَالنِّعَالِ وَيُطَافُ بِهِمْ فِي الْأَسْوَاقِ وَيُقَالُ: هَذَا جَزَاءُ مَنْ تَرَكَ الْكِتَابَ وَالسُّنَّةَ وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَى الْكَلَامِ.
 وَقَالَ:
 لَقَدْ اطَّلَعْت مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ عَلَى شَيْءٍ مَا كُنْت أَظُنُّهُ وَلَأَنْ يُبْتَلَى الْعَبْدُ بِكُلِّ ذَنْبٍ مَا خَلَا الشِّرْكَ بِاَللَّهِ خَيْرٌ لَهُ مِنْ أَنْ يُبْتَلَى بِالْكَلَامِ. وَقَدْ بُسِطَ تَفْسِيرُ كَلَامِهِ وَكَلَامِ غَيْرِهِ فِي مَوَاضِعَ وَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ مُرَادَهُمْ بِالْكَلَامِ هُوَ كَلَامُ الْجَهْمِيَّة الَّذِي نَفَوْا بِهِ الصِّفَاتِ وَزَعَمُوا أَنَّهُمْ يُثْبِتُونَ بِهِ حُدُوثَ الْعَالَمِ وَهِيَ طَرِيقَةُ الْأَعْرَاضِ.
 وَقَالَ أَحْمَد أَيْضًا:
 عُلَمَاءُ الْكَلَامِ زَنَادِقَةٌ وَمَا ارْتَدَى أَحَدٌ بِالْكَلَامِ فَأَفْلَحَ. وَكَلَامُ عَبْدِ الْعَزِيزِ بْنِ أَبِي سَلَمَةَ الماجشون مَبْسُوطٌ فِي هَذَا.
 وَذَكَرَ أَصْحَابُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ عَنْ أَبِي يُوسُفَ عَنْ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ قَالَ:
 لَا يَنْبَغِي لِأَحَدِ أَنْ يَنْطِقَ فِي اللَّهِ بِشَيْءِ مِنْ رَأْيِهِ وَلَكِنَّهُ يَصِفُهُ بِمَا وَصَفَ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ.
 وَقَالَ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ:
 أَتَانَا مِنْ خُرَاسَانَ ضَيْفَانِ كِلَاهُمَا ضَالَّانِ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُشَبِّهَةُ.
translated_text:
and asking about it is an innovation.” He disapproved of the newly introduced speculative theology.

It is reported from him and from Abū Yūsuf:
“Whoever seeks religion through speculative theology falls into heresy.”

Al-Shāfiʿī said:
“My judgment concerning the practitioners of speculative theology is that they should be beaten with palm branches and sandals, paraded through the marketplaces, and it should be proclaimed: ‘This is the recompense of those who abandon the Book and the Sunnah and turn to speculative theology.’”

He also said:
“I have discovered things among the practitioners of speculative theology that I had never imagined. For a servant to be afflicted with every sin except associating partners with Allah is better for him than to be afflicted with speculative theology.”

His statements and those of others have been explained at length in several places. It has been clarified that what they meant by speculative theology was the theology of the Jahmiyyah, through which they denied the divine attributes and claimed to establish that the universe began to exist—namely, the argument from accidents.

Ahmad also said:
“The scholars of speculative theology are heretics. No one who has clothed himself in speculative theology has ever prospered.”

The statements of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Salamah al-Mājishūn on this subject are extensive.

The followers of Abū Hanīfah related, through Abū Yūsuf, that Abū Hanīfah said:
“No one should say anything about Allah on the basis of his own opinion. Rather, he should describe Him as He has described Himself.”

Abū Hanīfah also said:
“Two guests came to us from Khurāsān, both astray: the Jahmiyyah and those who liken Allah to His creation.”

translated_text:
Abū ʿIsmah reported:
“I asked Abū Hanīfah, ‘Who belongs to the community?’ He replied, ‘Whoever gives precedence to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, loves ʿAlī and ʿUthmān, does not prohibit nabīdh (a drink made by steeping ingredients in water) prepared in earthenware jars, declares no one an unbeliever on account of a sin, accepts wiping over leather socks, believes that divine decree—both its good and its evil—is from Allah, and says nothing concerning Allah.’”

Khālid ibn Sabīh narrated that Abū Hanīfah said:
“Adherence to the community consists of seven things: giving precedence to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, loving ʿUthmān and ʿAlī, offering the funeral prayer for anyone among the people of the qiblah who dies having committed a sin, and saying nothing concerning Allah.”

I say:
His statement in these two reports, “saying nothing concerning Allah,” is explained in the report transmitted by Abū Yūsuf: “One should not say anything concerning Allah on the basis of one’s own opinion; rather, one should describe Him as He has described Himself.” Thus, the imams condemn anyone who speaks about the Lord’s attributes on any basis other than what the Messenger conveyed.

How much more, then, does this apply to those who claim that the Book and the Sunnah do not yield knowledge, and give precedence to their own opinions over them, despite those opinions being unsound in many respects!

Hishām narrated from Muhammad, from Abū Hanīfah and Abū Yūsuf—and this was also Muhammad’s own position—that they said:
“The Sunnah upon which the community’s practice rests is that no one among the people of the qiblah should be declared an unbeliever and excluded from Islam on account of a sin; that a person should not doubt his religion, saying, ‘I do not know whether I am a believer or an unbeliever’; that he should not espouse the doctrine of the Qadariyyah; and that he should not rise up

translated_text:
against the Muslims with the sword; that he should give precedence to those Companions of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who are to be given precedence, and acknowledge the superiority of those accorded it.”

They related that Abū Yūsuf said:
“The way of the people of the community, as we understand it, and the practice we found among the body of jurists who had not adopted religious innovations or wayward doctrines, is that one should neither revile any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—nor speak of their faults, nor recount the disputes that arose among them, thereby turning people’s hearts against them. One should have no doubt that they are believers. One should not declare any person among the people of the qiblah who professes Islam and believes in the Quran an unbeliever, nor exclude him from faith because of a sin he may have committed. One should neither espouse the doctrine of the Qadariyyah nor engage in religious disputation, for such disputation is among the gravest innovations. This is the position of the people of the Sunnah and the community.

“No one should ask concerning this, ‘How?’ or ‘Why?’ Someone who asks about it should receive no response other than being told not to ask; if he persists, one should refrain from sitting or walking with him. No one among the people of the Sunnah and the community should associate with any follower of wayward doctrines to the point of becoming his companion and confidant, for fear of being led astray, or of leading someone else astray through that association.”

He said:
“Religious disputation is an innovation, and the refutations that followers of wayward doctrines direct against one another are a newly introduced innovation. Had there been any merit in this, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and their followers would have preceded others in it, for they were better able to undertake it and had greater insight into it. And He said:

translated_text:
Allah Most High:

‘If they dispute with you, say, “I have submitted myself to Allah, as have those who follow me.”’

He did not command him to engage in disputation. Had He willed, He would have sent down arguments and told him, ‘Say such and such.’”

Abū Yūsuf said:
“Disregard the views of those given to disputation and the followers of doctrinal innovations among the Murji’ah, Rāfidah, Zaydiyyah, Mushabbihah, Shī‘ah, Khawārij, Qadariyyah, Mu‘tazilah, and Jahmiyyah.”

They said:
“It was also related that Muhammad said, ‘Abū Bakr and ‘Umar are superior to ‘Alī.’”

I say: What Abū Yūsuf stated concerning disputation resembles the statements of many leading scholars of the Sunnah, including Imam Ahmad and others. This subject calls for fuller discussion and detailed clarification, for which this is not the place. For this reason, Bishr ibn al-Walīd, a companion of Abū Yūsuf, loved Ahmad and was inclined toward him. Indeed, Abū Yūsuf was more inclined toward hadith than others were. And Allah knows best and is Most Wise.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section

The short surahs at the end of the Quran are interrelated. Sūrat Iqra’ (“Recite”) was the first revelation of the Quran. Hence it opens with the command to recite, closes with the command to prostrate, and speaks in between of prayer. Recitation is prayer’s finest utterance and its first after the opening takbīr; prostration is its finest action and its last before the closing salutation.

Thus, after he was commanded to recite, Sūrat al-Muddaththir (“The Cloaked One”) was revealed to him so that he would convey the message. He was told:

“Arise and warn.”

Through the first he became a prophet, and through the second he became a messenger. Hence he was addressed as “the cloaked one”: someone seeking warmth against the chill of terror and alarm caused by the magnitude of what had suddenly overwhelmed him. He had returned to Khadījah with the muscles between his neck and shoulders trembling, saying, “Cover me! Cover me!” It was thus as though he was being forbidden to seek warmth and commanded to rise and warn. Similarly, in Sūrat al-Muzzammil (“The Enwrapped One”), he was addressed as someone wrapped up for sleep when he was commanded to rise for prayer.

Having commanded recitation in this surah, Allah mentioned in the next the revelation of the Quran on the Night of Decree, and the descent of the angels and the Spirit. In Sūrat al-Ma‘ārij (“The Ways of Ascent”), He mentioned the ascent of the angels and the Spirit, and in Sūrat al-Naba’ (“The Tidings”), the standing of the angels and the Spirit. He thus mentioned ascent, descent, and standing; then

translated_text:
in the following surah, He mentioned its recitation to those being warned, saying:

“Reciting purified scriptures”
“containing upright writings.”

These three surahs thus form a connected treatment of the Quran: the command to recite it, the account of its revelation, and the Messenger’s recitation of it to those being warned. Then Sūrat al-Zalzalah (“The Earthquake”), al-‘Ādiyāt (“The Chargers”), al-Qāri‘ah (“The Striking Calamity”), and al-Takāthur (“Rivalry in Worldly Increase”) speak of the Last Day and its rewards and punishments. Both the Quran and the Last Day have been identified as “the great news.”

Then Sūrat al-‘Asr (“Time”), al-Humazah (“The Slanderer”), al-Fīl (“The Elephant”), Li-Īlāf (“For the Familiar Security”), Ara’ayt (“Have You Seen?”), al-Kawthar (“Abundance”), al-Kāfirūn (“The Disbelievers”), al-Nasr (“Victory”), and Tabbat (“May They Perish”) speak of deeds, both good and evil, although each surah has its own distinctive focus.

As for Sūrat al-Ikhlās (“Sincerity”) and the two surahs of refuge, al-Ikhlās contains praise of Allah, while the two surahs of refuge contain the servant’s supplication to his Lord to grant him refuge. Praise is coupled with supplication, just as Allah brought them together in the Mother of the Quran, which is divided between the Lord and the servant: half is praise of the Lord, and half is supplication on the servant’s part.

The connection here is clear. Belief in the Messenger begins with belief in the message he brought, namely the Quran. Then comes belief in its purpose and ultimate end: the bliss and punishment to which matters ultimately lead—that is, recompense. Then comes knowledge of the path to that end and the means of reaching it, namely deeds: good deeds, so that one may perform them, and evil deeds, so that one may avoid them.

Sūrat al-Bayyinah (The Clear Proof)

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

Concerning His saying, exalted is He:

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists would not desist until the clear proof came to them.”

This is a surah of immense significance, and reports have been transmitted concerning its merits. It is established in an authentic report that Allah commanded His Prophet to recite it to Ubayy ibn Ka'b. In the two Sahīh collections, Anas ibn Mālik reported that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said to Ubayy:

“Allah has commanded me to recite the Quran to you.”

He asked, “Did Allah name me to you?”

He replied, “Allah named you to me.”

Thereupon Ubayy began to weep.

Another version reads:

“Allah has commanded me to recite to you: ‘Those who disbelieved…’”

He asked, “Did He name me to you?”

He replied, “Yes.” So he wept.

In a version recorded by al-Bukhārī:

“And I was mentioned before the Lord of all worlds?”

He replied, “Yes.” Then his eyes overflowed with tears.

Qatādah said: “I was informed

that he recited to him: ‘Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture…’” Singling out this surah for recitation to Ubayy implies that it possesses distinctive qualities that warranted this choice.

His words, “to recite to you,” mean a recitation intended to convey, make heard, and teach—not a recitation undertaken to receive instruction and correction, as a student recites to a teacher. Some have mistakenly understood it in this latter sense and regarded it as an expression of humility. Abū Hāmid cited it as evidence of a learner’s humility, but this interpretation has no basis. It was to Gabriel that he would recite in this manner, reviewing the Quran with him every year, for Gabriel was the one who brought the Quran down to him. As for other people, they learned it from him. How, then, could he recite to any of them to have his recitation corrected, or recite as a student does?

Rather, his recitation to Ubayy ibn Ka'b was like his recitation of the Quran to humans and jinn. He did indeed recite the Quran to the jinn. Whenever he went out to the people, he would call them to Islam and recite the Quran to them. He would also recite it to people both during prayer and outside it.

Allah, exalted is He, says:

“So what is the matter with them that they do not believe, and when the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate?”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down

prostrate and weeping.” And He, exalted is He, says:

“Allah certainly bestowed a great favor upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting His verses to them.”

He mentions the same elsewhere. Thus, the Messenger recites Allah’s verses to the believers. The Prophet was commanded to single out Ubayy ibn Ka'b for recitation because of Ubayy’s merit and his particular mastery of the Quran. As is established in the authentic hadith collections, 'Umar said: “Ubayy is our best Quran reciter, and 'Alī our most skilled judge.”

It is also related in an authentic hadith that he said to Ibn Mas'ūd: “Recite the Quran to me.”

He replied: “Shall I recite it to you when it was revealed to you?”

He said: “I love to hear it from someone else.”

Ibn Mas'ūd’s recitation to him on this occasion was therefore intended to let him hear it, not to receive correction or instruction.

Regarding the meaning of Allah’s statement that neither of these two groups would break away, several Quran commentators have mentioned three interpretations. Does it mean that they would not abandon disbelief? Or does it mean that they did not reject Muhammad until he was sent, and thus had not broken away from Muhammad and belief in his prophethood until he was sent? Or does it mean that they would not be left alone until a messenger was sent to them?

translated_text:
Among those who mentioned this was Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī. He said:

“‘Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book’—meaning the Jews and Christians—and the polytheists, who worship idols, ‘would not break away,’ meaning separate or desist. One says, ‘I detached something, and it became detached,’ meaning that it separated. The meaning is that they would not abandon their disbelief and polytheism until the clear proof came to them. The wording is in the future tense, but its meaning is past. The clear proof is the Messenger, Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who made clear to them their misguidance and ignorance. This describes Allah’s favor upon those of the two groups who believed, since He delivered them through him.”

Al-Baghawī’s wording is similar. He said:

“They would not desist from their disbelief and polytheism. The linguists say that ‘breaking away’ means separating or departing. One says, ‘I detached something, and it became detached,’ meaning that it separated. ‘Until the clear proof comes to them’ is worded in the future tense, but its meaning is past: until the clear proof—the manifest evidence—came to them. This means Muhammad, who brought them the Quran, made clear to them their misguidance and ignorance, and called them to faith. Thus Allah delivered them through him from ignorance and misguidance.”

He mentioned no other interpretation.

Abū al-Faraj said:

“Some commentators held that the verse means that they did not disagree that Allah would send them a prophet until He sent him; then they became divided. Others said: They were not free of Allah’s proofs until the clear proof was established against them.”

translated_text:
He sent them a messenger to warn them, through whom the proof would be established against them and His favor perfected for those who believed. It is as though He said: ‘They were not [to](1) be left to themselves.’”

He said:

“There are parallels to this meaning in Allah’s Book.”

Al-Tha‘labī mentioned three interpretations. However, he attributed the third to someone who understood the intended meaning to be their destruction through the establishment of proof against them, and interpreted “breaking away” as meaning “perishing.”

He said:

“They were not ‘breaking away,’ meaning desisting from their disbelief and their association of partners with Allah. The linguists said it means ‘ceasing.’ The Arabs say, ‘So-and-so has not ceased doing such-and-such,’ meaning that he continues to do it. The basic meaning of fakk is ‘opening,’ as in unsealing a document or opening an anklet.

“‘Until the clear proof came to them’ means the manifest proof: Muhammad, who brought them the Quran, exposed their misguidance and ignorance, and called them to faith.”

He said:

“Ibn Kaysān said: ‘Its meaning is that these disbelievers did not abandon the description of Muhammad in their scripture until he was sent. When he was sent, they became divided concerning him.’”

He also said:

“The scholars said that the opening of the surah, up to His words, ‘containing upright scriptures,’ concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who believed. ‘Nor did they become divided’ concerns those among the People of the Book who did not believe after the proof had been established against them.”

He said:

“Some leading linguists said: ‘His words “breaking away” mean “perishing.” This derives from the expression, “A woman’s salā has come apart during childbirth,” meaning that it separates and does not join together again, so she perishes. The verse means that they would not perish in their state of denial until proof had been established against them through the sending of the Messenger and the revelation of the Book.’”

Al-Baghawī mentioned this interpretation and the first, then said: “The first is more correct.”

(I say: The second interpretation, which he related from Ibn Kaysān, is that of al-Farrā’. Al-Mahdawī presented it before the first, saying:

“‘Breaking away’ derives from the expression ‘one thing breaks away from another,’ meaning that it separates from it. The meaning is that they would not become divided except when the Messenger came to them, because they abandoned the accounts and descriptions of him that they possessed and disbelieved after the clear proofs.”

He said:

“On this interpretation, ‘breaking away’ does not require a predicate. This is supported by His words:

‘Nor did those who were given the Scripture become divided until after the clear proof had come to them.’”

He said:

“Mujāhid said: ‘The meaning is that they would not desist from their ways.’ It is also related from Mujāhid: ‘They would not believe until the clear proof came to them.’”

He said:

“Al-Farrā’ said: ‘They did not cease mentioning the references to the Prophet that they possessed until he appeared. When he appeared, they became divided and disagreed.’”

I say:

This is the interpretation he presented first. However, al-Farrā’ and Ibn Kaysān understood “breaking away” as their abandoning and ceasing to mention him, the reports concerning him, and the glad tidings of his coming. In other words, they did not abandon or forsake what they knew of the reports concerning him until he appeared; then they broke away.

The other account says:

“They would not ‘break away’—that is, become divided—until the Messenger came, because they abandoned the reports concerning him that they possessed.”

This is the meaning of what Abū al-Faraj related:

“They did not disagree that Allah would send them a prophet until he was sent; then they became divided.”

Thus, “breaking away” means either their separating from one another or their abandoning the knowledge and reports they possessed concerning him. This interpretation is weak and is certainly not what is intended by this verse. Allah did not refer to the People of the Scripture as a whole; rather, He mentioned the disbelievers among the polytheists and the People of the Scripture. It is well known that the polytheists did not know him, mention him, or find him described in their scriptures as the People of the Scripture did. Nor had they been united upon a single religion before his mission, only to become divided when he came.

It is therefore impossible to say:

“The polytheists had not abandoned their knowledge of Muhammad, their mention of him, or their belief in him, nor had they disagreed or become divided over this, until he was sent.”

This meaning is false with regard to the polytheists. Nor does it hold true of the People of the Scripture, for Allah mentioned only the disbelievers among them, saying:
