translated_text:
the Scripture did not become divided until after the clear evidence had come to them.” Had this been the intended meaning here, it would have been mere repetition.

The first interpretation is better known among the exegetes. Some, such as al-Baghawī and others, mention another interpretation. It is known from Mujāhid and al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas, as in the well-known commentary transmitted by Ibn Abī Najīh from Mujāhid. Concerning “breaking away,” he said: “Hypocrites; they would not believe until the truth became clear to them.” Al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas said: “They persisted in doubt and uncertainty until the clear evidence and the messengers came to them.”

This interpretation entails praising and commending them after the coming of the clear evidence. Those who held it therefore had to say: “This concerns those of the two groups who believed, explaining Allah’s favor upon them.” They understood His words:

“And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided”

as referring to those among them who did not believe in Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This too is weak.

For the People of the Scripture became divided and disagreed before Muhammad was sent to them, as Allah states in several places. The Most High says:

“We certainly gave the Children of Israel the Scripture, judgment, and prophethood, provided them with good things, and favored them above all peoples.”

“And We gave them clear proofs concerning the matter, and they did not differ until

after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual rivalry. Your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they differed.”

He also says:

“Then We set you upon a clear way concerning the religion, so follow it, and do not follow the desires of those who do not know.”

The Most High says:

“Mankind was one community. Then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warnings, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between people concerning that over which they differed.”

Then He says:

“None differed over it except those who had been given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual rivalry. Then Allah, by His permission, guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they had differed. Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.”

He thus states that Allah, by His permission, guided the believers to the truth concerning which people had differed. This disagreement therefore existed before the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came into being.

The Most High says:

“The Sabbath was imposed only upon those who differed concerning it. Your Lord will surely judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they differed.”

The Most High also says:

“We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good dwelling place and provided them with good things. They did not differ until knowledge had come to them. Your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they differed.”

Then the Most High says:

“If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so never be among those who doubt.”

The Most High says:

“By Allah, We certainly sent messengers to nations before you, but they were enticed by

Satan, who made their deeds seem fair to them. He is their ally today, and theirs will be a painful punishment.”

“We have sent down the Scripture to you only so that you may make clear to them that over which they differed, and as guidance and mercy for people who believe.”

The Most High thus states that He sent messengers to nations before Muhammad, that Satan made their deeds seem fair to them and was their ally when Muhammad was sent, and that He sent down the Scripture to them so that Muhammad might make clear to them that over which they differed.

The Most High says:

“Indeed, this Quran recounts to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ. And it is certainly guidance and mercy for the believers.”

He says to the community of Muhammad:

“Do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. For them there will be a tremendous punishment.”

This makes clear that they became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them, before Muhammad, and Allah has forbidden his community to be like them.

The Most High also says:

“From those who said, ‘We are Christians,’ We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of. So We stirred up enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection.”

He says of the Jews:

“We cast enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection.”

He also says:

“We scattered them throughout the earth as communities. Some of them were righteous, and some were otherwise.”

Hadiths have been transmitted through various chains in the Sunan collections and the Musnad, reporting that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Jews divided into seventy-one sects, and this community will divide into seventy-three sects.”

Although some, such as Ibn Hazm, judge these hadiths to be weak, most scholars have accepted them and affirmed their truth.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Leave me alone so long as I leave you alone. Those before you perished only because of their excessive questioning and their disagreements with their prophets. When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

It is also reported in the two Sahīh collections that he said:

“We are the last, but will be the foremost on the Day of Resurrection, although they were given the Scripture before us and we were given it after them. This, then, is their day concerning which they differed, and Allah guided us to it. In this, the people follow us: tomorrow is for the Jews, and the day after tomorrow for the Christians.”

It is known through mass transmission that the People of the Scripture differed and became divided before Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent. Indeed, the Jews split into sects before the Messiah came; then, when the Messiah came, they differed concerning him. The Christians subsequently developed further differences. How, then, can it be said that His words,

“Those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after the clear proof had come to them,”

refer to those among them who did not believe in Muhammad?

Furthermore, those who disbelieved in Muhammad are disbelievers, and they are the ones mentioned in His words:

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists would not desist until the clear proof came to them.”

the clear proof.” They had become divided and disagreed over what the prophets brought before Muhammad, and those among them who disbelieved had done so before Muhammad was sent.

Among them were also those who did not disbelieve, but believed in the prophets, as Allah Most High said:

“Among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and establish justice thereby.”

“We dispersed them throughout the earth into communities; among them are the righteous, and among them are those less so.”

Allah Most High also said:

“They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite Allah’s verses during the hours of the night, prostrating themselves.”

“They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and hasten to do good deeds. They are among the righteous.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Had they upheld the Torah, the Gospel, and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have received provision from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a community who follow a moderate course, but evil indeed is what many of them do.”

In Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, ʿIyād ibn Himār reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah looked upon the people of the earth and detested them, Arabs and non-Arabs alike, except for a remnant among the People of the Scripture. My Lord said to me, ‘Rise among Quraysh and warn them.’ I said, ‘My Lord, they would then smash my head until they left it like a loaf of bread.’ He said, ‘I shall test you and test others through you, and send down to you a Book that water cannot wash away, which you will recite asleep and awake. Send forth an army, and We shall send twice their number; and with those who obey you, fight those who disobey you.’”

The hadith is longer than this.

translated_text:
Our purpose here is to discuss the verse, so we say:

The third view is the soundest, both in wording and in meaning. As regards the wording, its significance and what it conveys, this expression is used when a person frees himself from something that binds him—his will, that is—and is imposed upon him. One says, “He broke free of it,” as with a captive or a slave held under the constraint of slavery or captivity. One says, “I released the captive, and he became free,” and “I freed a slave.” Allah Most High said:

“And what can make you know what the steep path is? It is the freeing of a slave.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī:

“Visit the sick, feed the hungry, and free the captive.”

It is also reported in the Sahīh that when ʿAlī was asked what was in the document, he said, “It contains blood money, the release of captives, and the ruling that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever.”

Thus, releasing someone means separating him from whoever subjugates him and exercises control over him against his will, and parting the two.

One also says, “So-and-so will not leave so-and-so alone until he gets him involved in such-and-such,” and “The one in charge will not let this man go until he does such-and-such.” Such expressions describe someone who persistently holds another in his grip and gains control over him, whether through power and coercion or through making things attractive and appealing and employing means by which the other becomes obedient to him.

And of someone held under another’s control, one says, “He cannot break free of this,” just as a captive or slave cannot break free of whoever holds him in subjection. Thus, His words:

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not to break free”

mean that they were not to be left to their own devices, doing whatever they desired without restraint, as someone who has broken free is no longer restrained. He did not say “mafkūkīn” (released), but rather “munfakkīn” (breaking free). This wording is better, for it negates an action on their part. Had He said “released,” the implied meaning would have been that they were not to be left unrestrained and alone, thus negating an action on the part of someone else.

The point is that they were not to be left without commands or prohibitions, with no messengers sent to them, doing whatever they wished in pursuit of their desires. The meaning is that Allah does not leave them alone or abandon them. He does not release them until He sends them a messenger. This resembles His words:

“Does man think that he will be left without purpose?”

That is, without being commanded or forbidden. Does he imagine that this will happen? It will never happen; rather, he must be given commands and prohibitions. Similar to this are His words, Most High:

“Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Quran so that you may understand. And indeed, it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom. Shall We then turn the Reminder away from you, disregarding you, because you are a transgressing people?”

This is a rhetorical question expressing rejection: Are We, because of your transgression, to cease sending down the Reminder and refrain from sending messengers? And who resents their being sent?

For the former denies their existence, while the latter entails hatred of them and aversion to what they brought. Allah Most High says:

“That is because they hated what Allah revealed, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

He also related the words of the believer from Pharaoh’s household:

“Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, yet you remained in doubt about what he brought you. Then, when he died, you said, ‘Allah will never send a messenger after him.’ Thus does Allah lead astray whoever is a transgressor, full of doubt.”

As for anyone who denies the messengers after they have been sent, his disbelief is evident. But someone may suppose that Allah will send him no messenger and that he will be left without purpose, neglected, neither commanded nor forbidden. This too is something Allah has condemned, when messengers must necessarily be sent and scriptures revealed, just as deeds must necessarily be recompensed with reward and punishment, and the Resurrection must take place. Thus He, glorified be He, rebukes those who suppose that this will not happen. Allah Most High says:

“We did not create the heaven and the earth and all that is between them without purpose. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve. So woe to those who disbelieve because of the Fire!”

“Or should We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth? Or should We treat the righteous like the wicked?”

Allah Most High also says:

“Did you then think that We created you without purpose and that you would not be returned to Us?”

Allah Most High also says:

“We did not create the heavens and the earth and all that is between them except in truth. The Hour is certainly coming, so pardon graciously.”

“Indeed, your Lord is the Creator, the All-Knowing.”

He also says:

“Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned, and they will not be wronged.”

translated_text:
And He says of those endowed with understanding:

“Those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: ‘Our Lord, You did not create this without purpose. Glory be to You! Protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’”

These and similar passages in the Quran show that commands and prohibitions, reward and punishment, and the Resurrection are inevitable. They rebuke anyone who supposes or imagines that these things will not occur. This entails that they must necessarily occur and that their not occurring is impossible.

This is agreed upon by those among the adherents of the religions who believe the messengers, whether Muslims or others, on the basis of accepting the report as true. Allah has foretold this, and His report is true. What He has foretold must therefore occur; it is necessary by virtue of His promise and His report. For if He knows that something will happen and has declared that it will happen, it must happen. Nothing can possibly be contrary to what He has known, declared, written, and decreed. Moreover, He has willed this: whatever He wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. Everything He wills must occur.

Whether, however, it may be said that His will renders this necessary is disputed.

Likewise, it is also disputed whether it may be said that this has become necessary because He has made it incumbent upon Himself, or because His wisdom requires it. Whatever He has sworn to do must occur. An oath encompasses the meaning of a declaration

and the sense of urging and demanding.

However, people disagree over whether the latter applies to Allah, as in His words:

“I will surely fill Hell with you and all those among them who follow you.”

And His words:

“And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would subject them to grievous torment.”

Those who say that His wisdom, His judgment, or His will necessitates this maintain that it may be known through reason. They say that reason may establish that messengers must necessarily be sent, and that this is necessary according to His judgment and wisdom. This is the position of many groups, or most of them.

Others say that none of this can be known except through revelation. This is the position of the Jahmiyyah and the Ashʿariyyah, whereas the former is the position of the Muʿtazilah, the Karrāmiyyah, and the Hanafīs, or most of them. Among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, some hold this view. The majority of jurists, however, together with the early generations, affirm divine wisdom and that His acts have underlying reasons. Only those among them who agree with the Jahmī determinists deny this, such as al-Ashʿarī and those who agree with him.

Likewise, the majority of them affirm that acts possess attributes by virtue of which they are good or evil and reprehensible. They do not regard their goodness and badness as a preference for one of two alternatives without any determining ground beyond sheer will, as the Jahmiyyah and those who agree with them maintain.

translated_text:
This is the position of the imams and the majority, just as they affirm divine decree and believe in it: Allah is the Creator of all things; whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. They accept neither the position of those among the Muʿtazilah and others who deny divine decree, nor that of the Jahmī determinists and others who deny the Lord’s wisdom.

Thus, they accept neither the position of the Qadariyyah who deny divine decree nor that of the determinist Qadariyyah, whose position entails denying commands and prohibitions, promises and threats, and recompense through reward and punishment—especially those among them who state this openly or say:

“For anyone who witnesses divine decree, commands and prohibitions, promises and threats cease to apply.”

The deniers of divine decree believed, in general, in what the messengers brought. They regarded as obligatory what Allah made obligatory and as forbidden what Allah forbade. They believed in Paradise and Hell and strove to follow the messengers. However, they erred in denying divine decree and supposing that affirming it contradicts commands and prohibitions, promises and threats. They also supposed that their belief that Allah is just and truthful could not be complete unless they denied divine decree and the release from the Fire of those guilty of major sins. They imagined that Allah had declared that He would never bring out of the Fire anyone whose sin merits punishment, nor ever show him mercy. Thus, they did not allow for the possibility that someone might be punished for his sin and then shown mercy. Rather, in their view, anyone whose sin merits punishment would never be shown mercy. Although they did not deliberately intend to deny the messengers, this position of theirs entails

translated_text:
contradicting the reports from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—which hadith scholars recognize as mass-transmitted, concerning sinners being brought out of the Fire and intercessors interceding for them. It also entails making people despair of Allah’s mercy, while denying the all-encompassing scope of Allah’s creation, will, and power: they claimed that some events lie beyond His power and are neither willed nor created by Him.

In this respect, they resembled the Magians, so much so that it was said:

“The Qadariyyah are the Magians of this community.”

Those at the opposite extreme withheld judgment concerning Allah’s statements altogether, even rejecting both kinds of general statement. Thus, they did not derive from His statements knowledge of the promises and threats He conveyed. They would not affirm with certainty the salvation of those whom Allah knows to have believed, done righteous deeds, and been among the most obedient to Him, if any one of them had committed a single minor sin. Nor would they affirm with certainty the punishment of those whom Allah knows to be the most wicked and evil members of the Muslim community. Rather, despite Allah’s knowledge of both groups, they considered it possible that He might punish people who had performed great good deeds for a minor sin with a punishment He inflicts on no one else in the Muslim community, and that He might admit the wicked members of the Muslim community into Paradise alongside the earliest forerunners in faith. A detailed discussion of both groups belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that this surah indicates what other passages of the Quran also indicate: Allah sends messengers to people to command and forbid them, sending them as bearers of glad tidings and warnings. As He, the Exalted, says:

“We send the messengers only as bearers of glad tidings and warnings.”

They warn those who do evil of the punishments for their deeds, and give those who believe and do righteous deeds glad tidings of everlasting bliss and “that they will have a good reward,” “in which they will remain forever.”

Thus, His words,

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not to be left alone until the clear evidence came to them,”

explain that Allah would not leave the disbelievers as they were, in their disbelief. Rather, He does not leave them alone without first sending them the Messenger as a bearer of glad tidings and warnings,

“so that He may repay those who do evil for what they have done and reward those who do good with the best.”

This is further clarified by the fact that hattā (“until”) is a particle marking an endpoint, and what follows that endpoint differs from what precedes it, as in His words:

“until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread,”

and His words,

“until they become pure,”

and His words,

“until she marries a husband other than him,”

and similar passages. If the intended meaning were that they would not desist from disbelief and believe until the truth became clear to them, it would follow that, after the clear evidence came, they all desisted and believed, since the wording encompasses them all.

Likewise, if the intended meaning were that they had agreed on affirming the Messenger’s truthfulness until he was sent, it would follow that they had all known of him before he was sent to them, and that they all became divided and disagreed after he was sent. Both implications are false. Many of them are unlettered and know the Scripture only through wishful notions; they were unaware of what the scriptures contained concerning his being sent and other matters. When he was sent, a great many of them believed in him; they did not all turn away from faith in him.

Thus, the verse does not contain blanket praise of them, as supposed by those who understood it to mean that they had not desisted from disbelief or come to faith until the truth became clear to them. Nor does it contain blanket condemnation of them, as supposed by those who understood that, when the Messenger came to them, they became divided and disagreed after having agreed on affirming his truthfulness. Rather, it praises those among them who believed in the Messenger, condemns those who did not believe, and declares that the Messenger would inevitably be sent to them, whereupon some would believe in him and others would disbelieve. Allah, the Exalted, says:

“We have favored some of those messengers over others. Among them were those to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some in rank. We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them. But they differed: some believed and others disbelieved. Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.”

Moreover, He must test those who believe in the messengers, thereby distinguishing the truthful from the liars. As Allah, the Exalted, says:

“Do people think they will be left to say, ‘We believe,’ without being tested?”

“We certainly tested those before them, so Allah will surely know those who are truthful, and He will surely know the liars.”

Then He says:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think they can escape Us? How badly they judge!”

When messengers are sent to people, each person falls into one of two categories: either someone who outwardly believes in them and must therefore be tested until the truthful can be distinguished from the liar; or someone who commits evil deeds and does not believe. Such a person cannot escape Allah; rather, He—glorified and exalted—is sure to seize him.

Thus, people fall into three categories in their response to the messengers: a believer inwardly and outwardly; a disbeliever who openly professes disbelief; and a hypocrite who outwardly professes faith while inwardly concealing disbelief. This division arose once the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, emigrated to Medina. At the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah, Allah, the Exalted, revealed four verses describing the believers, two verses describing the disbelievers, and ten-odd verses describing the hypocrites. But when he was in Mecca and the believers were oppressed, no one had any need

to resort to hypocrisy. Rather, some believers concealed their faith from many people. Others uttered words of disbelief under compulsion while their hearts remained firm in faith. Such a person is a believer both inwardly and outwardly. Although he outwardly professes disbelief before certain people under compulsion, or conceals his faith from them, he professes faith in private and among those he trusts, and fulfils whatever duties he can. Whatever he is unable to fulfil is waived for him.

For this reason, scholars, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal, said that hypocrisy was not possible for them; hypocrisy arose only in Medina. There were, however, people in Mecca whose hearts were diseased, as He says in the Meccan surah:

“And so that those given the Scripture and the believers may have no doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is disease and the disbelievers may say, ‘What does Allah intend by this as an example?’”

He—glorified is He—has stated that He would not leave those who profess faith without distinguishing the wicked from the good and testing them. As He, the Exalted, says:

“Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good.”

He also says:

“Or do you think that you will be left alone before Allah has made evident those among you who strive and take no confidants other than Allah, His Messenger, and the believers? And Allah is fully aware of what you do.”

And He, the Exalted, says:

“Or do you think that you will enter Paradise without experiencing the like of what befell those who passed away before you? They were afflicted with poverty and hardship and were so shaken that the messenger and those who believed with him said, ‘When will Allah’s help come?’ Indeed, Allah’s help is near.”

And there are other passages to the same effect.

Likewise, He would not leave those who disbelieved without sending them the Messenger with clear signs. This is the meaning of His words:

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists were not to be left alone until the clear evidence comes to them.”

When the clear evidence comes to them, some believe and others disbelieve.

If it is said that, beyond this, the verse also conveys the other meaning—that they would not find guidance, know the truth, and believe until the clear evidence came to them, since they have no way of knowing the truth except through a messenger who comes from Allah; or that they would not desist and heed admonition, even if they knew the truth, until someone came to them from Allah to remind them—then this meaning does not contradict the former.

This is unlike the interpretation of those who say: “The polytheists and the People of the Scripture had not abandoned their recognition of Muhammad or ceased mentioning him, nor were they divided concerning him. Rather, they were agreed upon believing in him until the clear evidence came to them; then they abandoned belief in him and became divided.” This is certainly not the intended meaning.

Among the things that clarify this is His wording, “until the clear evidence comes to them.” He did not say, “until it came to them.” Because those interpreters did not understand the meaning of the verse, they thought that the past tense was called for here, and that the intended meaning was: they did not depart from their previous state, whether disbelief or faith, until the clear evidence came to them. Thus, the wording “until the clear evidence comes to them” puzzled them. And it was said:

translated_text:
some of them: “Not all of it has yet come to them.” According to the correct meaning, however, the imperfect tense is appropriate here, as in Allah’s words:

“Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the evil from the good.”

The intended meaning is that they were not to be released and left alone until the clear evidence comes to them. He, glorified be He, said: “Those who disbelieved were not…” Although the particle lam gives the imperfect verb a past meaning, this applies when the verb stands alone. Thus, lam ya’ti and lam yadhhab mean mā atā (“he did not come”) and mā dhahaba (“he did not go”). But when one says, “He would not do this,” or, as Allah says:

“Allah would not forgive them, nor would He guide them to a way,”

the intended meaning is an enduring action, without restriction to a particular time. Saying, “So-and-so would not come until so-and-so went to him,” differs from saying, “So-and-so had not come until so-and-so went to him.” Likewise, saying, “So-and-so would not do this until such-and-such happens,” conveys a similar meaning, unlike saying, “So-and-so had not done it until so-and-so came.” Thus, the imperfect verb is negated, with an active participle as its predicate, denoting continuity.

The intended meaning is that they were not to be left alone, in the present or the future, until the clear evidence comes to them. Had the wording here been “until the clear evidence came to them,” it would not have been appropriate.

translated_text:
Likewise, if He had meant giving up disbelief and embracing faith, the wording would have been, “until the clear evidence comes to them”—meaning that they would not know the truth until a prophet comes to make it known to them, or would not heed admonition and act upon it until someone comes to admonish and remind them. This is therefore not a place for the past tense, unlike saying, “They remained disbelievers until he came to them.”

The verse thus states that clear evidence must be established and that they cannot be released without it. Its purpose is not merely to report that they were not released and then were released at some point in the past. It is as though He had said, “They would not be released until the clear evidence comes to them.” Here, however, He used the plural active participle, munfakkīn (“released”).

Having explained that messengers must be sent to those who disbelieved among the polytheists and the People of the Book, so that the proof might thereby be established against them, He, glorified be He, then explained that the People of the Book who believed in the messengers became divided only after the clear evidence had come to them and the proof had been established against them. Allah’s clear signs and His proof were thus established against both groups. He punished neither group until the clear evidence had come to them and the proof had been established against them, as in the account of Moses and those to whom he was sent. Allah did not leave Pharaoh and his people alone without sending Moses to them, nor did He punish them until after establishing the proof against them. Then, once the Children of Israel had believed in the Scriptures and the messengers, they became divided and fell into disagreement only

after the clear evidence had come to them. Thus, they had no excuse for this. For this reason, Muhammad’s community was forbidden to imitate them:

“And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them.”

The people to whom Muhammad was sent are likewise. Whoever disbelieved would not be released until the clear evidence came to him. Those among the nations who believed in Muhammad and then became divided and differed did so only after the clear evidence had come to them. All of them were commanded

“only to worship Allah, devoting their religion sincerely to Him, turning away from falsehood, to establish prayer and give zakah. That is the upright religion.”

The verse praises the Lord and describes His wisdom, justice, and proof: He does not leave them without sending them a messenger. As He said to the People of the Book:

“Our Messenger has come to you, making things clear to you after an interval between messengers, lest you say, ‘No bearer of good tidings or warner has come to us.’ Now a bearer of good tidings and a warner has come to you”—to the end of the verse.

It does not praise them for persisting in disbelief until the Messenger comes. At most, this means that they are not punished for it until the Messenger comes, not that they are praised for it until he comes. No rational person would say such a thing, nor has anyone said it—especially since the proof had already been established against the People of the Book through prophets before him.

A parallel wording occurs in His saying:

“And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship.”

This does not mean that you could not reach it in the past; rather, this is their constant condition. Thus, His words, “Those who disbelieved would not be released until it comes to them,” imply that this is always their condition.

The surah mentions the different classes of creation and what Allah has commanded all His servants. It explains that this is indispensable: messengers must be sent, scriptures revealed, and the blessed—the people of Paradise—and the wretched—the people of the Fire—made known. His words:

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists would not be released until the clear evidence comes to them—a messenger from Allah, reciting purified scriptures,”

form a statement explaining that the Messenger was sent to them all. His words:

“Those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after the clear evidence had come to them,”

establish the proof against the followers of revealed laws, condemn their divisions and disagreements, and explain that these arose after the clear evidence had come to them.

These two statements are paralleled by His saying:

“Mankind was one community; then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between people concerning that over which they differed.”

Then He said:

“None differed concerning it except those who were given it, after

clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual animosity. Then Allah, by His permission, guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed.”

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“He has ordained for you the religion He enjoined upon Noah, and which We have revealed to you, and which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: ‘Establish the religion and do not become divided in it.’ What you call them to is difficult for the polytheists to accept. Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns to Him.”

Then He said:

“They did not become divided until after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual animosity. Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord granting them respite until an appointed time, judgment would have been passed between them. Indeed, those who inherited the Scripture after them are in troubling doubt about it.”

And His saying:

“We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, but differences arose concerning it. Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, judgment would have been passed between them. Indeed, they are in troubling doubt about it,”

in Surah Hūd and Surah ‘Ayn Sīn Qāf.

Then He mentioned what all were commanded to do, saying:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah, devoting their religion sincerely to Him and inclining to the truth, to establish prayer and give zakah. That is the upright religion.”

Then He mentioned the final outcome of those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists, and the final outcome of those who believed and did righteous deeds.

Section

Regarding His saying:

“Those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after the clear proof had come to them.”

A group of commentators said: This refers to their division concerning Muhammad after they had been united in believing in him. Some of these commentators understood their division to mean that some believed while others disbelieved.

Al-Baghawī said: Then He mentioned those among the People of the Book who did not believe, saying:

“Those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after the clear proof had come to them.”

That is, the clear statement in their scriptures that he was a prophet sent by Allah. The commentators said: The People of the Book remained united in affirming Muhammad’s truthfulness until Allah sent him. Once he was sent, they became divided concerning him and disagreed: some believed in him, while others disbelieved in him.

A group of commentators gave a similar explanation of His saying:

“We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good dwelling place and provided them with good things. They did not differ until knowledge had come to them.”

Abū al-Faraj said: Ibn ‘Abbās said: They did not differ concerning Muhammad; they continued to affirm his truthfulness until knowledge came to them—meaning the Quran.

It is also reported from him that “until knowledge came to them” means Muhammad. According to this interpretation, “knowledge” here stands for what is known. This is explained by the fact that when he came to them

Then He says:

This interpretation is well known from Abū al-‘Āliyah, who narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka‘b. Ibn Abī Hātim and others narrated it from al-Rabī‘, from Abū al-‘Āliyah, from Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, who used to recite it:

the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners.” He explained that Allah sent the messengers and revealed the scriptures only when disagreement arose.

He said: He revealed the Scripture when disagreement arose.

“None differed over it except those who were given it.”

This means the Children of Israel, who were given the Scripture and knowledge.

“After clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual transgression.”

He says: They transgressed out of rivalry for this world, seeking its dominion, splendor, and adornment, vying over who among them would wield authority and command awe among the people. Thus they transgressed against one another and struck one another’s necks.

“Then Allah, by His permission, guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed.”

He says: Allah guided them when disagreement arose: they remained steadfast upon what the messengers had brought before the disagreement. They maintained sincere devotion to Allah alone, worshipping Him without associating any partner with Him, establishing prayer, and giving zakat. They adhered to the original way that had prevailed before the disagreement and kept apart from the disagreement. Thus they would be witnesses over mankind on the Day of Resurrection, testifying against the people of Noah, the people of Hūd, the people of Sālih, the people of Shu‘ayb, and Pharaoh’s people that their messengers had conveyed the message to them and that they had rejected their messengers.

I say:

The Quran speaks of two kinds of disagreement. In the first, all those who disagree are condemned, as in His words:

“Indeed, those who differ concerning the Scripture are in extreme dissension.”

And His words:

“They will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy.”

In the second, He praises the believers and condemns the disbelievers, as in His words:

“Had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after clear proofs had come to them. But they differed: some believed and some disbelieved. And had it been the will of

Allah, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.” And His words:

“These are two adversaries who have disputed concerning their Lord. For those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out.”

Through to His words:

“Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds.”

And His words:

“Indeed, those who believe, the Jews, the Sabians, the Christians, the Magians, and those who associate partners with Allah—Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Witness over all things.”

Since this is so, the division and disagreement among the People of the Scripture that He condemned involved condemnation of them all. He forbade imitating them, saying:

“Do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them.”

And He said:

“None differed over it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual transgression.”

This occurs when one group believes in some truth but rejects the truth held by another, and adds falsehood to the truth, as the Jews and Christians differed concerning the Messiah and other matters.

If someone says that the People of the Scripture did not become divided over Muhammad until after he was sent, meaning that some believed while others disbelieved—as some have said—then those condemned here are the disbelievers, not the believers. Thus, not everyone involved in the disagreement is condemned. Surah al-Takāthur

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section: “Surah al-Takāthur”

The words used in this surah,

“Until you visit the graves,”

draw attention to the fact that a visitor must leave the place he visits. This therefore points to the resurrection.

Then He says:

“No! You will soon know.”
“Then no! You will soon know.”

This foretells what they will know in the future. Hence, it is reported from Alī that this refers to punishment in the grave. Then He says:

“No! If only you knew with the knowledge of certainty!”

This refers to their knowing in the present, with the consequent left unstated. That is: the reality would be beyond description; you would know something momentous, and it would turn your attention away from what now distracts you. For distraction through rivalry for more arises only from heedlessness and a lack of certainty.

As He says:

“They denied Our signs and were heedless of them.”

It is also like the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much.”

The consequent of “if” is frequently omitted in the Quran to emphasize its magnitude and gravity, for it is too momentous

to be described or conceived merely by hearing words, for one who reports something is not like one who witnesses it firsthand. Hence He follows this with an oath affirming that they will see it: this is the certainty of sight, which surpasses a report that yields the knowledge of certainty. He says:

“You will surely see Hellfire.”

“Then you will surely see it with the certainty of sight.”

This statement refers to the future and is the response to an unstated oath, while the consequent of “if” is omitted, as explained above. This is one of the two interpretations.

According to the other, it is connected to “if.” But an objection is raised: the consequent of “if” must be in the past tense, so the wording would be: “You would have seen Hellfire.” This is like the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“If you remained in the state you are in when you are with me, the angels would shake hands with you in your streets and on your beds.”

If it were in the past tense, it would not take an emphatic ending. Rather, one says: “If he were to come, I would come.” The answer to this objection is that it is the response to an unstated oath, standing in place of the consequent of “if.” This is like His saying:

“And if you obey them, you are surely polytheists.”

There are parallels to this in the Quran and in Arabic speech. When a statement contains both an oath and a condition, each requiring a response, the response is given to whichever comes first. Here, that is the oath, which is the intended emphasis.

According to this interpretation, the meaning would be: “By Allah, if you knew with the knowledge of certainty, you would surely see Hellfire with your hearts.”

The first interpretation, however, is the well-known one. Some Quran commentators mention no other, and it is the interpretation they transmitted from their predecessors. What demonstrates its soundness and establishes that it is correct is that His words,

“Then you will surely see it,”

and,

“Then you will surely be questioned,”

are conjoined to what precedes them and therefore fall within its scope. Thus, if the first statement were dependent on the condition, the statements conjoined to it would be

likewise conditional. But this is untenable, because seeing it with the certainty of sight and being questioned about worldly blessings are not conditional upon knowing of it in this world with the knowledge of certainty.

Moreover, interpreting an unqualified reference to seeing as seeing with the heart is not customary Arabic usage. Furthermore, the condition would then be identical to its consequent: the meaning would be, “If you knew with the knowledge of certainty, you would see with your hearts.” Yet that is itself knowledge, so the meaning would be, “If you knew, you would know,” which conveys nothing. Even if beholding with the heart were intended to mean something beyond mere knowledge, it is already known that someone who knows a thing can bring himself to behold it with his heart. Moreover, even if this meaning conveyed something, it would not warrant an oath, for it is of little consequence.

Furthermore, in His words:

“If you knew with the knowledge of certainty,”

He does not specify the object of knowledge such that knowing it would necessarily entail knowing of Hellfire. If a particular object of knowledge is intended, nothing in the conditional clause indicates it so as to establish the connection. If the broader object of knowledge is intended—namely, what comes after death—then that entails knowledge of Hellfire and other things. This, however, is open to question.

For someone may ask: In His words:

“You will soon know,”

and:

“Then, no indeed! You will soon know,”

He does not specify

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

His words:

“Woe to every slanderer and backbiter.”

This means someone who maliciously attacks others and finds fault with them, as He says:

“A slanderer, going about spreading malicious gossip.”

And He says:

“Among them are those who criticize you concerning the distribution of charities.”

And He says:

“Those who criticize the believers who give charity voluntarily.”

Hamz (malicious criticism) is more severe, because hamz means a forceful thrust. From this comes the name of the letter hamzah, which is a sharp catch in the throat. Another instance is His saying:

“And say: ‘My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils.’”

Another is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan, from his goading, his blowing, and his spitting.”

He also said: “His goading is al-mūtah,” meaning a seizure. Thus hamz resembles taʿn (stabbing) in both expression and meaning, whereas lamz is akin to condemnation and fault-finding.  فَهَذِهِ خَمْسُ مَوَاضِعَ وَذَلِكَ نَاشِئٌ عَنْ حُبِّ الشَّرَفِ وَالْمَالِ فَإِنَّ مَحَبَّةَ الشَّرَفِ تُحْمَلُ عَلَى انْتِقَاصِ غَيْرِهِ بِالْهَمْزِ وَاللَّمْزِ وَالْفَخْرِ وَالْخُيَلَاءِ وَمَحَبَّةُ الْمَالِ تُحْمَلُ عَلَى الْبُخْلِ وَضِدُّ ذَلِكَ مَنْ أَعْطَى فَلَمْ يَبْخَلْ وَاتَّقَى فَلَمْ يَهْمِزْ وَلَمْ يَلْمِزْ وَأَيْضًا فَإِنَّ الْمُعْطِيَ نَفَعَ النَّاسَ وَالْمُتَّقِيَ لَمْ يَضُرَّهُمْ فَنَفَعَ وَلَمْ يَضُرَّ وَأَمَّا الْمُخْتَالُ الْفَخُورُ الْبَخِيلُ فَإِنَّهُ بِبُخْلِهِ مَنَعَهُمْ الْخَيْرَ وَبِفَخْرِهِ سَامَهُمْ الضُّرَّ فَضَرَّهُمْ وَلَمْ يَنْفَعْهُمْ وَكَذَلِكَ 
" الْهُمَزَةُ الَّذِي جَمَعَ مَالًا "
 وَنَظِيرُهُ قَارُونُ الَّذِي جَمَعَ مَالًا وَكَانَ مِنْ قَوْمِ مُوسَى فَبَغَى عَلَيْهِمْ.
 وَمَنْ تَدَبَّرَ الْقُرْآنَ وَجَدَ بَعْضَهُ يُفَسِّرُ بَعْضًا فَإِنَّهُ كَمَا قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ فِي رِوَايَةِ الوالبي:
 مُشْتَمِلٌ عَلَى الْأَقْسَامِ وَالْأَمْثَالِ وَهُوَ تَفْسِيرُ: مُتَشَابِهًا مَثَانِيَ.

denote someone to whom this is done. The same distinction occurs in analogous pairs such as duhkah (someone laughed at) and duhakah (someone who laughs often), and lu‘bah (someone played with) and lu‘abah (someone who plays often).] (*)

His words:

“Who amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it.”

He describes him as attacking people and finding fault with them, and as amassing wealth and repeatedly counting it. This parallels His words in Surah al-Hadīd:

“Allah does not love anyone who is conceited and boastful.”

“Those who are miserly.”

There is a passage with a similar meaning in Surah al-Nisā’. The slanderer and backbiter resembles the conceited boaster, while the one who amasses wealth and keeps counting it resembles the miser.

Another parallel to these two traits is His saying:

“A slanderer, going about spreading malicious gossip.”

“Withholding good, a transgressor, sinful.”

“Harsh and, moreover, ignoble.”

He describes him as arrogant and miserly. Likewise, He says:

“But as for the one who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient.”

These are five passages. Such conduct springs from the love of status and wealth: love of status drives a person to belittle others through slander, backbiting, boasting and conceit, while love of wealth drives him to miserliness. His opposite is someone who gives rather than being miserly, and fears Allah rather than slandering or backbiting.

Furthermore, the giver benefits people, while the person who fears Allah does not harm them: he thus brings benefit without causing harm. By contrast, the conceited, boastful miser deprives them of good through his miserliness and inflicts harm upon them through his boasting. He therefore harms them without benefiting them. The same applies to “the slanderer who amasses wealth.” Another example is Qārūn, who amassed wealth and belonged to the people of Moses, yet oppressed them.

Whoever reflects upon the Quran will find that its passages explain one another. For, as Ibn ‘Abbās said in the report transmitted by al-Wālibī, it encompasses categories and parables. This explains the description: “mutually consistent and oft-repeated.”

وَلِهَذَا جَاءَ كِتَابُ اللَّهِ جَامِعًا. كَمَا قَالَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
" 
{أُعْطِيت جَوَامِعَ الْكَلِمِ}
 "
 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{كِتَابًا مُتَشَابِهًا مَثَانِيَ}
 فَالتَّشَابُهُ يَكُونُ فِي الْأَمْثَالِ وَالْمَثَانِي فِي الْأَقْسَامِ فَإِنَّ التَّثْنِيَةَ فِي مُطْلَقِ التَّعْدِيدِ.
 كَمَا قَدْ قِيلَ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{ارْجِعِ الْبَصَرَ كَرَّتَيْنِ}
 وَكَمَا فِي قَوْلِ حُذَيْفَةَ 
" كُنَّا نَقُولُ بَيْنَ السَّجْدَتَيْنِ: رَبِّ اغْفِرْ لِي رَبِّ اغْفِرْ لِي "
 وَكَمَا يُقَالُ: فَعَلْت هَذَا مَرَّةً بَعْدَ مَرَّةٍ فَتَثْنِيَةُ اللَّفْظِ يُرَادُ بِهِ التَّعْدِيدُ؛ لِأَنَّ الْعَدَدَ مَا زَادَ عَلَى الْوَاحِدِ وَهُوَ أَوَّلُ التَّثْنِيَةِ وَكَذَلِكَ ثَنَيْت الثَّوْبَ أَعَمُّ مِنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَرَّتَيْنِ فَقَطْ أَوْ مُطْلَقَ الْعَدَدِ فَهُوَ جَمِيعُهُ مُتَشَابِهٌ يُصَدِّقُ بَعْضُهُ بَعْضًا لَيْسَ مُخْتَلِفًا بَلْ كُلُّ خَبَرٍ وَأَمْرٍ مِنْهُ يُشَابِهُ الْخَبَرَ لِاتِّحَادِ مَقْصُودِ الْأَمْرَيْنِ وَلِاتِّحَادِ الْحَقِيقَةِ الَّتِي إلَيْهَا مَرْجِعُ الْمَوْجُودَاتِ. فَلَمَّا كَانَتْ الْحَقَائِقُ الْمَقْصُودَةُ وَالْمَوْجُودَةُ تَرْجِعُ إلَى أَصْلٍ وَاحِدٍ وَهُوَ اللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ. كَانَ الْكَلَامُ الْحَقُّ فِيهَا خَبَرًا وَأَمْرًا مُتَشَابِهًا لَيْسَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْمُخْتَلِفِ الْمُتَنَاقِضِ. كَمَا يُوجَدُ فِي كَلَامِ أَكْثَرِ الْبَشَرِ وَالْمُصَنِّفُونَ الْكِبَارُ مِنْهُمْ يَقُولُونَ شَيْئًا ثُمَّ يَنْقُضُونَهُ وَهُوَ جَمِيعُهُ مَثَانِي؛
 لِأَنَّهُ اُسْتُوْفِيَتْ فِيهِ الْأَقْسَامُ الْمُخْتَلِفَةُ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ يَقُولُ:
 
{وَمِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنَا زَوْجَيْنِ}
 فَذِكْرُ الزَّوْجَيْنِ مَثَانِي وَالْإِخْبَارُ عَنْ الْحَقَائِقِ بِمَا هِيَ عَلَيْهِ بِحَيْثُ يَحْكُمُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ بِحُكْمِ نَظِيرِهِ وَهُوَ حُكْمٌ عَلَى الْمَعْنَى الْوَاحِدِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ خَبَرًا أَوْ طَلَبًا خِطَابٌ مُتَشَابِهٌ فَهُوَ مُتَشَابِهٌ مَثَانِي.
translated_text:
For this reason, the Book of Allah is comprehensive, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“I have been given concise, comprehensive speech.”

Allah Most High says:

“A Book, mutually consistent and oft-repeated.”

Its mutual consistency concerns its parallels, while its repetition concerns its categories, for the dual form can signify repetition in general. This interpretation has been given to His words:

“Look again, twice over.”

Likewise, Hudhayfah said, “Between the two prostrations, we used to say: ‘My Lord, forgive me; my Lord, forgive me.’” Similarly, one says, “I did this time after time.” Thus, doubling an expression can signify repetition, for number denotes what exceeds one, beginning with two. Likewise, “I folded the garment” can refer to folding it just twice or to folding it any number of times.

The whole Quran is mutually consistent: its parts confirm one another and are not discordant. Rather, every report and command in it accords with its reports, because both share a single purpose, and because the reality to which existing things ultimately refer is one. Since the realities sought and those that exist have a single source—Allah, glorified be He—truthful discourse about them, whether reporting or commanding, is mutually consistent. It is not discordant and contradictory, as is found in the speech of most people. Even their great authors say something and then contradict it.

The whole Quran is also oft-repeated, because all the different categories are fully covered within it. Allah says:

“And of everything We created pairs.”

Mentioning both members of a pair constitutes such repetition. Describing realities as they are, so that a thing receives the same judgment as its counterpart—a judgment concerning the single meaning they share, whether expressed as a statement or a directive—is mutually consistent discourse. Thus, it is mutually consistent and oft-repeated.

original_text:
وَهَذَا فِي الْمَعَانِي مِثْلُ الْوُجُوهِ وَالنَّظَائِرِ فِي الْأَلْفَاظِ فَإِنَّ كُلَّ شَيْئَيْنِ مِنْ الْأَعْيَانِ وَالْأَعْرَاضِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ إمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ أَحَدُهُمَا مِثْلَ الْآخَرِ أَوْ لَا يَكُونَ مِثْلَهُ فَهِيَ الْأَمْثَالُ وَجَمْعُهَا هُوَ التَّأْلِيفُ وَإِذَا جَاءَتْ بِلَفْظِ وَاحِدٍ كَانَتْ نَظَائِرَ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مِثْلَهُ فَهُوَ خِلَافُهُ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ ضِدًّا أَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ وَقَدْ يُقَالُ:
 إمَّا أَنْ يَجْمَعَهُمَا جِنْسٌ أَوْ لَا فَإِنْ لَمْ يَجْمَعْهُمَا جِنْسٌ فَأَحَدُهُمَا بَعِيدٌ عَنْ الْآخَرِ وَلَا مُنَاسَبَةَ بَيْنَهُمَا وَإِنْ جَمَعَهُمَا جِنْسٌ فَهِيَ الْأَقْسَامُ وَجَمْعُهَا هُوَ التَّصْنِيفُ وَدَلَالَةُ اللَّفْظِ الْوَاحِدِ عَلَى الْمَعَانِي الْمُخْتَلِفَةِ تُسَمَّى الْوُجُوهَ. وَالْكَلَامُ الْجَامِعُ هُوَ الَّذِي يَسْتَوْفِي الْأَقْسَامَ الْمُخْتَلِفَةَ وَالنَّظَائِرَ الْمُتَمَاثِلَةَ جَمْعًا بَيْنَ الْمُتَمَاثِلَيْنِ وَفَرْقًا بَيْنَ الْمُخْتَلِفَيْنِ. بِحَيْثُ يَبْقَى مُحِيطًا وَإِلَّا فَذِكْرُ أَحَدِ الْقِسْمَيْنِ أَوْ الْمِثْلَيْنِ لَا يُفِيدُ التَّمَامَ وَلَا يَكُونُ الْكَلِمُ مُحِيطًا وَلَا الْكَلِمُ جَوَامِعَ وَهُوَ فِعْلُ غَالِبِ النَّاسِ فِي كَلَامِهِمْ.
 وَالْحَقَائِقُ فِي نَفْسِهَا:
 مِنْهَا الْمُخْتَلِفُ وَمِنْهَا الْمُؤْتَلِفُ وَالْمُخْتَلِفَانِ بَيْنَهُمَا اتِّفَاقٌ مِنْ وَجْهٍ وَافْتِرَاقٌ مِنْ وَجْهٍ فَإِذَا أَحَاطَ الْكَلَامُ بِالْأَقْسَامِ الْمُخْتَلِفَةِ وَالْأَمْثَالِ الْمُؤْتَلِفَةِ كَانَ جَامِعًا وَبِاعْتِبَارِ هَذِهِ الْمَعَانِي كَانَتْ ضُرُوبُ الْقِيَاسِ الْعَقْلِيِّ الْمَنْطِقِيِّ ثَلَاثَةً: الْحَمْلِيَّاتُ وَالشَّرْطِيَّاتُ الْمُتَّصِلَةُ وَالشَّرْطِيَّاتُ الْمُنْفَصِلَةُ. فَالْأَوَّلُ لِلْحَقَائِقِ الْمُتَمَاثِلَةِ الدَّاخِلَةِ فِي الْقَضِيَّةِ الْجَامِعَةِ. وَالثَّانِي لِلْمُخْتَلِفَاتِ الَّتِي لَيْسَتْ مُتَضَادَّةً بَلْ تَتَلَازَمُ تَارَةً وَلَا تَتَلَازَمُ أُخْرَى.
translated_text:
In the realm of meanings, this corresponds to the multiple senses and parallel usages of words. Any two things—whether concrete entities, accidents, or otherwise—are either alike or unlike. Those that are alike are counterparts, and bringing them together constitutes composition. When they are expressed by the same word, they constitute parallel usages. If one is unlike the other, it differs from it, whether or not the two are opposites.

One may also say that either a genus encompasses them both or it does not. If no genus encompasses them, they are remote from one another, with no correspondence between them. If a genus encompasses them, they constitute its divisions, and bringing them together constitutes classification. A single word’s signifying different meanings is called its “multiple senses.”

Comprehensive discourse fully covers the different divisions and the corresponding counterparts, bringing together what is alike and distinguishing what is different, so that its coverage remains complete. Otherwise, mentioning only one of two divisions or counterparts does not achieve completeness: the discourse is neither all-encompassing nor comprehensive. Yet this is what most people do in their speech.

Realities themselves include both what differs and what accords. Two differing realities agree in one respect and differ in another. When discourse encompasses the different divisions and the corresponding counterparts, it is comprehensive. In view of these distinctions, rational, logical syllogisms take three forms: categorical syllogisms, conjunctive conditional syllogisms, and disjunctive conditional syllogisms. The first concerns similar realities subsumed under a comprehensive proposition. The second concerns differing realities that are not mutually opposed, but sometimes entail one another and sometimes do not.

original_text: وَالثَّالِثُ لِلْحَقَائِقِ الْمُتَضَادَّةِ الْمُتَنَافِيَةِ إمَّا وُجُودًا أَوْ عَدَمًا وَهِيَ النَّقِيضَانِ وَإِمَّا وُجُودًا فَقَطْ وَهُوَ أَعَمُّ مِنْ النَّقِيضَيْنِ وَإِمَّا عَدَمًا فَقَطْ وَهُوَ أَخَصُّ مِنْ النَّقِيضَيْنِ. فَالْحَمْلِيَّاتُ لِلْمِثْلَيْنِ وَالْأَمْثَالِ وَالشَّرْطِيَّاتُ الْمُنْفَصِلَةُ لِلْمُتَضَادَّيْنِ وَالْمُتَضَادَّاتِ وَيُسَمَّى التَّقْسِيمَ وَالسَّبْرَ وَالتَّرْدِيدَ وَالْبَيَانِيَّ وَالْمُتَّصِلَةُ لِلْخِلَافَيْنِ غَيْرِ الْمُتَضَادَّيْنِ وَيُسَمَّى التَّلَازُمَ.
translated_text:
The third concerns opposed realities that are mutually incompatible, whether in existence or nonexistence—in which case they are contradictories—or in existence alone, which is broader than contradiction, or in nonexistence alone, which is narrower than contradiction.

Thus, categorical syllogisms concern two or more similar realities, while disjunctive conditional syllogisms concern two or more opposed realities. Such reasoning is called division, testing, the posing of alternatives, and expository reasoning. Conjunctive conditional syllogisms concern two differing realities that are not opposites; this is called mutual entailment.

original_text:
سُورَةُ الْكَوْثَرِ

translated_text:
Surah al-Kawthar

Shaykh al-Islām Abū al-ʿAbbās Ahmad ibn ʿAbd al-Halīm ibn ʿAbd al-Salām ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

“Surah al-Kawthar”

How magnificent this surah is, and how abundant its benefits despite its brevity! Its true meaning is understood from its ending. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, cuts off whoever hates His Messenger from every good. He cuts off his remembrance, his family, and his wealth, so that he loses these in the Hereafter. He cuts his life off from good, so that he neither benefits from it nor stores up righteous deeds during it for his return to Allah. He cuts his heart off from good, so that it cannot comprehend goodness, nor does He make it fit to know Him, love Him, and believe in His messengers. He cuts off his deeds, so that He does not employ him in any act of obedience. He cuts him off from supporters, so that he finds neither supporter nor helper.

He cuts him off from all acts of devotion and righteous deeds, so that he neither savours them nor finds any sweetness in them. Even if he performs them outwardly, his heart wanders away from them. This is the recompense of anyone who hates some of what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought and rejects it on account of his own desires, someone he follows, his shaykh, his ruler, or his superior. Such is the person who hates the verses and hadiths concerning Allah’s attributes and interprets them in a way other than that intended by Allah

One of the clearest signs of his hatred and aversion toward them is that, when he hears Ahl al-Sunnah citing them as evidence for the truth they convey, he recoils, turns away, and draws back because of the hatred and aversion toward them in his heart. Who could hate the Messenger more than such a person? Likewise, those given to musical listening, who dance to singing, poetry, tambourines, and flutes, find the Quran tedious and burdensome when they hear it recited in their gatherings. What hatred could be greater than this? Apply the same reasoning to the other groups in this regard.

The same applies to anyone who gives precedence to people’s words and learning over the Quran and Sunnah. Were he not hateful toward what the Messenger brought, he would not do so. Some even forget the Quran after having memorized it, occupying themselves instead with the words of so-and-so and so-and-so. But those who hate and reject it most are those who disbelieve in it, deny it, and describe it as “tales of the ancients” and “magic handed down.” Such a person is cut off most severely and grievously. Everyone who hates it has a share of this severance in proportion to his hatred. Because these people hated and opposed it, Allah recompensed them by making all good hostile to them and cutting them off from it. He favoured His Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—with the opposite: He granted him al-Kawthar, which is part of the abundant good Allah bestowed upon him in this world

and in the Hereafter. Among what He granted him in this world were guidance, victory, support, joy of eye and soul, an uplifted heart, and such bliss in remembering and loving Him that no worldly pleasure could possibly compare with it. In the Hereafter, He granted him al-Wasīlah and the Praised Station, and made him and his community the first for whom the gate of Paradise would be opened. He also granted him the Banner of Praise and the great Cistern at the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, among other gifts. He made all believers his children, and he is a father to them. This is the very opposite of the condition of the one cut off, who hates him and hates what he brought.

His words, “Indeed, the one who hates you,” mean the one who detests you. The one cut off is someone whose line of descent is severed, who brings forth neither good nor righteous deeds: no good or righteous deed proceeds from him.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh was told, “There are people in the mosque who sit, and others gather around them.” He replied, “Whoever sits to receive people will have people gather around him. But the people of the Sunnah die while their memory lives on, whereas the people of innovation die and their memory dies with them.”

This is because the people of the Sunnah revived what the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought, and thus had a share in His words:

“And We have raised high your renown.”

The people of innovation hated what the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought, and thus had a share in His words:

“Indeed, the one who hates you is the one cut off.”

So beware, beware, O man, of hating anything that the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought, or rejecting it because of your own desires, or in defence of your school, or

For the only obedience to anyone that Allah has made obligatory is obedience to His Messenger and adherence to what he brought. Thus, if a servant were to oppose all creation while following the Messenger, Allah would not question him about opposing anyone. For whoever obeys or is obeyed is only to be obeyed in subordination to the Messenger; if he commanded something contrary to the Messenger’s command, he would not be obeyed. Understand this, then: listen, obey, and follow. Do not introduce innovations, lest you become cut off and your deeds be rejected. Indeed, there is no good in any deed cut off from following the Messenger, nor in the one who performs it. And Allah knows best.

As for His words, exalted is He:

“Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar.”

This verse indicates an abundant gift from a mighty, self-sufficient Giver of boundless bounty. It also indicates that He, exalted is He, His angels, and His host are with him.

He began the verse with inna (“indeed”), which conveys emphasis and affirms the truth of the statement. The verb appears in the past tense, indicating certainty and that this is an established reality. This is not negated by its indication that the granting of al-Kawthar had already been ordained in the original decree, when the destinies of all creatures were determined fifty thousand years before He created them.

He omitted the noun qualified by al-kawthar (“abundant”), making the expression more emphatically general by leaving it unspecified, and used the adjective instead. That is, He, glorified and exalted is He, said:

“Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar.”

He thus described it as abundant. The well-known al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise, as explicitly stated in authentic hadiths. Ibn ʿAbbās said that al-Kawthar is part of the abundant good that Allah granted him. And if the lowest-ranking of the inhabitants of

translated_text:
Paradise has the equivalent of ten times this world, what, then, must we think of what Allah has prepared there for the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him? Al-Kawthar is thus a sign and an indication of the manifold blessings Allah has prepared for him, their continuity and increase, and his lofty and exalted rank. That river, al-Kawthar, is the greatest of the rivers of Paradise, with the finest, freshest, and sweetest water, and is the highest of them. This is because He used the definite article, which indicates the perfection and completeness of what is named.

This is like saying, “Zayd is the learned man; Zayd is the brave man,” meaning that no one is more learned or braver than he is. Likewise, His words:

“Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar.”

These indicate that He has granted him all goodness, complete and abundant. If any member of his community receives a share of it, that share comes through the blessing of following him and taking him as an example. Moreover, he, peace and blessings be upon him, receives a reward equal to that person’s, without diminishing the follower’s reward in any way. This points to Allah Most High granting him, in Paradise, the equivalent of the rewards of his entire community, without diminishing their rewards, for he is the means of their guidance and salvation.

The servant should therefore—indeed, must—follow him, take him as an example, comply with his commands, and perform abundant righteous deeds: fasting, prayer, charity, and purification, so that the Messenger may receive a reward equal to his. For when the servant commits forbidden acts, the Messenger misses out on a reward equal to that for the good the servant has neglected. If the servant commits what is forbidden while abandoning what is commanded, his burden of sin grows heavier and his salvation becomes more difficult, because he has both committed the forbidden and abandoned the commanded. But if he performs what is commanded while committing what is forbidden, he will be among those for whom intercession is made

translated_text:
by the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, since he receives a reward equal to that person’s for fulfilling what was commanded. To Allah all creation will return, and with Him rests their reckoning. He knows their condition best—that is, the circumstances of His servants. His intercession is for those of his community who commit major sins. Whoever does good does so only because Allah enables him, while the wrongdoer has neither a defence nor an excuse.

The point is that al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise, and it forms part of the abundant good Allah has granted His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in this world and the Hereafter. This is in addition to the reward Allah grants him equal to the rewards of his community until the Day of Resurrection. Thus, whenever anyone reads, acquires knowledge, performs a righteous deed, teaches another, gives charity, performs Hajj, undertakes jihad, guards the frontiers, repents, remains patient, places his trust in Allah, or attains any spiritual station of the heart—such as reverent awe, fear, knowledge of Allah, or anything else—the Messenger receives a reward equal to his, without diminishing that person’s reward in any way. And Allah knows best.

As for His words:

“So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.”

Allah commanded him to combine these two great acts of worship: prayer and sacrifice. Both express nearness to Allah, humility, dependence upon Him, thinking well of Him, firm certainty, and the heart’s peaceful trust in Allah, His assurance, His command, His bounty, and His recompense. This is the opposite of the condition of those marked by arrogance and aversion, who consider themselves independent of Allah: those who bring no need before their Lord in prayer to ask Him to fulfil, and who do not offer sacrifices to Him out of fear of poverty, unwillingness to help the poor and give to them, and ill thoughts of their Lord. This is why Allah joined the two together in His words, Exalted is He:

“Say,

my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of all worlds.” Sacrifice here means slaughtering an animal seeking His pleasure.

The point is that prayer and sacrifice are the greatest acts by which one draws near to Allah. He introduces the command to perform them with the particle fa (“so”), indicating causation: performing these acts—prayer and sacrifice—is a means of giving thanks for the al-Kawthar and abundant good that Allah has granted him. These two acts of worship are the greatest expressions of the recipient’s gratitude to his Benefactor and worship of Him. Indeed, prayer is the pinnacle of worship and the ultimate goal.

It is as though He were saying:

“Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar”—

abundant good—and bestowed this blessing upon you so that you may perform these two acts of worship for Us in gratitude for Our favor upon you. They are also the reason for Our bestowing this favor upon you, so perform them for Us. Prayer and sacrifice are thus preceded by favor and followed by further favor.

The greatest act of worship involving wealth is sacrifice, and the greatest bodily act of worship is prayer. What comes together for the servant in prayer does not come together for him in any other act of worship, as those with living hearts and lofty aspirations know. Likewise, what comes together when he offers sacrifice—giving Allah precedence, thinking well of Him, firm certainty, and trust in what is in Allah’s hands—is truly remarkable when accompanied by faith and sincerity.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, obeyed his Lord’s command: he prayed frequently to his Lord and offered many sacrifices. During the Farewell Pilgrimage, he slaughtered sixty-three camels with his own hands, and he would offer sacrifices on the Eids and at other times.

These verses also indicate that you should pay no heed to people or to what you suffer at their hands; rather, pray to your Lord and sacrifice. They also allude to the condition of the hater who is cut off, whose prayer and sacrifice are devoted to other than Allah.

His words,

“Indeed, it is the one who hates you who is cut off,”

contain several forms of emphasis:

First: beginning the sentence with inna (“indeed”).

Second: using the separating pronoun, which reinforces the statement and conveys exclusivity.

Third: using the elative form for the predicate rather than a passive participle.

Fourth: making it definite with the definite article, indicating that this quality applies to him in its entirety and that he deserves this description more than anyone else. A similar example of emphasis occurs in His words:

“Do not fear; indeed, it is you who will have the upper hand.”

Among the surah’s subtle lessons is the shift in grammatical person in His words:

“So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.”

This indicates that your Lord deserves this worship and that it is fitting for you to worship Him and offer sacrifice to Him. And Allah knows best.

Surah al-Kāfirūn (The Disbelievers)

The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

In the surah “Say, O disbelievers,” scholars have offered several explanations for the repetition of the disavowal on both sides, where Allah says:

“I do not worship what you worship,
nor are you worshippers of what I worship.”

Then He says:

“Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped,
nor are you worshippers of what I worship.”

Among these explanations are two well-known views mentioned by many commentators: is the statement repeated for emphasis, or to deny such worship both now and in the future?

Abū al-Faraj said:

“There are two views concerning this repetition. The first is that it emphasizes the point and puts an end to their hopes of winning him over. This was al-Farrā’s view.

“We have treated this fully in Surah al-Rahmān. Ibn Qutaybah said: ‘The repetition in Surah al-Rahmān is for emphasis.’ He said: ‘It is the Arabs’ practice to repeat for emphasis and to ensure understanding, just as they employ brevity for ease

 تَكْرَارُ الْكَلَامِ فِي 
{قُلْ يَا أَيُّهَا الْكَافِرُونَ}
 .
translated_text:
and conciseness. For it is better for a learner or an orator to employ varied forms of expression than to confine himself to a single form throughout.

Someone may say, “By Allah, I will not do it; again, by Allah, I will not do it,” when he wishes to emphasize his refusal and extinguish any hope that he will do it. Similarly, when seeking brevity, he may say, “By Allah, I will do it,” leaving the negative “not” implicit. To a hurried messenger, one says, “Hurry, hurry!” and to an archer, “Shoot, shoot!”

A poet said:
“How many blessings you once enjoyed—how many, how many!”

Another said:
“Did you ask the hosts of Kindah,
on the day they fled, ‘Where? Where?’”

Sometimes they wish to emphasize a descriptive word but find it awkward to repeat the very same word, so they change one of its letters.’

Ibn Qutaybah said: ‘When Allah enumerated His blessings in this surah, reminded His servants of His favors, and drew their attention to His power, He placed each repeated statement between two blessings, so that they would understand those blessings and acknowledge them. It is like saying to someone: “Did I not give you lodging when you were an outcast? Do you deny this? Did I not take you on pilgrimage when you had never performed it before? Do you deny this?”’”

I say: Ibn Qutaybah said: “The repetition of the words in ‘Say, O disbelievers’

translated_text:

I say: The repetition of wording that he mentioned is indeed found in the speech of Arabs and non-Arabs alike, for all nations emphasize requests or statements by repeating their words. An example is the report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Allah, I will certainly campaign against Quraysh! Again, by Allah, I will certainly campaign against Quraysh! Again, by Allah, I will certainly campaign against Quraysh!”

He then said, “If Allah wills,” but he did not campaign against them.

It is also reported that, during the expedition to Tabūk, Hudhayfah was leading his mount while ‘Ammār was driving it from behind. A group of over ten men set out and ascended the mountain pass on their mounts, their faces veiled. They had intended to assassinate the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said to Hudhayfah, “Lead on! Lead on!” and to ‘Ammār, “Drive on! Drive on!”

There are many more examples of this, but nothing of this kind occurs in the Quran. The Quran has a unique character: no human speech resembles it, whether that of a prophet or anyone else, even though it was revealed in the Arabic language. No created being can produce a surah, or even part of a surah, like it. Thus, nowhere in the Quran is the very same wording repeated immediately after its first occurrence. Rather, in

Surah al-Rahmān, He repeats that address after each verse, rather than in uninterrupted succession. This manner of expression is loftier than the first. Likewise, the Quran’s narratives contain no repetition of the kind some have supposed. Nor does “Say, O disbelievers” contain any repeated wording except His saying:

“Nor are you worshippers of what I worship.”

Even here, a sentence separates the two occurrences.

They have compared what occurs in Surah al-Rahmān to the words of someone addressing a person whom he has treated well and showered with favours, but who denies them and shows ingratitude:

“Were you not poor, and did I not enrich you? Do you deny this? Were you not naked, and did I not clothe you? Do you deny this? Were you not unknown, and did I not make you known?”

And so forth. This is a closer comparison than consecutive repetition, as in the repeated oath.

Likewise, some say that one expression may be joined to another merely because the wording differs, as in the verse:

“He found her words a lie and a falsehood.”

There is nothing of this kind in the Quran. Allah never includes an additional word in it without an additional meaning, even if that meaning includes emphasis. Whatever additional wording occurs in such statements as His saying:

“So it was by mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them,”

and His saying:

“Before long, they will surely become regretful,”

and His saying:

“How little you take heed!”

conveys more meaning than would be conveyed without it. Thus, additional wording conveys additional meaning, and the strength of the wording corresponds to the strength of the meaning. The dammah (u-vowel) is stronger
